fragments.text: Height per unit x; it can exceed 1 provided areas are valid probabilities.

fragments.label: Median
fragments.text: A value m with equal probability on either side for a continuous distribution.

fragments.label: Support
fragments.text: The interval on which the density is non-zero.
Valid density functions

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A pdf f(x) must satisfy f(x)≥0 on its support and ∫f(x)dx=1 over the whole support. Use normalisation to find unknown constants, checking they keep the density non-negative.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A density value is not itself a point probability.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Outside the stated support, f(x)=0.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Normalisation: ∫ f(x) dx=1 over the support
Probabilities as areas

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: P(a < X < b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx after intersecting the requested interval with the support. For continuous X, endpoints make no difference: P(X=a)=0.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Draw the support and shade the required interval.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Use complements for awkward tails.
Percentiles

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: A pth percentile q satisfies ∫ from the lower support limit to q of f(x)dx=p/100. The median uses 0.5. Solve and select the root that lies within the support.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Do not assume median equals mean unless symmetry justifies it.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Reject algebraic roots outside the support.
Moments

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Calculate E(X)=∫xf(x)dx and E(X²)=∫x²f(x)dx over the support, then Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]². Interpret the mean in the same units as X and variance in squared units.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Normalise before calculating moments.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Keep exact values until the variance subtraction is complete.
Can a pdf exceed 1?

fragments.label: Can a pdf exceed 1?
fragments.text: Yes; only areas must be between 0 and 1, and total area must equal 1.
What is P(X=a) for continuous X?

fragments.label: What is P(X=a) for continuous X?
fragments.text: Zero.
How is the median found?

fragments.label: How is the median found?
fragments.text: Set the area from the lower support boundary to m equal to 0.5.
Which root of a percentile equation is valid?

fragments.label: Which root of a percentile equation is valid?
fragments.text: Only a root lying in the stated support.

Understand sampling distributions and construct confidence intervals to estimate an unknown population parameter. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Population
fragments.text: The full set about which an inference is made.

fragments.label: Sample
fragments.text: A subset observed to learn about the population.

fragments.label: Sampling distribution
fragments.text: The probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples.

fragments.label: Standard error
fragments.text: The standard deviation of a sampling distribution.

fragments.label: Confidence interval
fragments.text: A range generated by a method that captures the true parameter at a stated long-run rate.
Random samples and bias

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Every population member should have an appropriate chance of selection. Convenience, voluntary-response and incomplete-frame samples can be biased. Random numbers help choose units without personal judgement.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: A large biased sample is still biased.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Distinguish sampling variation from measurement error.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Sample mean moments: E(X̄)=μ; Var(X̄)=σ²/n
Sample mean distribution

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: If population mean is μ and variance σ², then E(X̄)=μ and Var(X̄)=σ²/n. X̄ is normal if the population is normal and approximately normal for large n by the CLT.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Standard error is σ/√n.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Increasing n reduces standard error by the square-root law.
Unbiased estimates

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Estimate μ by x̄. Estimate population variance with s²=Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1), equivalently [Σx²−(Σx)²/n]/(n−1). The n−1 correction makes the estimating process unbiased.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Use the sample variance requested, not the descriptive variance with denominator n.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Keep x̄ unrounded in the variance formula.
Confidence intervals

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: For known σ or a large sample, a confidence interval for μ is x̄±z*σ/√n, replacing σ by s for a large sample when needed. For a large-sample proportion p, use p̂±z*√[p̂(1−p̂)/n]. Interpret the confidence level as a property of the method.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: 90%, 95%, 99% use different central z-values.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: Give interval endpoints in context and sensible units.
What is the standard error of X̄?

fragments.label: What is the standard error of X̄?
fragments.text: σ/√n.
Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?

fragments.label: Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?
fragments.text: It corrects the systematic underestimation and makes the estimator unbiased.
What does a 95% confidence method mean?

fragments.label: What does a 95% confidence method mean?
fragments.text: Across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals produced by the method contain the true parameter.
What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?

fragments.label: What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?
fragments.text: It is halved.

Set up null and alternative hypotheses, use a critical region or p-value, and draw a conclusion in the context of the question. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Null hypothesis
fragments.text: H₀, the model or parameter value tested as the default claim.

fragments.label: Alternative hypothesis
fragments.text: H₁, the direction or difference supported if H₀ is rejected.

fragments.label: Significance level
fragments.text: The maximum chosen probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true.

fragments.label: Critical region
fragments.text: Test-statistic values that lead to rejection of H₀.

fragments.label: p-value
fragments.text: The probability under H₀ of an outcome at least as extreme as observed in the direction(s) of H₁.

fragments.label: Type I error
fragments.text: Rejecting a true H₀.

fragments.label: Type II error
fragments.text: Failing to reject a false H₀ under a specified alternative.
Setting up the test

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Define the parameter, write H₀ with equality, and make H₁ match the claim. 'Increased' gives an upper tail, 'decreased' a lower tail, and 'changed' two tails. The test calculation always uses the H₀ parameter.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Use population parameters, not sample statistics, in hypotheses.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Choose the tail before seeing the result.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Mean test statistic: Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n)
Discrete tests

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For X binomial or Poisson, find the probability of the observed result or something more extreme under H₀. Reject if that p-value is ≤α. A critical region is chosen so its H₀ probability is at most α; discreteness means the actual size may be smaller.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For two tails, identify both extremes rather than blindly doubling if the distribution is asymmetric.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: State the actual critical-region probability when requested.
Normal and mean tests

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Use a continuity-corrected normal approximation for binomial/Poisson when conditions hold. For a mean, standardise Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n), using s for σ in a large-sample setting as allowed, then compare with the relevant critical value or p-value.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Put μ₀ from H₀ in the numerator.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: A two-tailed α test places α/2 in each tail.
Errors and conclusions

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Type I probability is the rejection-region probability under H₀. Type II probability is the acceptance-region probability under a specified alternative. Finish with 'reject H₀' or 'do not reject H₀', followed by a contextual evidence statement—never say H₀ is proved.

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Power=1−P(Type II error).

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: The conclusion must use the direction in H₁.
Where does equality belong in hypotheses?

fragments.label: Where does equality belong in hypotheses?
fragments.text: In H₀.
What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?

fragments.label: What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?
fragments.text: A lower-tailed test.
What is a Type I error?

fragments.label: What is a Type I error?
fragments.text: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true.
How should a non-significant result be stated?

fragments.label: How should a non-significant result be stated?
fragments.text: Do not reject H₀; there is insufficient evidence for the contextual alternative claim.

Fetch–decode–execute cycle

fragments.text: 1. Address in the PC copies to the MAR; PC increments. 2. Instruction at that address fetched into the MDR, then copied to the CIR. 3. Decoded and executed, using the ACC for arithmetic where needed.

User-defined data types let a programmer represent a problem using meaningful structures instead of forcing everything into primitive types. At A2 you must know enumerated types, pointers, records and sets, understand why each is useful, and choose a suitable type for a scenario.

fragments.label: Enumerated type
fragments.text: A programmer-defined type whose values come from a fixed list of named constants.

fragments.label: Pointer
fragments.text: A variable that stores the address/reference of another data item.

fragments.label: Record
fragments.text: A composite type grouping named fields that may have different data types.

fragments.label: Set
fragments.text: An unordered collection of distinct values with operations such as union and intersection.

fragments.label: Dereference
fragments.text: Follow a pointer to access the data stored at the referenced address.
Enumerated types

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Use an enumeration when only a fixed set of states is valid. It makes programs self-documenting and prevents meaningless values from being assigned.

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text:
TYPE TState = (Waiting, Running, Complete)
DECLARE State : TState
State <- Running
Pointers

fragments.label: Pointers
fragments.text: Pointers make dynamic structures possible because a node can refer to another node without the items needing to be contiguous in memory. The pointer stores an address; dereferencing accesses the target value. A null pointer represents 'no target'.

fragments.label: Pointers
fragments.text:
TYPE TNodePointer = ^TNode
DECLARE Current : TNodePointer
Records

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: A record models one entity using several fields. Fields may have different types; records can contain arrays or other records, and arrays can contain records. This is ideal for students, products, employees and similar entities.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text:
TYPE TStudent
  DECLARE Name : STRING
  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
  DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:3] OF INTEGER
ENDTYPE
Sets

fragments.label: Sets
fragments.text: Sets are useful where membership matters but order and duplicates do not. Union combines members, intersection keeps common members, difference removes members of another set, and membership tests whether a value belongs to the set.
Choosing a type

fragments.label: Choosing a type
fragments.text: Base the choice on the data requirement: enum for fixed named choices; record for related fields; set for unique unordered membership; pointer for dynamic links. In an exam, justify the feature that fits the scenario rather than just defining the type.
enum=fixed named choices
pointer=address/reference
record=related fields
set=unique unordered values

File organisation describes how records are arranged on backing storage; file access describes how they are reached. You must compare serial, sequential and random organisation, understand direct access and indexing, and use hashing—including what happens when collisions occur.

fragments.label: Serial file
fragments.text: Records are stored in the order they arrive, with no ordering by key.

fragments.label: Sequential file
fragments.text: Records are stored in order of a key field.

fragments.label: Random file
fragments.text: Records are stored at locations calculated or chosen to allow direct access.

fragments.label: Index
fragments.text: A smaller structure mapping search keys to record locations.

fragments.label: Hash function
fragments.text: An algorithm that transforms a record key into a storage address.

fragments.label: Collision
fragments.text: Two different keys generate the same hash address.
Serial organisation

fragments.label: Serial organisation
fragments.text: Very simple for append-heavy data such as logs. New records can be added quickly, but finding one record usually means reading from the start until it is found.

fragments.label: Serial organisation
fragments.text: Example: a transaction log written in time order.
Sequential organisation

fragments.label: Sequential organisation
fragments.text: Records are kept sorted by a key. This is effective for batch processing in key order and allows ordered traversal. Insertion/update can be more expensive because ordering must be preserved.

fragments.label: Sequential organisation
fragments.text: Example: employee records stored in EmployeeID order for payroll processing.
Random organisation and direct access

fragments.label: Random organisation and direct access
fragments.text: The program can jump directly to a likely record location rather than reading every previous record. It suits systems that repeatedly retrieve individual records by a unique key.
Indexes

fragments.label: Indexes
fragments.text: An index stores keys plus pointers/addresses. Searching the smaller index identifies where the full record is stored. Extra storage and maintenance are required, especially when records are inserted or deleted.
Hashing

fragments.label: Hashing
fragments.text: A hash function transforms a key into an address. A good function is fast and spreads keys across the available range. The same function must be used on retrieval.

fragments.label: Hashing
fragments.text:
address <- Key MOD 1000
Key 47231 -> address 231
Collision resolution

fragments.label: Collision resolution
fragments.text: Because the address range is finite, collisions are unavoidable. The system needs a defined rule such as linear probing, an overflow area or chaining. Retrieval must follow the same collision rule used during insertion.

fragments.label: Collision resolution
fragments.text: If slot 231 is occupied, linear probing can test 232, 233, ... until a free slot is found.
serial=arrival order
sequential=key order
random=direct location
index=key->location
collision needs a rule

Binary floating-point representation stores a real number using a mantissa and an exponent. For Cambridge 9618 both fields are interpreted using two's complement. You must convert values, normalise them, and explain precision, range, rounding, overflow and underflow.

fragments.label: Mantissa
fragments.text: The signed significant part of a floating-point number; more mantissa bits give greater precision.

fragments.label: Exponent
fragments.text: The signed power of two controlling the position of the binary point; more exponent bits give greater range.

fragments.label: Normalisation
fragments.text: Rewriting a floating-point number in a standard form that uses the mantissa bits efficiently.

fragments.label: Rounding error
fragments.text: The difference caused when an exact value cannot be represented with the available bits.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: A value whose magnitude is too large for the available exponent range.

fragments.label: Underflow
fragments.text: A non-zero value too close to zero to be represented usefully with the available format.
Interpreting the format

fragments.label: Interpreting the format
fragments.text: Think of the value as mantissa multiplied by 2 raised to the exponent. Decode the exponent carefully, then move the binary point by that signed power.

fragments.label: Interpreting the format
fragments.text: value = mantissa x 2^exponent
Precision versus range

fragments.label: Precision versus range
fragments.text: More mantissa bits provide more significant binary digits, so nearby values can be distinguished more accurately. More exponent bits allow larger positive and negative exponents, expanding the representable range. With a fixed word length, increasing one usually reduces the other.
Normalisation

fragments.label: Normalisation
fragments.text: Normalisation avoids wasting mantissa bits on redundant sign bits. In two's-complement fractional form, a positive normalised mantissa begins with different leading sign/data bits (typically 01...) and a negative one typically begins 10....
Approximation and rounding

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding
fragments.text: Many denary fractions recur forever in binary, so finite storage keeps an approximation. Repeated arithmetic can accumulate small errors; this is why equality comparisons on calculated real values can be unreliable.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding
fragments.text: 0.1 in denary has a recurring binary fractional representation.
Overflow and underflow

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Overflow is a range failure at very large magnitude; underflow occurs near zero when the format cannot keep a meaningful non-zero representation. Increasing exponent bits changes range, not the significant precision of the mantissa.
mantissa->precision
exponent->range
value=mantissa x 2^exponent
normalise to use bits efficiently
finite binary can round

Protocols are agreed rules that let unlike hardware and software communicate reliably. At A2 the central model is the four-layer TCP/IP stack, plus the purposes of common application protocols such as HTTP, FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP and BitTorrent.

fragments.label: Protocol
fragments.text: An agreed set of rules for formatting, transmitting, receiving and interpreting data.

fragments.label: Protocol stack
fragments.text: A layered collection of protocols, each layer providing a defined service.

fragments.label: Encapsulation
fragments.text: Adding headers/control information as data passes down the stack.

fragments.label: Port number
fragments.text: A number used by the transport layer to identify an application/service on a host.

fragments.label: TCP/IP
fragments.text: The internet protocol suite organised into Application, Transport, Internet and Link layers.
Why layers are useful

fragments.label: Why layers are useful
fragments.text: Layering separates responsibilities. An application can use transport services without knowing network hardware details; local-network technology can change without redesigning every application. Standard interfaces improve interoperability, maintenance and troubleshooting.
Application layer

fragments.label: Application layer
fragments.text: Provides network services directly used by software. HTTP/HTTPS transfer web content, FTP transfers files, SMTP sends email, POP3/IMAP retrieve or manage email, and BitTorrent supports peer-to-peer distribution.
Transport layer

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Provides end-to-end application communication. TCP can segment data, number segments, detect loss, request retransmission and reassemble data. Port numbers identify the target application/service.
Internet layer

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Uses logical IP addressing and routing. Routers examine destination information and forward packets towards the destination network.
Link layer

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Handles frames and transmission across the local medium, including local hardware addressing and access to technologies such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
Encapsulation in practice

fragments.label: Encapsulation in practice
fragments.text: At the sender, application data moves down the stack and receives layer-specific control information; the receiver removes that information in reverse order and passes the reconstructed data up to the application.

fragments.label: Encapsulation in practice
fragments.text:
Sender: Application -> Transport -> Internet -> Link
Receiver: Link -> Internet -> Transport -> Application
Application=services
Transport=end-to-end
Internet=IP+routing
Link=local network
SMTP sends; POP3/IMAP receive/manage

Circuit switching reserves a dedicated end-to-end path before communication; packet switching divides a message into independently routed packets that share network links. You must compare both methods and explain the role of routers and packet headers.

fragments.label: Circuit switching
fragments.text: A dedicated communication path is reserved for the duration of a session.

fragments.label: Packet switching
fragments.text: A message is divided into packets that independently share network routes.

fragments.label: Router
fragments.text: A device that forwards packets between networks using destination information and routing data.

fragments.label: Packet header
fragments.text: Control information carried with a packet, such as destination and sequencing information.
Circuit switching

fragments.label: Circuit switching
fragments.text: A route is established first and remains reserved. It can offer predictable latency/bandwidth, but capacity is wasted when the connection is idle, and failure of the reserved path can interrupt the session.

fragments.label: Circuit switching
fragments.text: Traditional real-time telephone networks are the classic example.
Packet switching

fragments.label: Packet switching
fragments.text: A message is split into packets containing payload and control information. Packets may take different routes and arrive out of order; the destination uses sequence information to reconstruct the message. Missing/corrupt packets can be retransmitted.
Why packet switching suits the internet

fragments.label: Why packet switching suits the internet
fragments.text: Many users share the same links efficiently, and routing can work around congestion or failed paths. The trade-offs are variable delay, header overhead and the need to reorder/retransmit packets.
Routers

fragments.label: Routers
fragments.text: Each router examines destination information and selects a next hop using routing knowledge/tables. It does not need the entire message or one permanent end-to-end route.
circuit=dedicated route
packet=shared links
router chooses next hop
packets may arrive out of order
packet switching uses capacity efficiently

title: Processors, Parallel Processing and Virtual Machines

fragments.text: This topic extends CPU architecture to processor design choices, instruction pipelining, parallel architectures and virtual machines. The key is not memorising labels but explaining performance trade-offs and why a particular architecture suits a workload.

fragments.label: RISC
fragments.text: Reduced Instruction Set Computer: a small set of simple, usually fixed-format instructions.

fragments.label: CISC
fragments.text: Complex Instruction Set Computer: a larger set of more complex instructions/addressing modes.

fragments.label: Pipelining
fragments.text: Overlapping stages of several instruction executions to increase throughput.

fragments.label: SIMD
fragments.text: Single Instruction Multiple Data: the same instruction operates on many data items in parallel.

fragments.label: MIMD
fragments.text: Multiple Instruction Multiple Data: processors execute different instructions on different data.

fragments.label: Virtual machine
fragments.text: A software-created computer environment that behaves as a separate machine while sharing host hardware.
RISC versus CISC

fragments.label: RISC versus CISC
fragments.text: RISC favours simple instructions, many registers and predictable instruction formats, which can support efficient pipelining. CISC can perform more work per instruction and reduce instruction count, but decoding/execution is more complex. 'RISC is faster' is not a sufficient evaluation by itself.
Pipelining

fragments.label: Pipelining
fragments.text: Fetch, decode and execute for different instructions overlap. Once full, the pipeline can improve throughput because several instructions are in progress. A branch or interrupt may invalidate prefetched instructions, forcing a flush/refill and reducing the gain.
Flynn-style architectures

fragments.label: Flynn-style architectures
fragments.text: SISD is conventional one-instruction/one-data processing. SIMD applies one instruction to many data items, useful for image/vector workloads. MISD is rare. MIMD allows multiple processors/cores to run different instructions on different data and is common in parallel systems.
Massively parallel computing

fragments.label: Massively parallel computing
fragments.text: A very large number of processing units operate simultaneously on decomposed parts of a problem. It excels when work can be parallelised, but communication, synchronisation, load balancing and serial sections limit speed-up.
Virtual machines

fragments.label: Virtual machines
fragments.text: A hypervisor/virtualisation layer lets multiple guest systems share hardware. Benefits include isolation, testing, snapshots, server consolidation and running different operating systems. Costs include overhead, resource contention and dependence on the host/hypervisor.
RISC=simple instructions
CISC=complex instruction set
pipeline=overlap stages
SIMD=same instruction many data
MIMD=different instructions/data
VM=isolated software machine

A2 logic moves beyond basic gates to adders, flip-flops, Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps. You need to derive truth tables/circuits, understand one-bit storage, simplify expressions correctly and minimise circuits using K-maps.

fragments.label: Half adder
fragments.text: Adds two input bits and outputs Sum and Carry.

fragments.label: Full adder
fragments.text: Adds two bits plus CarryIn and outputs Sum and CarryOut.

fragments.label: Flip-flop
fragments.text: A bistable sequential circuit capable of storing one bit of state.

fragments.label: Karnaugh map
fragments.text: A visual map of truth-table outputs used to group adjacent values and minimise Boolean expressions.

fragments.label: De Morgan's laws
fragments.text: Rules that distribute NOT over AND/OR while swapping the operator.
Half and full adders

fragments.label: Half and full adders
fragments.text: For a half adder, Sum is A XOR B and Carry is A AND B. A full adder includes CarryIn so units can be chained to add multi-bit binary values.

fragments.label: Half and full adders
fragments.text: Half adder: S = A XOR B; C = A AND B
SR and JK flip-flops

fragments.label: SR and JK flip-flops
fragments.text: An SR flip-flop has Set/Reset control and stores output Q. A basic SR design has a forbidden/ambiguous input combination. The JK design resolves that case: when J=K=1 the output toggles. Flip-flops are building blocks for registers/counters/state memory.
Boolean algebra

fragments.label: Boolean algebra
fragments.text: Use identity, complement, absorption, idempotent and distributive laws plus De Morgan. A simplification is valid only if it preserves the truth table.

fragments.label: Boolean algebra
fragments.text:
NOT(A.B) = NOT A + NOT B
NOT(A+B) = NOT A . NOT B
Karnaugh maps

fragments.label: Karnaugh maps
fragments.text: Place outputs in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ by one variable. Group adjacent 1s in rectangles of size 1,2,4,8...; make groups as large as possible and allow wrap-around adjacency. Variables that change inside a group disappear from the simplified term.
Why simplify

fragments.label: Why simplify
fragments.text: Fewer terms/gates can reduce hardware cost, propagation delay, power use and opportunities for error. K-maps give a systematic visual way to find such reductions for small variable counts.
half adder=XOR+AND
full adder includes CarryIn
flip-flop stores 1 bit
De Morgan swaps AND/OR under NOT
K-map groups powers of 2

At A2 the operating system is primarily a resource manager. You need process states and scheduling, interrupts and the kernel, and memory management through virtual memory, paging, segmentation and page replacement—including why disk thrashing occurs.

fragments.label: Process
fragments.text: A program in execution together with its current state/resources.

fragments.label: Ready
fragments.text: Able to run but waiting for CPU time.

fragments.label: Blocked
fragments.text: Unable to continue until an event/resource becomes available.

fragments.label: Page
fragments.text: A fixed-size block used in paging/virtual memory.

fragments.label: Segment
fragments.text: A variable-size logical section of a program such as code, stack or data.

fragments.label: Disk thrashing
fragments.text: Excessive movement of pages between RAM and backing storage so little useful processing is done.
Process states

fragments.label: Process states
fragments.text: A running process can be pre-empted and return to Ready, or become Blocked while waiting for I/O. When the required event finishes, it returns to Ready. The scheduler chooses among ready processes, creating the appearance of concurrent execution on one CPU.
Scheduling algorithms

fragments.label: Scheduling algorithms
fragments.text: FCFS is simple arrival order but can make short jobs wait behind a long one. SJF chooses the shortest job and can reduce average wait but may starve long jobs. SRT is the pre-emptive version based on remaining time. Round Robin assigns time slices, improving responsiveness/fairness but causing more context switches when slices are very small.
Interrupts and kernel

fragments.label: Interrupts and kernel
fragments.text: An interrupt causes the CPU to preserve enough state and transfer control to an interrupt service routine. The kernel manages low-level resources/process states and can schedule another process before execution resumes.
Virtual memory and paging

fragments.label: Virtual memory and paging
fragments.text: Virtual memory uses backing storage to extend the apparent address space. If a required page is not in RAM, a page fault causes it to be loaded; another page may need replacement. Disk access is far slower than RAM, so frequent faults are expensive.
Segmentation

fragments.label: Segmentation
fragments.text: Segmentation divides memory into logical variable-size areas that match program structure. Paging uses fixed-size blocks. Segmentation gives logical organisation/protection benefits but variable sizes can make allocation more complex.
Disk thrashing

fragments.label: Disk thrashing
fragments.text: When too few useful pages remain in RAM, the system repeatedly loads pages that soon replace one another. Most time is spent swapping instead of executing. More RAM, fewer active processes or better working-set/page-replacement decisions can reduce it.
ready=CPU wait
blocked=event wait
RR=time slices
paging=fixed size
segmentation=logical variable size
thrashing=too many page swaps

Translation software turns source code into executable behaviour. At A2 you need interpreters and compiler stages—lexical analysis, syntax analysis, code generation and optimisation—plus grammar description using BNF/syntax diagrams and expression evaluation using Reverse Polish Notation.

fragments.label: Token
fragments.text: A classified unit produced during lexical analysis, e.g. keyword, identifier, literal or operator.

fragments.label: Lexeme
fragments.text: The actual character sequence that matches a token category.

fragments.label: Parser
fragments.text: The syntax-analysis component that checks tokens against grammar.

fragments.label: BNF
fragments.text: A formal notation that defines valid language structures using production rules.

fragments.label: RPN
fragments.text: Postfix notation where operators follow operands, allowing stack-based evaluation without brackets.

fragments.label: Optimisation
fragments.text: Transformation of generated/intermediate code to improve speed/size without changing its result.
Interpreter

fragments.label: Interpreter
fragments.text: An interpreter translates/executes source during runtime and normally does not produce a permanently stored complete executable. It is convenient for testing and portable source execution, but repeated translation can reduce execution speed.
Lexical analysis

fragments.label: Lexical analysis
fragments.text: The compiler scans source characters, groups them into tokens, discards irrelevant whitespace/comments where appropriate, recognises identifiers/literals and maintains symbol-table information. Invalid character sequences can be reported as lexical errors.
Syntax analysis

fragments.label: Syntax analysis
fragments.text: The parser checks whether the token stream fits the language grammar, often building a parse tree/internal representation. Missing delimiters or malformed statements are syntax errors; logical correctness is a different issue.
Code generation and optimisation

fragments.label: Code generation and optimisation
fragments.text: Once the source is valid, machine/intermediate instructions are generated. Optimisation can remove redundant work, improve instruction selection or reduce code size while preserving program behaviour.
BNF and syntax diagrams

fragments.label: BNF and syntax diagrams
fragments.text: Both define legal grammatical structures. BNF uses production rules with sequences, alternatives and recursive definitions. Exam questions may ask whether a string is valid or to complete a rule.

fragments.label: BNF and syntax diagrams
fragments.text:
<digit> ::= 0 | 1 | 2 | ... | 9
<number> ::= <digit> | <digit><number>
Reverse Polish Notation

fragments.label: Reverse Polish Notation
fragments.text: Push operands onto a stack. When an operator appears, pop its operands, apply it, then push the result. No brackets are needed because order is explicit.
lexical=chars->tokens
syntax=tokens->grammar
generation=target code
optimisation=same result better code
RPN uses stack

title: Encryption, Encryption Protocols and Digital Certificates

fragments.text: A2 security focuses on protecting communication and proving identity. You must compare symmetric/asymmetric encryption, understand public/private key use for confidentiality and digital signatures, explain certificates and TLS/SSL, and know the idea, strengths and limitations of quantum cryptography.

fragments.label: Plaintext
fragments.text: Readable original data before encryption.

fragments.label: Ciphertext
fragments.text: Encrypted data intended to be unreadable without the correct key.

fragments.label: Symmetric encryption
fragments.text: The same secret key is used for encryption and decryption.

fragments.label: Asymmetric encryption
fragments.text: A related public/private key pair is used for complementary operations.

fragments.label: Digital signature
fragments.text: Cryptographic evidence that helps verify sender authenticity and detect alteration.

fragments.label: Digital certificate
fragments.text: A digitally signed credential binding an identity to a public key.

fragments.label: Certificate Authority
fragments.text: A trusted organisation that verifies identity and signs digital certificates.
Symmetric encryption

fragments.label: Symmetric encryption
fragments.text: Fast and suitable for large amounts of data. The weakness is secure key distribution: both parties need the same secret key, and disclosure of it compromises confidentiality.
Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality

fragments.label: Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality
fragments.text: To send a secret message to Bob, encrypt using Bob's PUBLIC key. Only the matching Bob PRIVATE key should be able to decrypt it. Public keys may be distributed openly; private keys must remain secret.
Digital signatures

fragments.label: Digital signatures
fragments.text: For authentication/integrity, the sender uses their private key in the signing process. A recipient verifies using the sender's public key. In real systems a hash of the message is normally signed, so modification can be detected efficiently.
Certificates and trust

fragments.label: Certificates and trust
fragments.text: A certificate links a public key to an identified subject and is signed by a trusted CA. A client verifies the CA signature, validity dates and identity/hostname before trusting the key. This prevents an attacker from simply presenting an arbitrary public key as if it belonged to the genuine server.
TLS/SSL

fragments.label: TLS/SSL
fragments.text: TLS (historically SSL) protects client-server sessions such as HTTPS. Certificates authenticate the server; asymmetric cryptography helps establish secure session secrets; efficient symmetric encryption then protects bulk traffic. The protocol also helps detect tampering.
Quantum cryptography

fragments.label: Quantum cryptography
fragments.text: Quantum key-distribution techniques can reveal eavesdropping because observation disturbs quantum states. Potential strength is secure key exchange based on physical principles. Limitations include specialised hardware, cost, distance/infrastructure constraints and the fact that compromised endpoints/software remain vulnerable.
symmetric=one shared secret
asymmetric=public/private pair
recipient public->privacy
sender private->signature
certificate=identity+public key
TLS uses asymmetric trust + symmetric session encryption

The AI topic combines graph search with machine learning. You must use Dijkstra's and A* searches, understand artificial neural networks and deep learning, distinguish supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement learning, and explain the purpose of backpropagation and regression.

fragments.label: Graph
fragments.text: A set of vertices/nodes connected by edges, often with edge weights representing cost or distance.

fragments.label: Dijkstra's algorithm
fragments.text: A shortest-path method that repeatedly finalises the unvisited node with lowest accumulated distance.

fragments.label: A*
fragments.text: A search using f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining actual cost from start with a heuristic estimate to goal.

fragments.label: Supervised learning
fragments.text: Learning from labelled training examples.

fragments.label: Unsupervised learning
fragments.text: Discovering structure/patterns in unlabelled data.

fragments.label: Reinforcement learning
fragments.text: Learning a policy from rewards/penalties following actions.

fragments.label: Backpropagation
fragments.text: Propagating output error backward through a neural network to adjust weights.

fragments.label: Regression
fragments.text: A method for modelling/predicting a continuous numeric relationship.
Graphs as search spaces

fragments.label: Graphs as search spaces
fragments.text: Nodes represent states/locations and edges possible transitions. Weighted edges let algorithms compare routes by cost, time or distance.
Dijkstra's algorithm

fragments.label: Dijkstra's algorithm
fragments.text: Start with cost 0 at the source and infinity elsewhere. Repeatedly select the unvisited node with smallest temporary distance, update neighbouring distances if a cheaper path is found, then finalise the selected node. With non-negative edge weights it finds shortest paths.
A* search

fragments.label: A* search
fragments.text: A* evaluates f=g+h. g is exact cost from the start; h is a heuristic estimate of remaining cost. A useful admissible heuristic does not overestimate the true remaining cost, allowing A* to focus toward the goal while retaining shortest-path guarantees under appropriate conditions.

fragments.label: A* search
fragments.text: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
Artificial neural networks

fragments.label: Artificial neural networks
fragments.text: Artificial neurons combine weighted inputs, apply activation functions and pass outputs forward. Training adjusts weights so network output better matches the desired behaviour. Hidden layers let a network learn intermediate features.
Learning types

fragments.label: Learning types
fragments.text: Supervised learning uses labelled targets, e.g. spam/not-spam. Unsupervised learning finds clusters/structure without target labels. Reinforcement learning has an agent choose actions in an environment and learn from rewards/penalties rather than labelled answers for every step.
Deep learning, backpropagation and regression

fragments.label: Deep learning, backpropagation and regression
fragments.text: Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex representations. Backpropagation calculates how weights contributed to error and updates them to reduce loss. Regression predicts continuous values/relationships, unlike classification which assigns categories.
Dijkstra=lowest accumulated cost
A*: f=g+h
supervised=labels
unsupervised=patterns
reinforcement=rewards
backprop adjusts weights

A2 algorithms brings together searching, sorting, ADTs and efficiency. You need to write/trace linear search, binary search, insertion sort and bubble sort; manipulate stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees; explain graphs and dictionaries; and compare time/space complexity using Big O.

fragments.label: Big O
fragments.text: A notation describing how time or memory requirements grow as input size n grows.

fragments.label: Binary search tree
fragments.text: A tree ordered by key so smaller values are placed in one subtree and larger values in the other.

fragments.label: Dictionary
fragments.text: An ADT storing key-value pairs accessed by unique keys.

fragments.label: Stack
fragments.text: LIFO structure: last item added is first removed.

fragments.label: Queue
fragments.text: FIFO structure: first item added is first removed.
Linear and binary search

fragments.label: Linear and binary search
fragments.text: Linear search checks items one by one and works on unsorted data; worst-case time grows O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED range; worst case O(log n). The cost of initially sorting data may matter if only one search will ever be done.

fragments.label: Linear and binary search
fragments.text: Binary search: compare target with middle; discard one half; repeat until found or interval empty.
Bubble sort

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: Compare adjacent items and swap out-of-order pairs. After each pass an extreme element moves to its final end position. A swap flag can stop early if a pass makes no swaps. Worst-case behaviour is quadratic.
Insertion sort

fragments.label: Insertion sort
fragments.text: Maintain a sorted prefix. Take the next value, shift larger values right, and insert it into the correct location. It can be efficient on small/nearly sorted input but worst case is also O(n^2).
Stacks and queues

fragments.label: Stacks and queues
fragments.text: Array implementations need indices/pointers plus overflow/underflow tests. Stacks push/pop at the top. Queues enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front; circular queues reuse freed array positions without shifting every item.
Linked lists

fragments.label: Linked lists
fragments.text: Each node contains data plus link(s). Search follows links. Insert/delete often change only a few links once the position is known, avoiding array shifts, but traversal is usually sequential because nodes are not indexed by position.
Binary trees

fragments.label: Binary trees
fragments.text: Search compares a key and descends left/right. Insertion descends until a free child location. Performance depends on shape: a balanced tree can be efficient, while a severely skewed tree behaves much more like a list.
Graphs and dictionaries

fragments.label: Graphs and dictionaries
fragments.text: Graphs model arbitrary many-to-many relationships such as transport/social networks. Dictionaries map keys to values and can be implemented using hashing or tree structures. Choose implementation according to lookup, insertion, ordering and memory requirements.
Big O and trade-offs

fragments.label: Big O and trade-offs
fragments.text: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic. Big O describes growth, not exact seconds. Space complexity matters too: a faster algorithm can require more memory.
linear O(n)
binary O(log n)+sorted
bubble=adjacent swaps
insertion=sorted prefix
stack=LIFO
queue=FIFO
Big O=growth rate

Recursion is when a routine calls itself to solve a smaller version of a problem. A valid recursive solution needs a stopping/base case and guaranteed progress toward it. You must trace calls, explain the call stack and unwinding, and evaluate recursion against iterative alternatives.

fragments.label: Base case
fragments.text: A condition that returns a result without making another recursive call.

fragments.label: Recursive case
fragments.text: The part that calls the same routine on a smaller/closer-to-base problem.

fragments.label: Call stack
fragments.text: The LIFO stack storing active routine calls, parameters, local data and return points.

fragments.label: Unwinding
fragments.text: Returning from nested recursive calls in reverse order after the base case is reached.
Designing a recursive routine

fragments.label: Designing a recursive routine
fragments.text: Every possible recursive path must eventually reach a base case. The recursive case should reduce the problem—such as n becoming n-1 or a tree call moving to a child. Otherwise recursion continues until stack space is exhausted.

fragments.label: Designing a recursive routine
fragments.text:
FUNCTION Factorial(n)
  IF n=0 THEN
    RETURN 1
  ELSE
    RETURN n*Factorial(n-1)
  ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
Tracing calls

fragments.label: Tracing calls
fragments.text: Separate the downward call phase from the upward return phase. Each call waits while the next is evaluated; once the base result appears, returns are resolved in reverse order.

fragments.label: Tracing calls
fragments.text: Factorial(3) -> 3*Factorial(2) -> 3*2*Factorial(1) -> 3*2*1*Factorial(0) -> 6
Call stack

fragments.label: Call stack
fragments.text: Each active invocation needs a stack frame containing parameters/local variables and a return address. Because the stack is LIFO, the latest call finishes first during unwinding.
When recursion is useful

fragments.label: When recursion is useful
fragments.text: It is natural for recursively defined structures/problems such as trees, divide-and-conquer algorithms or nested directory structures. For simple repetition, iteration can use less memory because it avoids many active stack frames.
base case stops
recursive case reduces problem
call stack=LIFO
unwinding=returns backward
recursion suits recursive structures

A programming paradigm is a general style of solving/programming a problem. Cambridge requires low-level, imperative/procedural, object-oriented and declarative approaches. At A2 you should be able to reason about addressing modes, modular procedural code, class relationships and declarative facts/rules/goals.

fragments.label: Programming paradigm
fragments.text: A broad approach/style for representing computation and organising programs.

fragments.label: Imperative programming
fragments.text: Programs expressed as commands that update state in a defined control flow.

fragments.label: Encapsulation
fragments.text: Controlling access to an object's internal state through a public interface.

fragments.label: Inheritance
fragments.text: A class deriving attributes/methods from another class; an is-a relationship.

fragments.label: Polymorphism
fragments.text: The same method/interface producing class-specific behaviour.

fragments.label: Aggregation
fragments.text: A has-a relationship where an object contains/references objects of another class.

fragments.label: Declarative programming
fragments.text: Specifying facts/rules or a desired relationship rather than an explicit step-by-step algorithm.
Low-level programming and addressing

fragments.label: Low-level programming and addressing
fragments.text: Immediate addressing places a literal value in the instruction. Direct addressing gives the memory address of the operand. Indirect addressing points to a location that contains the operand address. Indexed addressing combines a base address with an index. Relative addressing forms an address relative to a reference such as the program counter.
Imperative/procedural programming

fragments.label: Imperative/procedural programming
fragments.text: Variables hold state, and sequence, selection and iteration determine control flow. Procedures/functions decompose the solution, use parameters and local variables, and improve reuse/testing.
Classes and objects

fragments.label: Classes and objects
fragments.text: A class is a blueprint containing attributes and methods; an object/instance has its own state. Private attributes protect invariants, while getters/setters or other public methods provide controlled interaction.

fragments.label: Classes and objects
fragments.text:
CLASS BankAccount
  PRIVATE Balance : REAL
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(Amount : REAL)
    Balance <- Balance + Amount
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS
Inheritance, polymorphism, aggregation

fragments.label: Inheritance, polymorphism, aggregation
fragments.text: Inheritance models is-a and can reuse/extend behaviour. Polymorphism allows a common method call to behave differently for subclasses. Aggregation/containment models has-a—for example a Team object contains Player objects. Use the relationship that matches the real model rather than forcing inheritance.
Declarative programming

fragments.label: Declarative programming
fragments.text: Facts record known relationships, rules derive new relationships and goals/queries ask what can be proven. The language/runtime chooses the search/evaluation steps rather than the programmer explicitly controlling each step.

fragments.label: Declarative programming
fragments.text:
parent(alex,bob).
parent(bob,carol).
grandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z).
Choosing a paradigm

fragments.label: Choosing a paradigm
fragments.text: Low-level code gives hardware control but low portability. Procedural code suits clear algorithms. OOP suits systems with interacting entities/state and reuse. Declarative approaches suit relation/rule-based problems. Real applications can combine paradigms.
imperative=commands/state
class->objects
inheritance=is-a
aggregation=has-a
polymorphism=same interface different behaviour
declarative=facts+rules+goals

This topic is practical programming: robustly process files and handle runtime exceptions. You need correct read/write/append behaviour, serial/sequential/random-file processing, and exception handling that responds to expected failures without hiding ordinary programming errors.

fragments.label: Exception
fragments.text: A runtime event/error condition that interrupts normal execution and may be caught by a handler.

fragments.label: Read mode
fragments.text: Opens a file to inspect existing contents without intentionally replacing them.

fragments.label: Write mode
fragments.text: Opens a file for output, typically creating/replacing contents depending on language/API.

fragments.label: Append mode
fragments.text: Adds new data after existing contents.

fragments.label: Exception handler
fragments.text: Code executed when a specified exception occurs.
File lifecycle

fragments.label: File lifecycle
fragments.text: Open the file using the mode that matches the task, perform operations, and ensure resources are closed even if a failure occurs. Wrong mode choice can erase data or make required updates impossible.
Serial and sequential processing

fragments.label: Serial and sequential processing
fragments.text: Read records one at a time until end-of-file. Serial files are processed in stored arrival order; sequential files exploit key order for tasks such as merges or ordered reports.
Random file processing

fragments.label: Random file processing
fragments.text: Use a record number/address, often derived from a key/hash, to seek directly to the target record. Updates and retrieval must use exactly the same organisation, record-size/addressing and collision conventions used when the file was created.
Exception handling

fragments.label: Exception handling
fragments.text: Handle failures that can reasonably occur at runtime: missing file, permission failure, invalid conversion, unavailable resource, etc. A handler might report the issue, retry, use a safe fallback or terminate cleanly.

fragments.label: Exception handling

fragments.text: Exceptions versus validation

fragments.label: Exceptions versus validation
fragments.text: Exception handling is not a replacement for normal conditions/validation. If a value can be checked normally before an operation, an IF may be clearer; exceptions are for exceptional runtime situations that interrupt the normal path.
read=inspect
write=output/replace
append=add at end
random=direct position
exception=runtime failure with handler

Enterprise begins with a problem or opportunity and combines scarce resources to create value. For exams, connect the entrepreneur's decisions to risk, finance, customers and the wider economy; a definition alone rarely explains whether a new venture is likely to succeed.

fragments.label: Business activity
fragments.text: Using resources to produce goods or services that satisfy needs and wants, usually while meeting an objective such as profit or social impact.

fragments.label: Factors of production
fragments.text: Land, labour, capital and enterprise: the inputs combined to produce goods and services.

fragments.label: Scarcity
fragments.text: The condition in which unlimited wants cannot all be satisfied from limited resources.

fragments.label: Opportunity cost
fragments.text: The benefit of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made.

fragments.label: Added value
fragments.text: The difference between a product's selling price and the cost of bought-in materials and components.

fragments.label: Entrepreneur
fragments.text: A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources and accepts the financial risk of starting and managing a venture.

fragments.label: Intrapreneur
fragments.text: An employee who uses entrepreneurial initiative inside an existing organisation, while the employer normally carries the financial risk.

fragments.label: Business plan
fragments.text: A document setting out a venture's idea, objectives, market, operations, people and financial forecasts.

fragments.label: Social enterprise
fragments.text: A revenue-earning business whose main objectives are social or environmental and which reinvests much of its surplus in those objectives.
Purpose of business activity

fragments.label: Purpose of business activity
fragments.text: A business transforms inputs into outputs. Land includes sites and natural resources; labour is human effort; capital includes finance and productive assets; enterprise coordinates the other inputs and accepts risk. Consumer goods are tangible products bought by final users, consumer services are intangible, and capital goods help other businesses produce.

fragments.label: Purpose of business activity
fragments.text: A successful transformation must be effective (meet customer needs) and efficient (limit wasted time, money and materials).

fragments.label: Purpose of business activity
fragments.text: The business environment is dynamic: technology, competitors, incomes, tastes and laws change, so the original idea may need adapting.

fragments.label: Purpose of business activity
fragments.text: Customers provide revenue, suppliers provide reliable inputs, and government provides rules, infrastructure and sometimes support.
Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

fragments.label: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
fragments.text: Every business decision uses resources that could have been used elsewhere. State the actual alternative forgone: saying only that there is an 'opportunity cost' is not analysis.

fragments.label: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
fragments.text: A start-up spending $20,000 on equipment cannot use the same money for promotion or additional working capital.

fragments.label: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
fragments.text: A manager using factory space for Product A gives up the contribution that Product B might have earned.

fragments.label: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
fragments.text: The best choice depends on objectives, expected return, risk and time, not only the lowest immediate cost.

fragments.label: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
fragments.text: Buying an automated cutter may raise output, but the opportunity cost is the marketing campaign forgone. If weak awareness is the true sales constraint, the machine may add capacity without adding revenue.
Creating and increasing added value

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: Higher added value gives room to pay wages and other costs and still earn profit, but it is not identical to profit because it ignores expenses such as rent, salaries and promotion.

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: Raise the selling price through branding, design, quality, convenience, personal service or after-sales support.

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: Reduce bought-in costs through negotiation, bulk purchasing, less waste or a different supplier.

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: Improve the product so customers perceive a meaningful difference rather than a cosmetic change.

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: Evaluate trade-offs: cheaper inputs may damage reliability; higher prices may reduce demand; added services also cost money.

fragments.label: Creating and increasing added value
fragments.text: A café buys ingredients for $2.40 and sells the meal for $8.50. Added value = $8.50 − $2.40 = $6.10 per meal. New packaging that costs $0.30 only improves added value if it supports a price rise or sufficient extra sales.
Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs

fragments.label: Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs
fragments.text: Entrepreneurs need initiative, self-confidence, resilience, creativity, calculated risk-taking, leadership and enough financial literacy to control cash. Intrapreneurs can innovate with an established firm's finance, brand and systems, but may have less freedom and may not receive the full reward.

fragments.label: Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs
fragments.text: Rewards include profit, independence, achievement and possible capital growth.

fragments.label: Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs
fragments.text: Risks include loss of savings, uncertain income, long hours, stress and unlimited liability in some legal forms.

fragments.label: Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs
fragments.text: A characteristic matters only when linked to action: resilience helps an owner learn from rejected prototypes and revise the product rather than abandon the venture.
From opportunity to surviving start-up

fragments.label: From opportunity to surviving start-up
fragments.text: An opportunity may come from a hobby, new technology, a gap in an existing market or a better location/service. It still needs customers willing and able to pay. Many new businesses fail because the idea is not researched, records and cash are poorly controlled, finance is insufficient, management lacks key skills or competition and external change are underestimated.

fragments.label: From opportunity to surviving start-up
fragments.text: Test demand with focused market research and a small-scale launch.

fragments.label: From opportunity to surviving start-up
fragments.text: Secure start-up capital and enough working capital for the period before cash receipts become reliable.

fragments.label: From opportunity to surviving start-up
fragments.text: Build a dependable supplier base and a clear source of differentiation.

fragments.label: From opportunity to surviving start-up
fragments.text: Monitor costs, cash, customer feedback and competitor actions rather than relying on enthusiasm alone.
Business plans: value and limits

fragments.label: Business plans: value and limits
fragments.text: A business plan makes assumptions explicit and can persuade banks or investors that managers understand the market and cash needs. Typical sections cover the business idea and objectives, owners and skills, market research and marketing plan, operations and location, staffing, finance required, cash-flow and profit forecasts, and risks.

fragments.label: Business plans: value and limits
fragments.text: Planning can reveal a cash shortage before launch and coordinate decisions.

fragments.label: Business plans: value and limits
fragments.text: External finance providers can judge repayment ability, security and management credibility.

fragments.label: Business plans: value and limits
fragments.text: Forecasts are estimates: optimistic sales, missing costs or sudden market change can make a polished plan misleading.

fragments.label: Business plans: value and limits
fragments.text: The plan should be reviewed and updated; writing one does not guarantee success.
Enterprise and economic development

fragments.label: Enterprise and economic development
fragments.text: New ventures may create employment, increase output and tax revenue, introduce innovation and competition, and grow into significant exporters. Failure is also part of enterprise: resources can be lost, but skills and competitive pressure may still improve the economy.

fragments.label: Enterprise and economic development
fragments.text: Governments may support enterprise through education, infrastructure, grants, advice, incubators and simpler regulation.

fragments.label: Enterprise and economic development
fragments.text: Support has an opportunity cost and may keep weak firms alive, so effectiveness depends on targeting and follow-up.
Social enterprise and the triple bottom line

fragments.label: Social enterprise and the triple bottom line
fragments.text: A social enterprise trades rather than depending only on donations. It balances economic sustainability with social and environmental outcomes: profit is needed to continue, but profit maximisation is not the dominant purpose.

fragments.label: Social enterprise and the triple bottom line
fragments.text: Economic: earn a surplus and remain financially viable.

fragments.label: Social enterprise and the triple bottom line
fragments.text: Social: create jobs, widen access or support disadvantaged groups.

fragments.label: Social enterprise and the triple bottom line
fragments.text: Environmental: reduce waste, pollution or resource use.

fragments.label: Social enterprise and the triple bottom line
fragments.text: Tension remains possible—for example, paying fair wages may raise costs, while a higher price may reduce access for low-income customers.
What are the four factors of production?

fragments.label: What are the four factors of production?
fragments.text: Land, labour, capital and enterprise.
How is added value calculated?

fragments.label: How is added value calculated?
fragments.text: Selling price minus the cost of bought-in materials and components.
Why is added value not the same as profit?

fragments.label: Why is added value not the same as profit?
fragments.text: Profit also deducts other business costs, including wages, rent, interest and promotion.
What is opportunity cost?

fragments.label: What is opportunity cost?
fragments.text: The benefit of the next-best alternative forgone.
How does an intrapreneur differ from an entrepreneur?

fragments.label: How does an intrapreneur differ from an entrepreneur?
fragments.text: An intrapreneur innovates inside an existing organisation, which usually provides resources and bears the financial risk.
Name the three parts of the triple bottom line.

fragments.label: Name the three parts of the triple bottom line.
fragments.text: Economic, social and environmental outcomes.
Give two reasons a business plan may not predict success.

fragments.label: Give two reasons a business plan may not predict success.
fragments.text: It is based on estimates and may use optimistic or incomplete assumptions; external conditions can also change.

Business structure covers both where activity sits in the economy and the legal form chosen by its owners. The strongest answers compare control, liability, continuity, finance, profit sharing and legal requirements in the exact context—not simply whether a form is 'large' or 'small'.

fragments.label: Primary sector
fragments.text: Businesses that extract or harvest natural resources, such as farming, fishing and mining.

fragments.label: Secondary sector
fragments.text: Businesses that manufacture or construct goods by transforming raw materials and components.

fragments.label: Tertiary sector
fragments.text: Businesses that provide services to consumers or other organisations.

fragments.label: Private sector
fragments.text: The part of the economy owned and controlled by individuals or private organisations.

fragments.label: Public sector
fragments.text: Organisations owned or controlled by the state, often providing services or pursuing social objectives.

fragments.label: Limited liability
fragments.text: Owners can normally lose only the amount invested in the company; their personal assets are protected from company debts.

fragments.label: Separate legal identity
fragments.text: The company has legal existence apart from its owners and can own assets, make contracts and be sued in its own name.

fragments.label: Sole trader
fragments.text: A business owned and controlled by one person, who normally has unlimited liability.

fragments.label: Partnership
fragments.text: A business owned by two or more people who share finance, responsibilities and returns under an agreement.

fragments.label: Private limited company
fragments.text: An incorporated company whose shares cannot be offered to the general public and whose shareholders have limited liability.

fragments.label: Public limited company
fragments.text: An incorporated company permitted to offer shares to the public, often through a stock exchange.

fragments.label: Franchise
fragments.text: An agreement allowing a franchisee to use the franchisor's brand and business system in return for fees and compliance with rules.

fragments.label: Co-operative
fragments.text: An organisation owned and controlled by members for their mutual benefit, usually with democratic voting.

fragments.label: Joint venture
fragments.text: A separate project or business owned by two or more organisations that share resources, control, risks and returns.
Economic sectors and structural change

fragments.label: Economic sectors and structural change
fragments.text: Primary businesses supply resources, secondary businesses transform them and tertiary businesses provide services. A product may pass through all three—for example, cotton farming, clothing manufacture and retailing. Sector classification depends on the main activity, not the product name.

fragments.label: Economic sectors and structural change
fragments.text: Industrialisation is an increase in the importance of manufacturing as investment, infrastructure and skills develop.

fragments.label: Economic sectors and structural change
fragments.text: Deindustrialisation is a relative decline in manufacturing, often as productivity rises, production moves abroad or demand shifts toward services.

fragments.label: Economic sectors and structural change
fragments.text: Rising incomes, urbanisation, technology and outsourcing usually increase tertiary activity; this does not mean primary and secondary output disappear.
Private, public and mixed economies

fragments.label: Private, public and mixed economies
fragments.text: Private-sector owners usually pursue profit, growth or personal objectives and bear commercial risk. Public-sector organisations are accountable to government and may prioritise access, quality, employment or strategic control. Most economies are mixed: markets allocate many resources while the state owns, regulates or funds selected activities.

fragments.label: Private, public and mixed economies
fragments.text: A free-market economy relies mainly on private ownership and price signals.

fragments.label: Private, public and mixed economies
fragments.text: A command economy relies mainly on state ownership and planning.

fragments.label: Private, public and mixed economies
fragments.text: Public ownership does not remove the need for efficiency or finance; private ownership does not mean the business ignores law or stakeholders.
Unincorporated ownership: sole traders and partnerships

fragments.label: Unincorporated ownership: sole traders and partnerships
fragments.text: A sole trader has speed, privacy, direct customer contact and full control, but limited finance, workload pressure, lack of continuity and unlimited liability can constrain growth. A partnership pools finance, skills and workload, yet profit and decisions must be shared and partners may be bound by one another's actions.

fragments.label: Unincorporated ownership: sole traders and partnerships
fragments.text: A partnership agreement should state capital contributions, profit sharing, duties, decision rules, dispute procedures and what happens if a partner leaves.

fragments.label: Unincorporated ownership: sole traders and partnerships
fragments.text: Unlimited liability matters most where debts, legal claims or long-term contracts are large.

fragments.label: Unincorporated ownership: sole traders and partnerships
fragments.text: Small scale can support flexibility and personal service, but it is not automatically more efficient or less risky.
Incorporated ownership: private and public companies

fragments.label: Incorporated ownership: private and public companies
fragments.text: Incorporation creates separate legal identity, continuity and limited liability. A private limited company can sell shares privately and protect owner control through transfer restrictions. A public limited company can raise very large sums from public share issues, but faces disclosure, regulation, flotation cost and possible loss of control.

fragments.label: Incorporated ownership: private and public companies
fragments.text: Shareholders own a company and elect directors; directors manage it. Their objectives may differ, creating a divorce between ownership and control.

fragments.label: Incorporated ownership: private and public companies
fragments.text: Share finance is permanent capital, but new shares dilute ownership and future profit may be paid as dividends.

fragments.label: Incorporated ownership: private and public companies
fragments.text: Limited liability reduces owner risk but does not protect directors from every personal guarantee or unlawful act.
Franchising

fragments.label: Franchising
fragments.text: The franchisee buys the right to operate a proven format. The franchisor provides a brand, training, systems and often national promotion; the franchisee supplies local capital and management. This can speed expansion for the franchisor and reduce start-up uncertainty for the franchisee.

fragments.label: Franchising
fragments.text: Franchisee benefits: recognised name, established product, training, purchasing support and a tested model.

fragments.label: Franchising
fragments.text: Franchisee drawbacks: initial fee, continuing royalties, restricted decisions and reputation risk from other outlets.

fragments.label: Franchising
fragments.text: Franchisor benefits: rapid growth using franchisees' capital and local knowledge.

fragments.label: Franchising
fragments.text: Franchisor drawbacks: monitoring cost, less direct control and brand damage if a franchisee performs badly.
Co-operatives, joint ventures and other collaborative forms

fragments.label: Co-operatives, joint ventures and other collaborative forms
fragments.text: A producer, worker or consumer co-operative exists for member benefit and often uses one-member-one-vote, which may strengthen commitment but slow decisions and limit external investment. A joint venture combines complementary skills, technology, finance or market access for a defined purpose.

fragments.label: Co-operatives, joint ventures and other collaborative forms
fragments.text: Joint-venture benefits: shared cost and risk, local knowledge, faster entry and combined expertise.

fragments.label: Co-operatives, joint ventures and other collaborative forms
fragments.text: Joint-venture risks: conflict over objectives, culture, contribution, control, profit sharing and intellectual property.

fragments.label: Co-operatives, joint ventures and other collaborative forms
fragments.text: A social enterprise is distinguished by its main objective, not by one fixed legal form.
Choosing an appropriate structure

fragments.label: Choosing an appropriate structure
fragments.text: A justified recommendation weighs the owners' desired control and return against finance required, risk, continuity, skill needs, speed of decisions, legal formalities, disclosure and growth plans. The importance of each factor changes with context.

fragments.label: Choosing an appropriate structure
fragments.text: A high-risk manufacturer needing expensive equipment may value incorporation and access to share capital.

fragments.label: Choosing an appropriate structure
fragments.text: A professional service may value a partnership because complementary expertise and client relationships matter.

fragments.label: Choosing an appropriate structure
fragments.text: A first-time owner may prefer a franchise when brand recognition and operating support are worth the fees and reduced freedom.

fragments.label: Choosing an appropriate structure
fragments.text: Recommend → use case evidence → explain the benefit → recognise the main drawback → judge why the benefit matters more for this business.
What distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary activity?

fragments.label: What distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary activity?
fragments.text: Extraction/harvesting, transformation/construction, and service provision respectively.
What two protections usually follow incorporation?

fragments.label: What two protections usually follow incorporation?
fragments.text: Separate legal identity and limited liability.
Why can a partnership raise more finance than a sole trader?

fragments.label: Why can a partnership raise more finance than a sole trader?
fragments.text: More owners can contribute capital and may provide more security or expertise to lenders.
What is the divorce between ownership and control?

fragments.label: What is the divorce between ownership and control?
fragments.text: Shareholders own the company, while directors make many management decisions and may pursue different objectives.
Why may a franchise reduce risk but also reduce profit?

fragments.label: Why may a franchise reduce risk but also reduce profit?
fragments.text: It provides a tested brand/system, but fees and royalties take revenue and rules limit local decisions.
Give two benefits and two risks of a joint venture.

fragments.label: Give two benefits and two risks of a joint venture.
fragments.text: Shared resources/risk and local expertise; possible conflict and loss of control or knowledge.

Business size has no single perfect measure. Exams reward selecting a measure that fits the industry, explaining why growth occurs and distinguishing the advantages of scale from the management and financial problems growth can create.

fragments.label: Revenue
fragments.text: Income earned from sales over a period: selling price multiplied by quantity sold.

fragments.label: Capital employed
fragments.text: The long-term finance invested in the business and used to generate its operations.

fragments.label: Market share
fragments.text: One business's sales as a percentage of total sales in its defined market.

fragments.label: Internal growth
fragments.text: Expansion using the business's own activities, such as increasing output, opening outlets or launching products.

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Expansion by combining or working with another organisation, such as a merger, takeover or joint venture.

fragments.label: Merger
fragments.text: Two businesses agree to combine into one organisation.

fragments.label: Takeover
fragments.text: One business acquires control of another business.

fragments.label: Economies of scale
fragments.text: Reductions in average cost that may occur as the scale of operations increases.

fragments.label: Diseconomies of scale
fragments.text: Increases in average cost caused by an organisation becoming too large or difficult to manage.
Measuring business size

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Revenue, employees, capital employed, output and market share show different dimensions. The best measure depends on the purpose and industry: employee count understates an automated factory, while revenue may exaggerate a retailer selling high-value goods at a thin margin.

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Revenue is easy to compare but affected by prices, inflation and exchange rates.

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Employee numbers suit labour-intensive activities but ignore hours, skills and outsourcing.

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Capital employed suits capital-intensive firms but asset values and leasing policies differ.

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Output can compare similar producers but not a bank with a manufacturer.

fragments.label: Measuring business size
fragments.text: Market share shows competitive position but depends on how the market and geography are defined.
Why businesses seek growth

fragments.label: Why businesses seek growth
fragments.text: Growth may increase profit, market power, status, survival prospects and access to finance. It can spread risk across products or markets and support economies of scale. Managers may also seek growth for salary, authority or prestige even when owner returns do not improve.
