fragments.label: Why businesses seek growth
fragments.text: Greater market share can strengthen bargaining power with suppliers and retailers.

fragments.label: Why businesses seek growth
fragments.text: A larger customer base can reduce dependence on one buyer or region.

fragments.label: Why businesses seek growth
fragments.text: Growth is a means, not a guaranteed objective: revenue can rise while cash flow, quality or profit falls.
Internal growth

fragments.label: Internal growth
fragments.text: Internal growth is usually gradual and easier to control: the firm can retain its culture and finance expansion from retained profit. It may come from new products, additional capacity, more outlets, e-commerce, promotion or entry into new geographic markets.

fragments.label: Internal growth
fragments.text: Benefits: lower integration risk, management retains control, and expansion can match available finance and demand.

fragments.label: Internal growth
fragments.text: Drawbacks: slower market entry, all development risk is carried by one firm, and competitors may move first.
External growth

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Mergers and takeovers can provide immediate capacity, customers, employees, brands, technology or distribution. Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage, vertical integration joins different stages in the supply chain, and conglomerate integration joins unrelated activities.

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Horizontal: may raise market share and remove competition, but regulators may object.

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Backward vertical: may secure inputs and quality, but ties the firm to its own supplier operation.

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Forward vertical: may improve access to customers and retain retail margin, but requires new capabilities.

fragments.label: External growth
fragments.text: Conglomerate: spreads risk, but managers may lack expertise and synergies may be weak.
Advantages of small businesses

fragments.label: Advantages of small businesses
fragments.text: Small firms can offer personal service, rapid communication, flexible decisions and specialised niche products. Owners stay close to customers and employees, helping quick adaptation. These strengths matter most where customisation, trust or local knowledge is valued.

fragments.label: Advantages of small businesses
fragments.text: Limitations include weak bargaining power, fewer specialist managers, limited finance, dependence on key people and less ability to spread risk.

fragments.label: Advantages of small businesses
fragments.text: Small does not automatically mean low cost: lack of purchasing economies can make unit cost higher.
Advantages of large businesses

fragments.label: Advantages of large businesses
fragments.text: Large firms may gain purchasing, technical, financial, marketing and managerial economies of scale. A wide product or geographic portfolio can spread risk, and brand recognition or distribution power can create barriers to entry.

fragments.label: Advantages of large businesses
fragments.text: Potential drawbacks include slow decisions, weak communication, loss of personal service, employee alienation and coordination cost.

fragments.label: Advantages of large businesses
fragments.text: Market power may attract regulation and public criticism.
Problems of rapid growth

fragments.label: Problems of rapid growth
fragments.text: Overtrading occurs when sales and operations expand faster than working capital. The firm may have profitable orders but lack cash to pay suppliers and wages. Rapid recruitment can dilute culture and training; new layers slow communication; quality may fall; debt and fixed costs increase; and an acquired business may resist integration.

fragments.label: Problems of rapid growth
fragments.text: Plan cash and capacity before accepting major orders.

fragments.label: Problems of rapid growth
fragments.text: Delegate with clear accountability and strengthen systems as complexity rises.

fragments.label: Problems of rapid growth
fragments.text: Use staged growth, appropriate long-term finance and post-merger integration targets.

fragments.label: Problems of rapid growth
fragments.text: Sales rising quickly is not enough. Check whether receivables and inventory are absorbing cash faster than suppliers and lenders are willing to finance them.
Why is employee count a weak size measure for an automated firm?

fragments.label: Why is employee count a weak size measure for an automated firm?
fragments.text: Automation allows high output and revenue with relatively few employees.
How is market share calculated?

fragments.label: How is market share calculated?
fragments.text: Business sales divided by total market sales, multiplied by 100.
What is the difference between a merger and takeover?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a merger and takeover?
fragments.text: A merger is an agreed combination; a takeover is one firm acquiring control of another.
What is backward vertical integration?

fragments.label: What is backward vertical integration?
fragments.text: Combining with or acquiring a supplier at an earlier stage of the supply chain.
How can growth create a cash crisis?

fragments.label: How can growth create a cash crisis?
fragments.text: Inventory, wages and capacity may need paying before cash is collected from increased sales.
Give two advantages small firms can retain.

fragments.label: Give two advantages small firms can retain.
fragments.text: Personal customer service and fast, flexible decisions, among others.

Objectives translate purpose into priorities and measures. High-scoring answers explain why an objective fits the business's stage and stakeholders, how a decision helps achieve it, and what the business may sacrifice in the process.

fragments.label: Aim
fragments.text: A broad, long-term statement of what a business wants to achieve.

fragments.label: Objective
fragments.text: A specific target used to direct and measure progress toward an aim.

fragments.label: Strategy
fragments.text: A medium- to long-term plan for achieving an objective.

fragments.label: Tactic
fragments.text: A short-term action used to implement a strategy.

fragments.label: SMART objective
fragments.text: A target that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant/realistic and time-limited.

fragments.label: Profit maximisation
fragments.text: Seeking the greatest possible difference between total revenue and total cost.

fragments.label: Profit satisficing
fragments.text: Seeking a level of profit sufficient to satisfy owners while also meeting other objectives.

fragments.label: Management by objectives
fragments.text: Coordinating and motivating staff by translating corporate objectives into agreed divisional, departmental and individual targets.

fragments.label: Mission statement
fragments.text: A public statement of an organisation's central purpose, values and direction.

fragments.label: Corporate social responsibility
fragments.text: Considering social and environmental effects and stakeholder responsibilities in business decisions.

fragments.label: Ethics
fragments.text: Moral principles that influence what a business considers right or acceptable.
Why objectives matter

fragments.label: Why objectives matter
fragments.text: Objectives provide direction, coordinate departments, motivate and assess performance, support resource allocation and give stakeholders a basis for judging the business. They are valuable only when understood, accepted and supported by resources.

fragments.label: Why objectives matter
fragments.text: Corporate objectives should be translated into compatible functional and individual targets.

fragments.label: Why objectives matter
fragments.text: Regular review compares actual performance with the target and triggers corrective action.

fragments.label: Why objectives matter
fragments.text: Poorly designed targets can cause dysfunctional behaviour—for example, a sales target that encourages excessive discounting and weak profit.
Common objectives and their trade-offs

fragments.label: Common objectives and their trade-offs
fragments.text: Survival is common for new or threatened firms. Profit provides finance and owner return; growth may increase scale and market power; market-share targets strengthen position; shareholder-return targets focus on dividends and share value. Some owners choose satisficing to preserve leisure, control or service quality.

fragments.label: Common objectives and their trade-offs
fragments.text: Lowering price may support sales and market share but reduce contribution per unit.

fragments.label: Common objectives and their trade-offs
fragments.text: Rapid growth may increase long-term profit but reduce short-term cash and dividends.

fragments.label: Common objectives and their trade-offs
fragments.text: Cost reduction may support survival but damage quality, motivation or stakeholder trust.
SMART objectives

fragments.label: SMART objectives
fragments.text: Specific states exactly what will change; measurable gives evidence; achievable tests resources and conditions; relevant links to the wider aim; time-limited sets a deadline. 'Improve sales' is weak; 'increase online revenue in Vietnam by 8% by 31 December while maintaining gross margin' is much more useful.

fragments.label: SMART objectives
fragments.text: Too easy: little motivation or improvement.

fragments.label: SMART objectives
fragments.text: Too difficult: demotivation, manipulation of data or unsafe shortcuts.

fragments.label: SMART objectives
fragments.text: A target can be SMART but still strategically wrong if it measures the wrong outcome.
Management by objectives

fragments.label: Management by objectives
fragments.text: Senior objectives are divided into targets for divisions, departments, managers and employees. Ideally managers and staff agree targets, resources and review dates, which clarifies how each role contributes and can increase ownership.

fragments.label: Management by objectives
fragments.text: Benefits: coordination, clearer responsibility, motivation and measurable appraisal.

fragments.label: Management by objectives
fragments.text: Limits: time-consuming negotiation, conflicting targets, narrow focus and rapid obsolescence in a dynamic environment.

fragments.label: Management by objectives
fragments.text: Success needs communication, reliable measures, employee participation and corrective support—not targets alone.
Mission statements

fragments.label: Mission statements
fragments.text: A mission communicates what the organisation stands for and can align employees and reassure stakeholders. It is broader and less measurable than an objective.

fragments.label: Mission statements
fragments.text: Useful when it is distinctive, credible and reflected in resource decisions.

fragments.label: Mission statements
fragments.text: Weak when it is vague public relations language, conflicts with actual conduct or becomes outdated as the business changes.
Why objectives change

fragments.label: Why objectives change
fragments.text: Objectives reflect internal conditions and the external environment. A start-up may move from survival to growth; recession may reverse that shift. Ownership, business size, cash position, competition, technology, regulation, stakeholder pressure and leadership can all reset priorities.

fragments.label: Why objectives change
fragments.text: Communicating change reduces uncertainty and allows department targets and budgets to be updated.

fragments.label: Why objectives change
fragments.text: Changing too frequently can confuse employees; refusing to change can make objectives irrelevant.
Ethics and corporate social responsibility

fragments.label: Ethics and corporate social responsibility
fragments.text: An ethical decision may go beyond minimum law—for example safer sourcing, fairer pay or rejecting misleading promotion. This can raise short-run cost but strengthen reputation, recruitment, loyalty, access to contracts and long-run risk control.

fragments.label: Ethics and corporate social responsibility
fragments.text: Potential costs: higher inputs, monitoring, training and loss of business where rivals use lower standards.

fragments.label: Ethics and corporate social responsibility
fragments.text: Potential benefits: differentiation, stakeholder trust, lower legal/reputation risk and long-term sustainability.

fragments.label: Ethics and corporate social responsibility
fragments.text: The impact depends on customer willingness to pay, credibility, competitor conduct and whether claimed standards are independently verified.
Decision-making cycle

fragments.label: Decision-making cycle
fragments.text: A disciplined decision begins with objectives, defines the issue, gathers relevant data, develops options, compares quantitative and qualitative effects, selects and implements an option, then reviews the outcome against the original target.

fragments.label: Decision-making cycle
fragments.text: Quantitative evidence can compare cost, revenue and cash; qualitative evidence covers ethics, morale, risk and reputation.

fragments.label: Decision-making cycle
fragments.text: Review matters because assumptions may be wrong and implementation may differ from the plan.
What is the difference between an aim and an objective?

fragments.label: What is the difference between an aim and an objective?
fragments.text: An aim is broad and long-term; an objective is a specific target used to measure progress.
What does SMART stand for?

fragments.label: What does SMART stand for?
fragments.text: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant/realistic and time-limited.
Why might owners choose profit satisficing?

fragments.label: Why might owners choose profit satisficing?
fragments.text: They may value sufficient income alongside independence, leisure, control, quality or other stakeholder aims.
How does management by objectives work?

fragments.label: How does management by objectives work?
fragments.text: Corporate aims are translated into agreed targets for divisions, departments and individuals, then performance is reviewed.
Why can CSR improve long-run profit?

fragments.label: Why can CSR improve long-run profit?
fragments.text: It may strengthen trust, loyalty, recruitment and risk control, though it can raise short-run cost.
Give two reasons objectives change.

fragments.label: Give two reasons objectives change.
fragments.text: Examples include business age, recession, competition, ownership, finance, leadership, law or stakeholder pressure.

Stakeholder questions are about power, conflict and consequences. Identify exactly what each group wants, trace how a decision affects them, and judge whose interests should carry most weight in the particular situation.

fragments.label: Stakeholder
fragments.text: Any person or group with an interest in, or affected by, a business's decisions and performance.

fragments.label: Internal stakeholder
fragments.text: A stakeholder inside the organisation, such as owners, managers or employees.

fragments.label: External stakeholder
fragments.text: A stakeholder outside the organisation, such as customers, suppliers, lenders, government or the local community.

fragments.label: Shareholder
fragments.text: A person or institution owning shares in a company.

fragments.label: Accountability
fragments.text: The duty to explain decisions, accept responsibility for outcomes and provide relevant information to those affected.

fragments.label: Stakeholder conflict
fragments.text: A situation in which satisfying one group's objective makes another group's objective harder to achieve.

fragments.label: Pressure group
fragments.text: An organised group seeking to influence business or government decisions without directly controlling the organisation.
Stakeholder objectives

fragments.label: Stakeholder objectives
fragments.text: Owners seek return, growth and controlled risk; managers may seek pay, status and successful performance; employees value fair pay, security, conditions, development and satisfaction. Customers seek safe, reliable value; suppliers want repeat orders and prompt payment; lenders want interest and repayment; government wants legal compliance, jobs, output and tax; communities want employment with limited disruption and pollution.

fragments.label: Stakeholder objectives
fragments.text: Objectives within one group can differ: short-term investors may prefer dividends while founding owners favour reinvestment.

fragments.label: Stakeholder objectives
fragments.text: A stakeholder's stated objective does not show its power to achieve it.
How decisions create different effects

fragments.label: How decisions create different effects
fragments.text: One expansion decision can benefit employees through promotion, suppliers through larger orders and government through tax, yet reduce dividends, increase lender risk and create community traffic or pollution. Cover both direct and knock-on effects.

fragments.label: How decisions create different effects
fragments.text: Short-term and long-term effects may differ: training costs reduce current profit but can improve productivity and job security later.

fragments.label: How decisions create different effects
fragments.text: Different members of a group may experience opposite effects: automation can improve safety for retained staff while making other roles redundant.
Sources of stakeholder conflict

fragments.label: Sources of stakeholder conflict
fragments.text: Resources are limited, so higher wages may reduce short-run profit; lower prices may conflict with supplier or employee payments; a new factory may create jobs but harm residents; prompt debt repayment may restrict investment. Conflict can also come from different time horizons and risk preferences.

fragments.label: Sources of stakeholder conflict
fragments.text: Compromise options include staged change, consultation, retraining, compensation, environmental controls and sharing productivity gains.

fragments.label: Sources of stakeholder conflict
fragments.text: Compromise has a cost and may satisfy no group fully; delay can be worse when urgent action is required.
Stakeholder power and influence

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Influence depends on legal rights, financial dependence, scarcity of the stakeholder's resource, ability to organise, access to information, public support and urgency. A lender has power when finance is scarce; skilled employees have power when replacement is difficult; customers have power where substitutes are plentiful.

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Employees can negotiate, resign or take industrial action.

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Customers can switch, complain, review or boycott.

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Suppliers can change price, quality, credit or delivery terms.

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Government can tax, regulate, fine, subsidise or grant permission.

fragments.label: Stakeholder power and influence
fragments.text: Owners can vote, replace directors or withhold capital.
Accountability in practice

fragments.label: Accountability in practice
fragments.text: Accountability is more than publicity. It includes accurate reports, consultation, complaint processes, contracts, audits, legal compliance and measurable social/environmental commitments. Meeting responsibilities can strengthen trust and reduce disruption.

fragments.label: Accountability in practice
fragments.text: Customers: honest information, safe products, reliable service and remedies.

fragments.label: Accountability in practice
fragments.text: Employees: contracts, fair treatment, safe conditions, pay and development.

fragments.label: Accountability in practice
fragments.text: Suppliers/lenders: truthful financial information and agreed payment.

fragments.label: Accountability in practice
fragments.text: Community/government: compliance, tax, environmental control and transparent impact reporting.
Prioritising stakeholders

fragments.label: Prioritising stakeholders
fragments.text: Managers should compare stakeholder power, legitimacy and urgency, then connect the choice to long-term objectives. Prioritising lenders during a liquidity crisis may preserve the entire firm; prioritising customers after a safety failure may rebuild trust; consulting residents may be essential before seeking planning permission.

fragments.label: Prioritising stakeholders
fragments.text: Shareholder primacy focuses on owner return and clear accountability.

fragments.label: Prioritising stakeholders
fragments.text: Stakeholder approaches argue that long-run success depends on relationships with all essential groups.

fragments.label: Prioritising stakeholders
fragments.text: The best judgement is contextual: identify which relationship is most critical and what happens if it breaks down.
Changing objectives and stakeholder outcomes

fragments.label: Changing objectives and stakeholder outcomes
fragments.text: Moving from growth to survival can mean cancelled supplier orders, redundancies and lower owner returns. Moving toward CSR may benefit employees and communities but raise costs or prices. Changing objectives should therefore be communicated with reasons, timelines and mitigation.

fragments.label: Changing objectives and stakeholder outcomes
fragments.text: Unexplained change increases uncertainty and resistance.

fragments.label: Changing objectives and stakeholder outcomes
fragments.text: Credible consultation can improve information and implementation, but does not remove the need for difficult decisions.
What is the difference between a shareholder and stakeholder?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a shareholder and stakeholder?
fragments.text: A shareholder owns part of a company; a stakeholder is any group interested in or affected by the business.
Why can employees and owners conflict over wages?

fragments.label: Why can employees and owners conflict over wages?
fragments.text: Higher wages benefit employees but raise costs and can reduce short-run profit or dividends.
What determines stakeholder influence?

fragments.label: What determines stakeholder influence?
fragments.text: Legal rights, dependence, resource scarcity, organisation, information, public support and urgency.
Give two ways customers can influence a business.

fragments.label: Give two ways customers can influence a business.
fragments.text: They can switch purchases, complain, post reviews or organise a boycott.
What does business accountability require?

fragments.label: What does business accountability require?
fragments.text: Explaining decisions, providing reliable information, accepting responsibility and responding to outcomes.
How can a business reduce conflict over a factory closure?

fragments.label: How can a business reduce conflict over a factory closure?
fragments.text: Consult early, give notice and compensation, offer redeployment or retraining, and explain the financial need.

Human resource management makes sure the business has the right number of people with the right skills at the right time. Exam answers should connect workforce decisions to cost, flexibility, motivation, productivity, quality and the organisation's future needs.

fragments.label: Human resource management
fragments.text: Planning, recruiting, developing, rewarding and managing people so the organisation can meet its objectives.

fragments.label: Workforce planning
fragments.text: Forecasting the number and skills of employees required and preparing how to meet that need.

fragments.label: Job description
fragments.text: A document stating the job title, duties, responsibilities, working conditions and reporting relationships.

fragments.label: Person specification
fragments.text: A profile of the qualifications, skills, experience and personal qualities required from the successful applicant.

fragments.label: Induction training
fragments.text: An introduction for a new employee to the organisation, role, colleagues, procedures and safety requirements.

fragments.label: Labour turnover
fragments.text: The rate at which employees leave an organisation during a period.

fragments.label: Absenteeism
fragments.text: The proportion of scheduled working time lost because employees are absent.

fragments.label: Dismissal
fragments.text: Ending an employee's contract because of conduct, capability or another attributable reason, subject to law and procedure.

fragments.label: Redundancy
fragments.text: Ending employment because the job is no longer required, rather than because the employee is at fault.

fragments.label: Trade union
fragments.text: An organisation representing employees' interests in areas such as pay, conditions, rights and training.

fragments.label: Collective bargaining
fragments.text: Negotiation between an employer and employee representatives over terms and conditions of employment.
Workforce planning

fragments.label: Workforce planning
fragments.text: Workforce planning compares forecast labour demand with current labour supply by number, location and skill. Demand depends on sales forecasts, production methods, technology, growth, labour productivity and budgets; supply depends on turnover, retirement, promotion, training and the external labour market.

fragments.label: Workforce planning
fragments.text: A shortage may be met through recruitment, overtime, training, redeployment, flexible contracts, automation or outsourcing.

fragments.label: Workforce planning
fragments.text: A surplus may be managed through natural wastage, reduced overtime, redeployment, retraining, reduced hours, voluntary redundancy or compulsory redundancy.

fragments.label: Workforce planning
fragments.text: Forecasts are uncertain, so plans should include alternative demand scenarios and critical-skill priorities.
Recruitment documents and the recruitment process

fragments.label: Recruitment documents and the recruitment process
fragments.text: A clear job analysis leads to a job description and person specification. The vacancy can then be advertised, applications screened, candidates selected, references checked, an offer made and performance reviewed after appointment.

fragments.label: Recruitment documents and the recruitment process
fragments.text: The job description helps applicants understand the role and gives managers criteria for appraisal.

fragments.label: Recruitment documents and the recruitment process
fragments.text: The person specification reduces subjective selection but should contain only criteria genuinely relevant to performance.

fragments.label: Recruitment documents and the recruitment process
fragments.text: An application form gives comparable data; a CV may reveal more individuality but uses inconsistent formats.

fragments.label: Recruitment documents and the recruitment process
fragments.text: Poor specification increases the chance of costly labour turnover and weak performance.
Internal and external recruitment

fragments.label: Internal and external recruitment
fragments.text: Internal recruitment fills a vacancy from the existing workforce. It is quicker and cheaper, the candidate is known and promotion can motivate, but it limits new ideas, creates another vacancy and may cause rivalry. External recruitment widens the skill pool and brings fresh experience, but advertising, selection and induction cost more and performance is less certain.

fragments.label: Internal and external recruitment
fragments.text: Use internal recruitment where company knowledge and continuity matter.

fragments.label: Internal and external recruitment
fragments.text: Use external recruitment where new expertise, greater diversity or organisational change is needed.

fragments.label: Internal and external recruitment
fragments.text: The appropriate method depends on urgency, seniority, skill scarcity, cost and the quality of current employees.
Selection and employment contracts

fragments.label: Selection and employment contracts
fragments.text: Selection may combine interviews with skills, aptitude, personality, work-sample or group tests. Interviews allow follow-up and cultural assessment but can be biased and may predict performance poorly. Work samples often test job ability more directly, while references verify history rather than future potential.

fragments.label: Selection and employment contracts
fragments.text: A contract normally states job title, start date, hours, pay, benefits, duties, holiday and notice.

fragments.label: Selection and employment contracts
fragments.text: Selection should use consistent criteria and more than one source of evidence.

fragments.label: Selection and employment contracts
fragments.text: Employers must follow relevant equality, data and employment laws; the precise legal rules vary by country.
Flexible employment

fragments.label: Flexible employment
fragments.text: Full-time permanent staff can build commitment, continuity and firm-specific skill but create a stable labour cost. Part-time, temporary, flexitime, remote and zero-hours arrangements can match labour to demand and widen recruitment, yet may weaken security, communication and training.

fragments.label: Flexible employment
fragments.text: Part-time: useful for peak periods and employees needing shorter hours; more people may be needed for the same coverage.

fragments.label: Flexible employment
fragments.text: Temporary/fixed-term: useful for projects or seasonal demand; commitment and continuity can be lower.

fragments.label: Flexible employment
fragments.text: Flexitime/remote work: can improve retention and access to talent; coordination, supervision and cybersecurity need managing.

fragments.label: Flexible employment
fragments.text: Zero-hours: highly flexible where demand is uncertain; income insecurity may reduce loyalty and availability.
Training and development

fragments.label: Training and development
fragments.text: Induction reduces early mistakes and helps a recruit settle. On-the-job training uses real equipment and is tailored and relatively cheap, but output and quality may suffer while training and poor habits can be passed on. Off-the-job training uses specialists away from normal work and may bring recognised skills, but fees, travel and lost working time raise cost.

fragments.label: Training and development
fragments.text: Training can raise skill → productivity and quality → lower unit cost/complaints → stronger competitiveness.

fragments.label: Training and development
fragments.text: It can motivate by showing investment in employees and supporting promotion.

fragments.label: Training and development
fragments.text: A trained employee may leave, so retention and opportunities matter alongside the course itself.
Dismissal, redundancy, equality and diversity

fragments.label: Dismissal, redundancy, equality and diversity
fragments.text: Dismissal concerns the individual; redundancy concerns the role. Both require fair, lawful procedures. Redundancy can reduce a structural labour surplus but brings payments, lost skills, survivor anxiety and reputation risk. Equality prevents irrelevant discrimination; diversity uses differences in background and perspective as an organisational resource.

fragments.label: Dismissal, redundancy, equality and diversity
fragments.text: Redeployment, retraining, natural wastage and voluntary redundancy may reduce harm before compulsory redundancy.

fragments.label: Dismissal, redundancy, equality and diversity
fragments.text: Diverse teams may understand wider customers and challenge groupthink, but inclusion and fair processes are needed to convert diversity into performance.

fragments.label: Dismissal, redundancy, equality and diversity
fragments.text: Unfair treatment can cause legal cost, absenteeism, turnover and recruitment difficulty.
Measuring and improving workforce performance

fragments.label: Measuring and improving workforce performance
fragments.text: Labour productivity measures output relative to employees, labour turnover measures exits, and absenteeism measures lost working time. Trends and benchmarks are more informative than one number, and the data show symptoms rather than causes.

fragments.label: Measuring and improving workforce performance
fragments.text: Possible causes of poor performance include weak selection, inadequate training, low motivation, poor equipment, unsafe conditions, unclear objectives and ineffective management.

fragments.label: Measuring and improving workforce performance
fragments.text: Responses include appraisal, coaching, training, job redesign, teamworking, better resources, fair rewards and management by objectives.

fragments.label: Measuring and improving workforce performance
fragments.text: High turnover can bring new ideas and remove weak performers, but usually raises recruitment and training cost and loses experience.

fragments.label: Measuring and improving workforce performance
fragments.text: If 18 employees leave an average workforce of 120, labour turnover = 18 ÷ 120 × 100 = 15%. Do not conclude motivation is poor until comparing past years, competitors and the reasons people left.
Trade unions and collective bargaining

fragments.label: Trade unions and collective bargaining
fragments.text: Trade unions provide collective voice, negotiate pay and conditions, support members, offer training and may organise industrial action. Employers may gain an efficient communication channel and more orderly consultation, but fear higher labour costs or reduced management freedom.

fragments.label: Trade unions and collective bargaining
fragments.text: Union power rises when skills are scarce, membership is high, production is busy and disruption would be costly.

fragments.label: Trade unions and collective bargaining
fragments.text: It falls when unemployment and replacement supply are high or the business can relocate or automate.

fragments.label: Trade unions and collective bargaining
fragments.text: Constructive recognition and no-strike or dispute procedures may reduce disruption, but outcomes depend on trust and enforcement.
What comes first: job description or person specification?

fragments.label: What comes first: job description or person specification?
fragments.text: Job analysis informs both; the job description states the role, while the person specification states the candidate requirements.
How is labour turnover calculated?

fragments.label: How is labour turnover calculated?
fragments.text: Employees leaving during the period divided by average employees, multiplied by 100.
What distinguishes redundancy from dismissal?

fragments.label: What distinguishes redundancy from dismissal?
fragments.text: Redundancy occurs because the job is no longer required; dismissal is linked to the employee's conduct, capability or another attributable reason.
Why might internal recruitment motivate staff?

fragments.label: Why might internal recruitment motivate staff?
fragments.text: It provides visible promotion and career opportunities.
What is the main trade-off of off-the-job training?

fragments.label: What is the main trade-off of off-the-job training?
fragments.text: Specialist or recognised learning versus course cost and lost working time.
What is collective bargaining?

fragments.label: What is collective bargaining?
fragments.text: Negotiation between an employer and worker representatives over employment terms and conditions.

Motivation affects the effort, persistence and care employees bring to work. Theories are not labels to memorise: use each one to explain a practical reward or job-design decision, then judge whether it fits the workforce, task and culture.

fragments.label: Motivation
fragments.text: The internal and external forces that cause people to act toward a goal with effort and persistence.

fragments.label: Piece rate
fragments.text: Payment based on the number of acceptable units produced.

fragments.label: Commission
fragments.text: Payment linked to the value or number of sales made.

fragments.label: Profit sharing
fragments.text: A reward giving employees a share of business profit, usually in addition to normal pay.

fragments.label: Job rotation
fragments.text: Moving employees between tasks to increase variety and flexibility.

fragments.label: Job enlargement
fragments.text: Adding more tasks of a similar level to widen a job.

fragments.label: Job enrichment
fragments.text: Increasing responsibility, autonomy, challenge and opportunities for achievement within a job.

fragments.label: Hygiene factors
fragments.text: Herzberg's conditions that can cause dissatisfaction when inadequate but do not by themselves create lasting motivation.

fragments.label: Motivators
fragments.text: Herzberg's job-content factors—such as achievement, recognition and responsibility—that can create satisfaction.

fragments.label: Expectancy
fragments.text: Vroom's belief that additional effort will improve performance.
Why motivation matters

fragments.label: Why motivation matters
fragments.text: A motivated workforce is more likely to attend, stay, accept responsibility, suggest improvements and maintain quality. That can raise labour productivity, reduce recruitment and wastage costs, improve customer experience and protect reputation. Motivation does not guarantee performance: employees also need ability, resources and clear direction.

fragments.label: Why motivation matters
fragments.text: Low motivation can produce absenteeism, labour turnover, lateness, errors, accidents, weak service and resistance.

fragments.label: Why motivation matters
fragments.text: Different employees value money, security, social belonging, achievement, autonomy and purpose differently.
Taylor: scientific management and economic reward

fragments.label: Taylor: scientific management and economic reward
fragments.text: Taylor treated pay as the central motivator and sought the most efficient method by selecting a task, timing its elements, identifying the quickest method, training employees in it, supervising performance and paying by results. Piece rate can lift measurable output where quality is easy to check.

fragments.label: Taylor: scientific management and economic reward
fragments.text: Strengths: clear standard, direct reward-effort link and possible productivity gains in repetitive work.

fragments.label: Taylor: scientific management and economic reward
fragments.text: Limits: quantity may displace quality/safety, teamwork and service are hard to measure, repetitive work can demotivate, and money is not the only need.
Mayo: social needs and participation

fragments.label: Mayo: social needs and participation
fragments.text: The Hawthorne studies led Mayo to emphasise attention, consultation, teamwork, informal groups and social relationships. Employees may respond because they feel observed and valued, and group norms can strongly influence output.

fragments.label: Mayo: social needs and participation
fragments.text: Use team briefings, consultation, supportive supervision and opportunities for employee voice.

fragments.label: Mayo: social needs and participation
fragments.text: Groups can also set low output norms, and participation may be slow or incompatible with urgent, tightly controlled work.
Maslow: hierarchy of needs

fragments.label: Maslow: hierarchy of needs
fragments.text: Maslow arranged needs from physiological and safety through social, esteem and self-actualisation. A manager should identify the currently unsatisfied need and offer a matching condition: adequate pay, security, belonging, recognition or development. Once a lower need is reasonably satisfied, a higher need may become more influential.

fragments.label: Maslow: hierarchy of needs
fragments.text: The model reminds managers that pay alone is incomplete.

fragments.label: Maslow: hierarchy of needs
fragments.text: People do not always move in the same order, may pursue several needs together and differ by culture and life stage.
Herzberg: hygiene and motivators

fragments.label: Herzberg: hygiene and motivators
fragments.text: Hygiene factors include pay, policy, supervision, relationships, security and conditions. Poor hygiene causes dissatisfaction, but improving it only removes dissatisfaction. Lasting motivation comes from achievement, recognition, meaningful work, responsibility, advancement and growth—often delivered through job enrichment.

fragments.label: Herzberg: hygiene and motivators
fragments.text: Pay still matters if it is perceived as unfair; it is simply not enough by itself in Herzberg's model.

fragments.label: Herzberg: hygiene and motivators
fragments.text: Enrichment requires skill, trust and support; unwanted responsibility can create stress rather than motivation.
McClelland and Vroom

fragments.label: McClelland and Vroom
fragments.text: McClelland proposed learned needs for achievement, affiliation and power. High-achievement employees value challenging but attainable tasks and feedback; affiliation-oriented employees value relationships; power-oriented employees value influence and leadership. Vroom argues that motivation depends on expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance leads to reward) and valence (the employee values the reward).

fragments.label: McClelland and Vroom
fragments.text: A valuable bonus will not motivate if employees think the target is impossible.

fragments.label: McClelland and Vroom
fragments.text: A reachable target will not motivate if managers do not reliably deliver the promised reward.

fragments.label: McClelland and Vroom
fragments.text: Individual diagnosis makes these theories useful but also harder to administer consistently.
Financial methods

fragments.label: Financial methods
fragments.text: Time rate or salary provides predictable income and suits work where output is hard to measure, but weak performers may receive the same pay. Piece rate and commission create a direct output or sales incentive, but can harm quality, advice and teamwork. Bonuses can reward targets; profit sharing connects staff to overall success but individual effort has a weak link to total profit. Fringe benefits can aid recruitment and retention.

fragments.label: Financial methods
fragments.text: Design measures that cannot be achieved by sacrificing safety, quality or long-term customer value.

fragments.label: Financial methods
fragments.text: Rewards must be large, fair, timely and understood enough to change behaviour.

fragments.label: Financial methods
fragments.text: Pay systems need affordable base security as well as incentives where appropriate.
Non-financial methods and job design

fragments.label: Non-financial methods and job design
fragments.text: Rotation increases variety and multi-skilling but may only move boredom. Enlargement adds similar tasks; enrichment adds autonomy and responsibility. Teamworking satisfies social needs and combines ideas, while participation and delegation can build trust and esteem. Recognition, training, promotion and flexible work can also motivate.

fragments.label: Non-financial methods and job design
fragments.text: Non-financial does not mean cost-free: training, redesign, consultation and extra responsibility require time and support.

fragments.label: Non-financial methods and job design
fragments.text: Methods must fit task interdependence, employee competence and the manager's willingness to release control.
Choosing a motivation package

fragments.label: Choosing a motivation package
fragments.text: Begin with evidence: pay complaints, turnover interviews, errors, missed targets or employee surveys. Identify the cause, then combine fair hygiene factors with meaningful rewards and job design. Review productivity, quality, absence and turnover after implementation.

fragments.label: Choosing a motivation package
fragments.text: Production line: measured incentives plus quality safeguards, team targets and rotation may fit.

fragments.label: Choosing a motivation package
fragments.text: Creative professionals: autonomy, recognition, mastery and purpose may matter more than piece rate.

fragments.label: Choosing a motivation package
fragments.text: Sales staff: commission can focus effort, but include customer satisfaction or profit margin to discourage unsuitable selling.
What is the key risk of piece-rate pay?

fragments.label: What is the key risk of piece-rate pay?
fragments.text: Employees may maximise quantity at the expense of quality, safety, waste or teamwork.
What did Mayo emphasise?

fragments.label: What did Mayo emphasise?
fragments.text: Attention, consultation, teamwork, social relationships and group norms.
What is the difference between Herzberg's hygiene factors and motivators?

fragments.label: What is the difference between Herzberg's hygiene factors and motivators?
fragments.text: Poor hygiene causes dissatisfaction; motivators such as achievement and responsibility create positive satisfaction.
How does job enrichment differ from job enlargement?

fragments.label: How does job enrichment differ from job enlargement?
fragments.text: Enrichment adds autonomy, challenge and responsibility; enlargement adds more tasks at a similar level.
What three perceptions make up Vroom's model?

fragments.label: What three perceptions make up Vroom's model?
fragments.text: Expectancy, instrumentality and valence.
Why may profit sharing have a weak motivational effect?

fragments.label: Why may profit sharing have a weak motivational effect?
fragments.text: An individual's effort may have little visible effect on total company profit, and the payment can be delayed.

Management coordinates people and resources so objectives become results. Detailed answers distinguish functions, roles and leadership approaches, then choose what fits the urgency, workforce skill, risk and culture of the case.

fragments.label: Management
fragments.text: Coordinating people and resources through planning, organising, directing and controlling to achieve objectives.

fragments.label: Leadership
fragments.text: Influencing and motivating people to work toward a shared direction or objective.

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Passing authority to a subordinate to perform a task while the manager retains ultimate accountability.

fragments.label: Authority
fragments.text: The formal right to make decisions, give instructions and use resources.

fragments.label: Responsibility
fragments.text: The obligation to carry out an assigned task.

fragments.label: Accountability
fragments.text: Being answerable for a decision or result.

fragments.label: Autocratic leadership
fragments.text: A leader makes decisions centrally and expects instructions to be followed.

fragments.label: Democratic leadership
fragments.text: A leader involves employees in discussion and decision-making while normally retaining final responsibility.

fragments.label: Laissez-faire leadership
fragments.text: A leader gives capable employees substantial freedom to decide how work is completed.

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence
fragments.text: The ability to recognise and manage one's own emotions and understand and respond effectively to others.
Functions of management

fragments.label: Functions of management
fragments.text: Managers set objectives and plan how to achieve them; organise people, finance and physical resources; direct and motivate employees; coordinate interdependent work; and control by comparing actual performance with targets and correcting deviations.

fragments.label: Functions of management
fragments.text: Planning without control gives no evidence that the plan worked.

fragments.label: Functions of management
fragments.text: Control is not only punishment: it includes measurement, feedback, support and corrective action.

fragments.label: Functions of management
fragments.text: Coordination prevents departments optimising their own targets while damaging the whole business.
Mintzberg's interpersonal roles

fragments.label: Mintzberg's interpersonal roles
fragments.text: As figurehead, the manager performs symbolic and formal duties. As leader, the manager recruits, motivates and develops people. As liaison, the manager builds internal and external relationships that move information and resources.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's interpersonal roles
fragments.text: One meeting may involve several roles; the classification helps explain what the manager is doing and why.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's interpersonal roles
fragments.text: The importance of each role varies by level, organisation and situation.
Mintzberg's informational roles

fragments.label: Mintzberg's informational roles
fragments.text: As monitor, the manager gathers relevant internal and external information. As disseminator, the manager passes useful information to colleagues. As spokesperson, the manager represents the organisation to outsiders.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's informational roles
fragments.text: Information must be timely, accurate, relevant and directed to people able to act.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's informational roles
fragments.text: Too much uncontrolled information can slow decisions as much as too little.
Mintzberg's decisional roles

fragments.label: Mintzberg's decisional roles
fragments.text: As entrepreneur, the manager develops improvements and opportunities; as disturbance handler, responds to crises and conflict; as resource allocator, decides priorities; and as negotiator, represents the organisation in agreements.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's decisional roles
fragments.text: A resource-allocation decision should link to stated objectives and opportunity cost.

fragments.label: Mintzberg's decisional roles
fragments.text: Disturbance handling is reactive, while the entrepreneur role is proactive.
Delegation

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Effective delegation defines the result, grants enough authority and resources, sets limits and review points, and holds the subordinate responsible while the manager remains accountable. It reduces manager workload, speeds local decisions, develops staff and enriches jobs.

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Risks include inconsistent decisions, employee error, unclear authority and a manager's fear of losing control.

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Delegation works best with competence, trust, information, training and a clear reporting system.

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Passing a task without authority or resources is not effective delegation.
Leadership styles

fragments.label: Leadership styles
fragments.text: Autocratic leadership is fast, clear and useful in crisis, confidential decisions or with inexperienced staff, but may reduce ideas and motivation. Democratic leadership uses employee knowledge and builds commitment but takes time. Laissez-faire can release expert creativity and speed specialist decisions but risks drift and weak coordination.

fragments.label: Leadership styles
fragments.text: No style is universally best. Consider urgency, risk, workforce competence, task complexity, culture, location and need for innovation.

fragments.label: Leadership styles
fragments.text: Managers may use different styles in different decisions rather than displaying one fixed style.
McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y

fragments.label: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
fragments.text: Theory X assumes employees dislike work, avoid responsibility and need direction and control. Theory Y assumes work can be satisfying and employees can exercise self-direction, creativity and responsibility when conditions support it. These are managerial assumptions, not permanent labels for two types of person.

fragments.label: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
fragments.text: Theory X assumptions often lead to close supervision and financial control.

fragments.label: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
fragments.text: Theory Y assumptions support participation, delegation and enrichment.

fragments.label: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
fragments.text: Management behaviour can become self-fulfilling: distrust may reduce initiative, appearing to confirm Theory X.
Emotional intelligence and manager effectiveness

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence and manager effectiveness
fragments.text: Self-awareness helps a manager judge strengths and emotional triggers; self-management supports calm and integrity; social awareness helps interpret others; relationship skills support persuasion, conflict resolution and teamwork.

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence and manager effectiveness
fragments.text: Emotional intelligence can improve acceptance and implementation of difficult decisions.

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence and manager effectiveness
fragments.text: It does not replace technical knowledge, evidence or willingness to make unpopular choices.
Making and reviewing decisions

fragments.label: Making and reviewing decisions
fragments.text: Good management defines the objective and problem, gathers evidence, generates alternatives, compares quantitative and qualitative consequences, decides, communicates responsibilities, implements and reviews. Participation may improve information; a clear deadline prevents analysis from becoming delay.

fragments.label: Making and reviewing decisions
fragments.text: Effective managers adjust when evidence changes rather than defending the original plan.

fragments.label: Making and reviewing decisions
fragments.text: A high-quality decision can still fail through weak implementation, so review should separate decision quality from execution.
What are the five broad management functions?

fragments.label: What are the five broad management functions?
fragments.text: Planning, organising, directing, coordinating and controlling.
Which Mintzberg category includes figurehead, leader and liaison?

fragments.label: Which Mintzberg category includes figurehead, leader and liaison?
fragments.text: Interpersonal roles.
What must accompany responsibility in effective delegation?

fragments.label: What must accompany responsibility in effective delegation?
fragments.text: Enough authority, resources, information and clear review points.
When is autocratic leadership most defensible?

fragments.label: When is autocratic leadership most defensible?
fragments.text: Where speed, safety, secrecy or inexperienced employees make central direction important.
What is the central difference between Theory X and Theory Y?

fragments.label: What is the central difference between Theory X and Theory Y?
fragments.text: They are contrasting management assumptions about employees' attitude to work, responsibility and self-direction.
Name the four broad elements of emotional intelligence.

fragments.label: Name the four broad elements of emotional intelligence.
fragments.text: Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and relationship/social skills.

Marketing identifies, anticipates and satisfies customer requirements profitably. The exam focus is how market information changes decisions about customers, products and objectives—not advertising alone.

fragments.label: Marketing
fragments.text: The management process of identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer requirements profitably.

fragments.label: Marketing objective
fragments.text: A specific target for marketing activity that contributes to the business's overall objectives.

fragments.label: Market orientation
fragments.text: Basing product and marketing decisions on researched customer needs and market conditions.

fragments.label: Product orientation
fragments.text: Prioritising product quality, innovation or technical strength and then finding customers for the output.

fragments.label: Demand
fragments.text: The quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period.

fragments.label: Supply
fragments.text: The quantity producers are willing and able to offer at a given price over a period.

fragments.label: Market size
fragments.text: Total sales in a defined market over a period, measured by value or volume.

fragments.label: Market growth
fragments.text: The percentage change in the size of a market over a period.

fragments.label: Market share
fragments.text: One business's sales as a percentage of total sales in the defined market.

fragments.label: Niche market
fragments.text: A small, specialised segment with needs not fully served by mass-market offers.

fragments.label: Market segmentation
fragments.text: Dividing a market into groups with similar characteristics or needs so each can be targeted more effectively.

fragments.label: Unique selling point
fragments.text: A meaningful feature or benefit that differentiates an offer from competitors.
Role and objectives of marketing

fragments.label: Role and objectives of marketing
fragments.text: Marketing research identifies needs and competitor conditions; product design, price, promotion, distribution and service then create and deliver value. It also maintains relationships and anticipates change. Objectives may include sales, market share, awareness, retention, new markets, new products, brand image and profit.

fragments.label: Role and objectives of marketing
fragments.text: Objectives should be measurable, time-limited and consistent with finance, operations and overall strategy.

fragments.label: Role and objectives of marketing
fragments.text: A market-share campaign that overwhelms capacity or destroys contribution conflicts with wider business performance.

fragments.label: Role and objectives of marketing
fragments.text: Customer loyalty can reduce repeat-promotion cost and provide feedback, but loyalty schemes must create incremental profit rather than reward purchases that would happen anyway.
Market and product orientation

fragments.label: Market and product orientation
fragments.text: A market-oriented business researches needs before committing resources, reducing mismatch risk and supporting adaptation. Research is costly and uncertain, and customers may not imagine breakthrough products. A product-oriented business builds on technical expertise and quality; it may create innovation customers did not request, but can waste development spending if the product solves no valued problem.

fragments.label: Market and product orientation
fragments.text: Asset-led marketing starts from existing brand, technology, distribution or skills and finds offers that use those strengths.

fragments.label: Market and product orientation
fragments.text: Societal marketing considers long-run consumer and social welfare as well as immediate demand and profit.

fragments.label: Market and product orientation
fragments.text: Many successful firms combine orientations: product expertise generates possibilities and market evidence selects/refines them.
Changing markets and competition

fragments.label: Changing markets and competition
fragments.text: Customer needs shift with income, demographics, lifestyles, technology, fashion and social values. Globalisation, e-commerce and improved transport expose firms to more competitors and price comparison. Businesses respond through research, innovation, relationship marketing, lower cost, improved service and clearer differentiation.

fragments.label: Changing markets and competition
fragments.text: Reacting fastest is useful only if the response is accurate and affordable.

fragments.label: Changing markets and competition
fragments.text: Existing customer data may miss new segments or reinforce past assumptions.
Demand, supply and equilibrium

fragments.label: Demand, supply and equilibrium
fragments.text: Demand normally falls as price rises; supply normally rises as price rises. A change in the product's own price is a movement along a curve. Income, tastes, population, advertising and substitute prices can shift demand; production cost, tax, subsidy, technology, weather and supplier disruption can shift supply.

fragments.label: Demand, supply and equilibrium
fragments.text: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and unsold stock puts downward pressure on price.

fragments.label: Demand, supply and equilibrium
fragments.text: Below equilibrium, excess demand and shortages put upward pressure on price.

fragments.label: Demand, supply and equilibrium
fragments.text: A shift in demand or supply creates a new equilibrium price and quantity; explain the cause before the result.
Market size, growth and share

fragments.label: Market size, growth and share
fragments.text: Market size helps judge opportunity and calculate share. Growth indicates whether total demand is expanding; share indicates relative competitive position. Use value or volume consistently and define product, customer and geography carefully.

fragments.label: Market size, growth and share
fragments.text: High share may strengthen supplier bargaining, retailer support and brand credibility.

fragments.label: Market size, growth and share
fragments.text: A growing market can support sales without share gains; a firm can gain share while its sales fall if the total market contracts faster.

fragments.label: Market size, growth and share
fragments.text: Published estimates may be incomplete, outdated or use a different market definition.

fragments.label: Market size, growth and share
fragments.text: A firm sells $18m in a $120m market. Market share = 18 ÷ 120 × 100 = 15%. If the market was $100m last year, market growth = (120 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 20%.
Mass and niche marketing

fragments.label: Mass and niche marketing
fragments.text: Mass marketing targets a broad market with a standard offer, supporting high volume, wide distribution and economies of scale, but competition is intense and promotion expensive. Niche marketing focuses on a narrow segment, enabling specialisation, close customer knowledge and possibly premium prices, but the market is small and the business may depend on one changing segment.

fragments.label: Mass and niche marketing
fragments.text: A successful niche can attract larger competitors.

fragments.label: Mass and niche marketing
fragments.text: Digital channels can make small global niches economically reachable.

fragments.label: Mass and niche marketing
fragments.text: The choice depends on resources, differentiation, market size, competition and production flexibility.
Market segmentation

fragments.label: Market segmentation
fragments.text: Consumer markets may be segmented by age, gender, income/social group, location, lifestyle, values, behaviour and usage. Industrial markets may use industry, organisation size, location, purchase volume, required specification or buying process. Effective segments are identifiable, measurable, reachable, substantial and meaningfully different.

fragments.label: Market segmentation
fragments.text: Benefits: more relevant products/messages, less wasted promotion, stronger conversion and identification of gaps.

fragments.label: Market segmentation
fragments.text: Costs: research, smaller production runs, multiple campaigns and possible confusion between variants.

fragments.label: Market segmentation
fragments.text: Avoid stereotypes: segment variables are evidence for different needs, not proof of how every individual behaves.
Marketing and added value

fragments.label: Marketing and added value
fragments.text: Brand, design, packaging, convenience, service, guarantees and a credible USP can increase willingness to pay or repeat purchase. Added value rises only if the increase in selling price or value created exceeds extra bought-in input cost; profit rises only after all added marketing costs are considered.

fragments.label: Marketing and added value
fragments.text: A distinctive claim must be relevant and believable.

fragments.label: Marketing and added value
fragments.text: Premium packaging can strengthen perception but may conflict with environmental expectations.
What three activities are captured in the core definition of marketing?

fragments.label: What three activities are captured in the core definition of marketing?
fragments.text: Identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer requirements profitably.
How does product orientation differ from market orientation?

fragments.label: How does product orientation differ from market orientation?
fragments.text: Product orientation starts with technical/product strengths; market orientation starts with researched customer needs.
How is market growth calculated?

fragments.label: How is market growth calculated?
fragments.text: Change in market size divided by the previous market size, multiplied by 100.
Can share rise while sales fall?

fragments.label: Can share rise while sales fall?
fragments.text: Yes, if the overall market contracts by a greater percentage than the firm's sales.
What makes a useful market segment?

fragments.label: What makes a useful market segment?
fragments.text: It should be identifiable, measurable, reachable, substantial and different enough to require a distinct response.
Why may niche customers accept a higher price?

fragments.label: Why may niche customers accept a higher price?
fragments.text: A specialised offer may meet their needs more closely and face fewer direct substitutes.

Market research reduces uncertainty by collecting and interpreting evidence about customers, competitors and markets. It does not remove risk: the quality of the decision depends on the question, sample, method, timing and how honestly the evidence is interpreted.

fragments.label: Market research
fragments.text: Collecting, analysing and interpreting information about a market, customer or marketing decision.

fragments.label: Primary research
fragments.text: New first-hand data collected for the business's specific research objective.

fragments.label: Secondary research
fragments.text: Existing data originally collected for another purpose and reused for the current decision.

fragments.label: Quantitative data
fragments.text: Numerical data that can be measured and statistically analysed.

fragments.label: Qualitative data
fragments.text: Non-numerical evidence about opinions, motives, perceptions and explanations.

fragments.label: Sample
fragments.text: A subset of a target population selected for research.

fragments.label: Sampling frame
fragments.text: A list or source from which a sample is selected.

fragments.label: Bias
fragments.text: A systematic influence that makes evidence unrepresentative or pushes results in a particular direction.

fragments.label: Reliability
fragments.text: The extent to which a method would produce consistent results if repeated.

fragments.label: Validity
fragments.text: The extent to which the research measures what the decision actually requires.
Purpose and research process

fragments.label: Purpose and research process
fragments.text: Research can estimate demand, identify segments, test price or packaging, understand dissatisfaction, track competitors and forecast change. A disciplined process defines the decision/problem, specifies information needed, sets budget and method, collects data, analyses patterns, reports limitations, acts and reviews.

fragments.label: Purpose and research process
fragments.text: A vague objective collects interesting data that may not support a decision.

fragments.label: Purpose and research process
fragments.text: Start with secondary data where useful, then use primary research to fill specific gaps.

fragments.label: Purpose and research process
fragments.text: Research cost should be proportionate to the value and reversibility of the decision.
Primary and secondary research

fragments.label: Primary and secondary research
fragments.text: Primary evidence is specific, current and confidential but costs time and money. Secondary evidence is faster, cheaper and useful for market scale or trends, but may be outdated, use different definitions or come from a biased source.

fragments.label: Primary and secondary research
fragments.text: Internal secondary sources: sales records, website analytics, complaints, loyalty data, financial and inventory records.

fragments.label: Primary and secondary research
fragments.text: External sources: government statistics, industry reports, trade associations, competitors, academic studies and commercial databases.

fragments.label: Primary and secondary research
fragments.text: Triangulation—using different sources and methods—can reveal inconsistencies and improve confidence.
Questionnaires and interviews

fragments.label: Questionnaires and interviews
fragments.text: Questionnaires can reach many respondents and standardised questions are easy to compare. Poor wording, low response, dishonest answers and self-selection can bias results. Interviews allow clarification, probing and observation of tone, but interviewer influence, cost and small samples can reduce generalisability.

fragments.label: Questionnaires and interviews
fragments.text: Avoid leading, loaded, double-barrelled, ambiguous and overly technical questions.

fragments.label: Questionnaires and interviews
fragments.text: Provide exhaustive, non-overlapping response options and a sensible scale.

fragments.label: Questionnaires and interviews
fragments.text: Pilot the instrument with a small group before full collection.

fragments.label: Questionnaires and interviews
fragments.text: Weak: 'Don't you agree our excellent new package is worth more?' Better: 'How likely are you to buy this package at $4.00?' followed by a balanced five-point scale.
Focus groups, observation and test marketing

fragments.label: Focus groups, observation and test marketing
fragments.text: Focus groups generate detailed reactions and interaction but dominant participants and moderator bias can distort findings. Observation records actual behaviour rather than claimed behaviour, yet cannot explain motives. Test marketing measures real response in a limited area, reducing national-launch risk but costing time and alerting competitors.

fragments.label: Focus groups, observation and test marketing
fragments.text: Match the method to the question: observation for store movement, interviews for motives, test markets for actual purchase response.

fragments.label: Focus groups, observation and test marketing
fragments.text: Ethical research protects consent, privacy and data security.
Quantitative and qualitative evidence

fragments.label: Quantitative and qualitative evidence
fragments.text: Quantitative evidence estimates how many, how often or how much and supports tables, averages and comparisons. Qualitative evidence explains why and helps discover ideas, language and motives. The methods are complementary: qualitative findings can design a questionnaire, while quantitative results test how widespread those findings are.

fragments.label: Quantitative and qualitative evidence
fragments.text: Large numerical datasets are not automatically valid; the wrong sample or measure can produce precise but misleading results.

fragments.label: Quantitative and qualitative evidence
fragments.text: Qualitative depth does not prove prevalence across the market.
Sampling methods

fragments.label: Sampling methods
fragments.text: Random sampling gives each member a known/equal chance when a complete frame exists. Stratified sampling selects in proportion to relevant groups, improving representation but requiring population data. Quota sampling instructs researchers to fill group targets quickly, but interviewer choice introduces bias. Convenience sampling is fast and cheap but often least representative.

fragments.label: Sampling methods
fragments.text: Sample size affects sampling error, but representativeness matters as much as size.

fragments.label: Sampling methods
fragments.text: The target population and sampling frame should match the market decision.

fragments.label: Sampling methods
fragments.text: Non-response can bias even a well-designed random sample if respondents differ from non-respondents.
Reliability, validity and bias

fragments.label: Reliability, validity and bias
fragments.text: Reliability improves with clear standardised questions, trained researchers and consistent coding. Validity improves when questions measure the actual decision and respondents understand and answer truthfully. Bias may come from wording, interviewer behaviour, location, timing, sample selection, non-response and sponsor interest.

fragments.label: Reliability, validity and bias
fragments.text: A result can be reliable but invalid—for example, a consistent survey of existing customers used to estimate non-customer demand.

fragments.label: Reliability, validity and bias
fragments.text: Report confidence and limitations rather than hiding uncertainty.
Information technology and data

fragments.label: Information technology and data
fragments.text: Online surveys, analytics, social listening, customer databases and automated dashboards collect data rapidly and cheaply and permit personalisation. They also create self-selection, duplicate responses, privacy, security and interpretation risks. Digital behaviour shows what occurred, not always why.

fragments.label: Information technology and data
fragments.text: Clean data, consistent definitions and access controls are essential.

fragments.label: Information technology and data
fragments.text: Combine behavioural analytics with targeted qualitative research before a major decision.
What makes data primary?

fragments.label: What makes data primary?
fragments.text: It is newly collected first-hand for the business's current research purpose.
Can secondary data be internal?

fragments.label: Can secondary data be internal?
fragments.text: Yes—sales, complaints, loyalty, website and inventory records are examples.
Why pilot a questionnaire?

fragments.label: Why pilot a questionnaire?
fragments.text: To identify unclear wording, missing options, timing and coding problems before full collection.
How does stratified sampling improve representation?

fragments.label: How does stratified sampling improve representation?
fragments.text: It selects respondents from relevant subgroups in proportions matching the population.
Can research be reliable but invalid?

fragments.label: Can research be reliable but invalid?
fragments.text: Yes; it may consistently measure the wrong population or concept.
What is the main limit of observation?

fragments.label: What is the main limit of observation?
fragments.text: It records behaviour but usually cannot explain motives.

The marketing mix coordinates product, price, promotion and place for a defined target market. Each decision changes the effectiveness of the others, so exam evaluation should test whether the whole mix is consistent with the objective, customer, competition, product stage, capacity and budget.

fragments.label: Marketing mix
fragments.text: The coordinated product, price, promotion and place decisions used to meet the needs of a target market.

fragments.label: Brand
fragments.text: A name, symbol, design or set of associations that identifies and differentiates an offer.

fragments.label: Product life cycle
fragments.text: The pattern of introduction, growth, maturity/saturation and decline that a product's sales may follow.

fragments.label: Extension strategy
fragments.text: A change intended to prolong a product's sales, such as repositioning, promotion, redesign or a new market.

fragments.label: Price skimming
fragments.text: Launching at a high price to earn high margins from less price-sensitive early buyers.

fragments.label: Penetration pricing
fragments.text: Launching at a low price to gain customers and market share quickly.

fragments.label: Price discrimination
fragments.text: Charging different customer groups different prices for the same or very similar product when resale can be limited.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.

fragments.label: Above-the-line promotion
fragments.text: Paid mass-media communication that the business does not fully control at the point of customer response.

fragments.label: Below-the-line promotion
fragments.text: Targeted promotional activity such as sales promotions, direct marketing, sponsorship or personal selling.

fragments.label: Channel of distribution
fragments.text: The route and intermediaries through which a product passes from producer to final customer.

fragments.label: Customer relationship marketing
fragments.text: Activities designed to build long-term customer satisfaction, loyalty and repeat purchases.
Product: benefits, differentiation and portfolio

fragments.label: Product: benefits, differentiation and portfolio
fragments.text: Customers buy benefits rather than technical features alone. Product decisions include function, quality, design, brand, packaging, service, warranty and range. Consumer products may be convenience, shopping or speciality goods; industrial products are bought for organisational use. A strong USP should solve a valued problem and be difficult to copy.

fragments.label: Product: benefits, differentiation and portfolio
fragments.text: Branding supports recognition, trust, repeat purchase and premium pricing but needs consistent quality and promotion.

fragments.label: Product: benefits, differentiation and portfolio
fragments.text: Packaging protects and informs as well as promotes; excessive packaging can increase cost and environmental criticism.

fragments.label: Product: benefits, differentiation and portfolio
fragments.text: A product portfolio spreads risk and shares brand/distribution resources, but too many variants increase complexity and cannibalisation.
Product life cycle

fragments.label: Product life cycle
fragments.text: Introduction usually has low sales, high launch promotion and possible losses. Growth brings rising sales and competitors. Maturity/saturation has high but slowing sales, intense competition and pressure to differentiate. Decline brings falling sales as needs or technology change. Cash flow and suitable mix decisions differ at each stage.

fragments.label: Product life cycle
fragments.text: Extension strategies include new users/markets, redesign, new uses, promotions, price changes and updated packaging.

fragments.label: Product life cycle
fragments.text: The life cycle is descriptive, not a fixed timetable; fashion, management action and external shocks alter the pattern.

fragments.label: Product life cycle
fragments.text: Businesses may withdraw a declining product, harvest it or retain it because it supports a range or niche.
Pricing methods

fragments.label: Pricing methods
fragments.text: Cost-plus adds a markup to unit cost and is simple but ignores willingness to pay and rivals. Competitive pricing follows market prices but can create price wars. Skimming suits distinctive innovation and recovers development cost, yet attracts rivals. Penetration builds trial/share but may signal low quality and make later increases difficult. Promotional/loss-leader pricing creates traffic but lowers immediate margin. Psychological pricing uses customer perception; price discrimination extracts different willingness to pay but requires separation and can be seen as unfair.

fragments.label: Pricing methods
