fragments.text: Contribution pricing accepts an order above variable cost so it contributes to fixed cost, but repeated low prices may fail to cover total cost.

fragments.label: Pricing methods
fragments.text: Choose using objective, costs, competition, brand, product stage, capacity and PED.
Price elasticity of demand

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: PED is normally negative because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions; exams often discuss its magnitude. If |PED| > 1, demand is elastic and a price fall tends to increase total revenue. If |PED| < 1, demand is inelastic and a price rise tends to increase total revenue, assuming other factors remain unchanged.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Demand is more elastic when close substitutes exist, the purchase is a large share of income, buyers have time to switch and loyalty is weak.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: It is more inelastic for necessities, addictive products, small expenditures, urgent needs and strongly differentiated brands.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: PED is an estimate and can change by price range, segment and time; revenue is not profit because cost also changes.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Price rises from $20 to $22 (+10%) and demand falls from 5,000 to 4,000 (−20%). PED = −20% ÷ 10% = −2, so demand is elastic. Revenue falls from $100,000 to $88,000.
Promotion objectives and methods

fragments.label: Promotion objectives and methods
fragments.text: Promotion informs, persuades, reminds and builds brand. Advertising can reach a large audience but is costly and hard to personalise. Sales promotions create short-run trial or clear inventory but may train customers to wait for deals. Personal selling explains complex products and builds relationships but has high cost per contact. Direct marketing is targeted but may be ignored; sponsorship transfers event associations but gives limited message control; public relations can be credible but coverage is uncertain.

fragments.label: Promotion objectives and methods
fragments.text: Select media using the target audience, message complexity, reach, frequency, cost, measurability and product stage.

fragments.label: Promotion objectives and methods
fragments.text: Evaluate using incremental sales/contribution, awareness, enquiries, conversion and retention—not reach alone.

fragments.label: Promotion objectives and methods
fragments.text: A promotional budget may be affordable, percentage-of-sales, competitor-based or objective-and-task; only the last starts from what must be achieved.
Place and distribution channels

fragments.label: Place and distribution channels
fragments.text: Direct distribution (producer → customer) gives control, customer data and no intermediary margin, but the producer funds selling, delivery, storage and reach. Retailers provide convenience, display and local access but take margin and control. Wholesalers break bulk and serve many small retailers, reducing the producer's logistics burden but adding distance from customers.

fragments.label: Place and distribution channels
fragments.text: Agents bring specialist or foreign-market knowledge without taking ownership of goods, in return for commission.

fragments.label: Place and distribution channels
fragments.text: Choose using perishability, purchase frequency, customer location, technical explanation, order size, desired control, competitor channels and cost.

fragments.label: Place and distribution channels
fragments.text: Omnichannel distribution should coordinate inventory, pricing and service across stores, websites and marketplaces.
Digital marketing and e-commerce

fragments.label: Digital marketing and e-commerce
fragments.text: Websites, search, email, social media, marketplaces and creators can target segments, measure response, update messages quickly and reach global customers. Direct online selling may reduce premises and intermediary cost. However, competition and price transparency rise, cyber/privacy risks matter, platform fees or algorithms create dependence, and customers cannot always inspect products.

fragments.label: Digital marketing and e-commerce
fragments.text: Viral reach can be cheap and rapid but the business cannot fully control the message or reaction.

fragments.label: Digital marketing and e-commerce
fragments.text: Use data responsibly and judge conversion, customer acquisition cost and repeat value rather than likes alone.
Relationship marketing and the 4Cs

fragments.label: Relationship marketing and the 4Cs
fragments.text: Relationship marketing aims to retain profitable customers through reliable quality, service, complaints recovery, useful communication, loyalty rewards and personalisation. Retention can cost less than constant acquisition and can generate referrals and data, but not every unprofitable customer should be retained at any cost.

fragments.label: Relationship marketing and the 4Cs
fragments.text: Customer solution corresponds to product; cost to customer includes time, delivery and use as well as price.

fragments.label: Relationship marketing and the 4Cs
fragments.text: Communication is two-way rather than promotion only; convenience looks at the whole buying and service journey.

fragments.label: Relationship marketing and the 4Cs
fragments.text: The 4Cs force the business to view the 4Ps from the customer's perspective.
Building an integrated mix

fragments.label: Building an integrated mix
fragments.text: A premium technical product needs quality, credible specialist promotion, selective or direct distribution and a price that supports its position. A mass convenience product needs accessible distribution, repeat availability, simple communication and a competitive price. Contradictions waste resources and confuse positioning.

fragments.label: Building an integrated mix
fragments.text: Check internal fit with finance, capacity, people and brand; check external fit with target needs, rivals and the environment.

fragments.label: Building an integrated mix
fragments.text: Change one element only after tracing its effect on the rest—for example, a promotion that doubles demand may cause stockouts and reputational damage.
What are the four Ps?

fragments.label: What are the four Ps?
fragments.text: Product, price, promotion and place.
When is demand price elastic?

fragments.label: When is demand price elastic?
fragments.text: When the absolute PED value is greater than 1, so quantity changes proportionately more than price.
Why can price skimming attract competitors?

fragments.label: Why can price skimming attract competitors?
fragments.text: High margins signal an attractive opportunity.
What is an extension strategy?

fragments.label: What is an extension strategy?
fragments.text: A change intended to prolong product sales, such as redesign, repositioning, promotion or a new market.
What is the main producer trade-off in direct distribution?

fragments.label: What is the main producer trade-off in direct distribution?
fragments.text: More control, data and retained margin versus responsibility for reach, selling, delivery, storage and returns.
How do the 4Cs change perspective?

fragments.label: How do the 4Cs change perspective?
fragments.text: They view product, price, promotion and place as customer solution, customer cost, communication and convenience.
Why does a revenue-maximising price not necessarily maximise profit?

fragments.label: Why does a revenue-maximising price not necessarily maximise profit?
fragments.text: Changing price and volume also changes variable cost, capacity use and possibly fixed cost.

Operations transforms inputs into goods and services that customers value. Exam answers should connect method, technology, labour and productivity decisions to capacity, unit cost, quality, flexibility and the ability to meet demand.

fragments.label: Operations management
fragments.text: Managing the resources, processes and systems that create and deliver goods and services.

fragments.label: Transformation process
fragments.text: Converting inputs such as materials, labour, information and capital into outputs.

fragments.label: Productivity
fragments.text: Output produced relative to the inputs used over a period.

fragments.label: Efficiency
fragments.text: Using inputs with minimum waste, time or cost.

fragments.label: Effectiveness
fragments.text: Achieving the intended objective or customer outcome.

fragments.label: Labour-intensive production
fragments.text: Operations in which human labour provides a high proportion of the productive input.

fragments.label: Capital-intensive production
fragments.text: Operations relying heavily on machinery, equipment and technology.

fragments.label: Job production
fragments.text: Producing a single or customised item to a customer's specific requirements.

fragments.label: Batch production
fragments.text: Producing a group of identical items before switching the process to another batch.

fragments.label: Flow production
fragments.text: Producing standardised output continuously through a sequence of connected stages.

fragments.label: Mass customisation
fragments.text: Using flexible technology and standard components to produce personalised variations at near mass-production cost.

fragments.label: Intellectual capital
fragments.text: Useful organisational knowledge embodied in employees, systems, data, processes and relationships.
The transformation process

fragments.label: The transformation process
fragments.text: Inputs include materials, land, labour, capital, information, time and ideas. Transformation may physically manufacture, transport, store, inform or provide an experience. Outputs include goods, services and waste. Feedback about quality, cost and customer satisfaction helps control the process.

fragments.label: The transformation process
fragments.text: Operations must deliver the required quantity, quality, cost, speed, dependability and flexibility.

fragments.label: The transformation process
fragments.text: An efficient operation can still be ineffective if it produces something customers do not want.

fragments.label: The transformation process
fragments.text: Marketing forecasts demand, HR supplies skills and finance funds assets and working capital; operations decisions cannot be isolated.
Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness

fragments.label: Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness
fragments.text: Higher labour productivity means more output per employee or labour hour. If wages and quality are controlled, labour cost per unit may fall. However, productivity can rise because of technology or product mix rather than greater employee effort, and output counts can hide quality or service differences.

fragments.label: Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness
fragments.text: Efficiency measures the input-output relationship; effectiveness measures whether the intended result was achieved.

fragments.label: Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness
fragments.text: A call centre can shorten calls efficiently but become less effective if problems remain unresolved.

fragments.label: Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness
fragments.text: Use multiple measures: productivity, unit cost, defects, delivery time, complaints and customer outcomes.

fragments.label: Productivity, efficiency and effectiveness
fragments.text: Output rises from 8,000 to 9,600 units while employees rise from 40 to 48. Productivity remains 200 units per employee, so the 20% output growth is not a productivity improvement.
Improving productivity

fragments.label: Improving productivity
fragments.text: Training, motivation, better layout, reliable materials, maintenance, standardised methods, automation, quality at source and improved information can raise output from existing inputs. The bottleneck must be diagnosed before investing.

fragments.label: Improving productivity
fragments.text: Training may reduce errors and increase flexibility but costs time and money.

fragments.label: Improving productivity
fragments.text: Automation can increase speed and consistency but creates fixed cost, maintenance, skills and obsolescence risks.

fragments.label: Improving productivity
fragments.text: Pressure to work faster may increase defects, accidents and turnover, reducing effective productivity.
Labour-intensive and capital-intensive operations

fragments.label: Labour-intensive and capital-intensive operations
fragments.text: Labour-intensive operations suit customisation, personal service, variable demand and settings where labour is available and equipment is costly. Capital-intensive operations suit large, stable volumes and standardisation, providing speed and consistency but requiring high investment and utilisation.

fragments.label: Labour-intensive and capital-intensive operations
fragments.text: Labour strengths: initiative, empathy, flexibility and easier custom work. Risks: wage cost, absence, variable quality and training time.

fragments.label: Labour-intensive and capital-intensive operations
fragments.text: Capital strengths: continuous operation, precision, standard quality and lower variable labour cost. Risks: high fixed cost, breakdowns, inflexibility and technological obsolescence.

fragments.label: Labour-intensive and capital-intensive operations
fragments.text: Most organisations use a mix: the question is which task should be automated and where human judgement creates more value.
Job production

fragments.label: Job production
fragments.text: Job production delivers a one-off or highly customised output, such as a tailored suit, consultancy project or custom machine. Skilled employees may gain satisfaction and customers may pay a premium, but planning is complex, production is slow and unit cost high.

fragments.label: Job production
fragments.text: Best where requirements vary, volume is low and differentiation supports price.

fragments.label: Job production
fragments.text: Errors are costly because work and materials may be unique.
Batch production

fragments.label: Batch production
fragments.text: Batch production balances variety with some repetition. Resources make a quantity of one design, then are reset for another. It suits bakery products, clothing variants and components where demand is regular but not large enough for continuous flow.

fragments.label: Batch production
fragments.text: Strengths: product variety, some specialisation and less total exposure if one product's demand falls.

fragments.label: Batch production
fragments.text: Weaknesses: setup/changeover downtime, work-in-progress and inventory, scheduling complexity and inconsistent batches.

fragments.label: Batch production
fragments.text: Larger batches reduce changeovers but increase inventory risk.
Flow production and mass customisation

fragments.label: Flow production and mass customisation
fragments.text: Flow production gives rapid, high-volume, standardised output and can exploit automation and purchasing economies. A breakdown at one connected stage can stop the line, work may be repetitive and high fixed cost makes low utilisation expensive. Mass customisation uses modular designs and flexible computer-controlled systems to combine variety with scale.

fragments.label: Flow production and mass customisation
fragments.text: Flow needs stable, high demand and reliable inputs.

fragments.label: Flow production and mass customisation
fragments.text: Mass customisation requires accurate customer data, modular components, skilled systems and coordinated supply; too many choices can destroy efficiency.
Technology and process innovation

fragments.label: Technology and process innovation
fragments.text: CAD speeds accurate design and modification; CAM controls production equipment; automation performs processes with limited human intervention; information systems coordinate demand, inventory and scheduling. Technology can improve productivity, flexibility, quality and speed and enable new products.

fragments.label: Technology and process innovation
fragments.text: Costs include purchase, integration, training, cybersecurity, maintenance, downtime, redundancy and rapid obsolescence.

fragments.label: Technology and process innovation
fragments.text: A technological investment is worthwhile only if additional contribution and savings justify the cost and risk.

fragments.label: Technology and process innovation
fragments.text: Employee consultation and retraining can reduce resistance and preserve useful knowledge.
Choosing an operations method

fragments.label: Choosing an operations method
fragments.text: Use product uniqueness, target volume, demand stability, finance, required quality, delivery speed, workforce skills and technology. Then consider whether the method supports marketing promises and cash-flow capacity.

fragments.label: Choosing an operations method
fragments.text: Changing method causes disruption, retraining, inventory movement and possible redundancy before benefits arrive.

fragments.label: Choosing an operations method
fragments.text: Flexibility has value under uncertain demand, but spare capability and multi-skilled labour also cost money.
What is the difference between efficiency and effectiveness?

fragments.label: What is the difference between efficiency and effectiveness?
fragments.text: Efficiency minimises input waste; effectiveness achieves the intended objective or customer outcome.
How is labour productivity calculated?

fragments.label: How is labour productivity calculated?
fragments.text: Output in a period divided by employees or labour hours, as specified.
Which production method suits one-off customised output?

fragments.label: Which production method suits one-off customised output?
fragments.text: Job production.
What causes downtime in batch production?

fragments.label: What causes downtime in batch production?
fragments.text: Equipment and processes must be changed or reset between batches.
Why does flow production need stable demand?

fragments.label: Why does flow production need stable demand?
fragments.text: High fixed cost and specialised capacity become expensive when output and utilisation are low.
What allows mass customisation?

fragments.label: What allows mass customisation?
fragments.text: Flexible technology, modular/standard components, accurate customer information and coordinated processes.

Inventory protects production and sales against uncertainty but ties up cash and creates storage, damage and obsolescence costs. The correct level depends on demand variability, lead time, supplier reliability, perishability and the cost of a stockout.

fragments.label: Inventory
fragments.text: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods held by a business.

fragments.label: Raw-material inventory
fragments.text: Inputs held before they enter production.

fragments.label: Work in progress
fragments.text: Partly completed output still within the production process.

fragments.label: Finished-goods inventory
fragments.text: Completed products awaiting sale or distribution.

fragments.label: Buffer inventory
fragments.text: The minimum safety stock intended to absorb unexpected demand or delivery delay.

fragments.label: Reorder level
fragments.text: The inventory level at which a replenishment order is placed.

fragments.label: Lead time
fragments.text: The time between placing an order and receiving it ready for use.

fragments.label: Reorder quantity
fragments.text: The amount ordered each time inventory reaches the reorder level.

fragments.label: Just in time
fragments.text: An inventory system in which materials arrive and output is completed only when needed, minimising inventory held.

fragments.label: Stockout
fragments.text: A shortage in which the business cannot meet production or customer demand from available inventory.
Why businesses hold inventory

fragments.label: Why businesses hold inventory
fragments.text: Raw materials prevent production stopping when deliveries vary; work in progress connects stages with different speeds; finished goods allow immediate customer delivery and absorb demand peaks. Bulk orders may also earn discounts and protect against expected price rises.

fragments.label: Why businesses hold inventory
fragments.text: The value of insurance stock is greater where stockouts stop an entire process or permanently lose customers.

fragments.label: Why businesses hold inventory
fragments.text: Perishable, fashionable or technology products face high obsolescence risk, so excess inventory is especially costly.
Costs and risks of inventory

fragments.label: Costs and risks of inventory
fragments.text: Inventory ties up working capital that could pay debts or earn a return elsewhere. It requires space, handling, insurance, security and sometimes refrigeration; it may deteriorate, become obsolete or be stolen. More inventory can therefore weaken liquidity even when it appears as an asset.

fragments.label: Costs and risks of inventory
fragments.text: Ordering too little increases delivery cost and stockout risk.

fragments.label: Costs and risks of inventory
fragments.text: Ordering too much lowers order frequency but raises average inventory and cash tied up.

fragments.label: Costs and risks of inventory
fragments.text: The objective is an economic service level, not automatically zero inventory.
Reading an inventory-control chart

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: Inventory falls as materials are used or products sold. At the reorder level a new order is placed. During lead time, inventory continues falling toward buffer stock. When the reorder quantity arrives, the vertical rise takes inventory toward its maximum level.

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: Reorder level must cover expected usage during lead time plus an allowance for uncertainty.

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: A steeper downward line means faster usage; a wider horizontal lead-time gap means slower delivery.

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: If demand or lead time increases, an unchanged reorder level raises stockout risk.

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: A delayed delivery is shown by inventory continuing below the expected arrival point, using buffer stock.

fragments.label: Reading an inventory-control chart
fragments.text: Usage is 80 units per day, lead time is 5 days and desired buffer inventory is 120 units. Reorder level = (80 × 5) + 120 = 520 units.
Setting control levels

fragments.label: Setting control levels
fragments.text: Maximum level is constrained by storage, cash, perishability and order size. Buffer inventory depends on uncertainty and the cost of disruption. Reorder level depends on usage during lead time plus buffer stock. Reorder quantity balances order/delivery cost against holding cost and supplier discounts.

fragments.label: Setting control levels
fragments.text: Reliable real-time data reduces uncertainty but cannot prevent physical supply disruption.

fragments.label: Setting control levels
fragments.text: Seasonality should change expected usage and may require planned pre-building of inventory.
Just-in-time inventory management

fragments.label: Just-in-time inventory management
fragments.text: JIT seeks continuous flow with raw materials arriving only when needed, little work in progress and finished goods moving quickly to customers. It reduces working capital, storage, waste and hidden defects and frees space, but makes interruption immediately visible and potentially severe.

fragments.label: Just-in-time inventory management
fragments.text: Requirements: reliable nearby suppliers and transport, consistent quality, accurate demand information, disciplined scheduling, flexible multi-skilled employees and dependable equipment/IT.

fragments.label: Just-in-time inventory management
fragments.text: Frequent small deliveries may increase transport cost and environmental impact.

fragments.label: Just-in-time inventory management
fragments.text: A supplier failure, traffic disruption or sudden demand spike can stop production and damage customer trust.
Improving inventory performance

fragments.label: Improving inventory performance
fragments.text: Use accurate forecasts, point-of-sale data, inventory records, barcode/RFID systems, supplier performance measures, ABC prioritisation, quality at source and regular review of slow-moving lines. Work with suppliers on shared forecasts and delivery reliability rather than simply transferring risk.

fragments.label: Improving inventory performance
fragments.text: Reduce buffer inventory only after lead-time variability and defect rates have fallen.

fragments.label: Improving inventory performance
fragments.text: Dispose of obsolete stock, but judge discounts against brand effects and recovered cash.

fragments.label: Improving inventory performance
fragments.text: Track stockout frequency, inventory days/turnover, waste and service level together.
What are the three broad forms of inventory?

fragments.label: What are the three broad forms of inventory?
fragments.text: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods.
What triggers a replenishment order?

fragments.label: What triggers a replenishment order?
fragments.text: Inventory reaching the reorder level.
What happens during lead time?

fragments.label: What happens during lead time?
fragments.text: Inventory continues to be used between placing and receiving an order.
Why hold buffer inventory?

fragments.label: Why hold buffer inventory?
fragments.text: To absorb unexpected demand or delivery delay and reduce stockout risk.
What does JIT require from suppliers?

fragments.label: What does JIT require from suppliers?
fragments.text: Frequent, reliable, correctly timed deliveries of consistent quality.
Why can inventory weaken liquidity?

fragments.label: Why can inventory weaken liquidity?
fragments.text: Cash is tied up in goods and may not be available when short-term payments fall due.

Capacity utilisation compares actual output with potential output. Both unused and overloaded capacity create costs, so managers need to judge whether demand is temporary or permanent before changing resources or outsourcing work.

fragments.label: Capacity
fragments.text: The maximum output a business can produce in a period with its current resources under normal conditions.

fragments.label: Capacity utilisation
fragments.text: Actual output as a percentage of maximum potential output.

fragments.label: Full capacity
fragments.text: Operating at or very close to the maximum sustainable output of current resources.

fragments.label: Excess capacity
fragments.text: A situation in which actual output is below the level the organisation is equipped to produce.

fragments.label: Capacity shortage
fragments.text: Insufficient current resources to meet demand at the required time or standard.

fragments.label: Rationalisation
fragments.text: Reorganising operations—often closing or combining sites and reducing resources—to remove excess capacity and lower cost.

fragments.label: Outsourcing
fragments.text: Contracting an external organisation to perform an activity previously or potentially undertaken inside the business.

fragments.label: Business-process outsourcing
fragments.text: Contracting a business function such as payroll, customer support, IT or logistics to an external specialist.

fragments.label: Core activity
fragments.text: An activity central to the organisation's customer value and competitive advantage.
Calculating and interpreting capacity utilisation

fragments.label: Calculating and interpreting capacity utilisation
fragments.text: Capacity utilisation shows how intensely current facilities, equipment and labour are being used. A higher percentage may spread fixed cost across more units; a low percentage signals idle resources. The theoretical maximum may differ from sustainable practical capacity because maintenance, breaks, product mix and quality requirements consume time.

fragments.label: Calculating and interpreting capacity utilisation
fragments.text: Always state the percentage and what it means in units or spare capacity where possible.

fragments.label: Calculating and interpreting capacity utilisation
fragments.text: Compare over time and with demand forecasts; one high month may be seasonal rather than permanent.

fragments.label: Calculating and interpreting capacity utilisation
fragments.text: A plant capable of 24,000 units per month produces 18,000. Capacity utilisation = 18,000 ÷ 24,000 × 100 = 75%, leaving 6,000 units (25%) unused.
High or full capacity

fragments.label: High or full capacity
fragments.text: High utilisation can lower average fixed cost, signal strong demand and support employee security. It also leaves little room for rush orders, maintenance, training or error. Continuous pressure may create overtime cost, breakdowns, queues, quality failure and missed delivery.

fragments.label: High or full capacity
fragments.text: A hotel may value a high occupancy rate, yet 100% occupancy prevents accepting profitable late bookings and intensifies service pressure.

fragments.label: High or full capacity
fragments.text: Optimal utilisation is often below 100% when flexibility and reliability have value.
Excess capacity

fragments.label: Excess capacity
fragments.text: Low utilisation raises fixed cost per unit and may demotivate employees or signal weak demand. Short-term causes include seasonality, a temporary downturn or maintenance; long-term causes include structural demand decline, lost competitiveness, excess expansion or new technology.

fragments.label: Excess capacity
fragments.text: Short-term responses: flexible hours, maintenance/training, temporary promotions, pre-building non-perishable inventory or temporary closure.

fragments.label: Excess capacity
fragments.text: Long-term responses: new products/markets, sell or lease assets, close capacity, retrain/redeploy staff or relocate.

fragments.label: Excess capacity
fragments.text: Producing unwanted inventory does not solve excess capacity; it converts spare capacity into tied-up cash and holding cost.
Capacity shortages

fragments.label: Capacity shortages
fragments.text: A shortage can be handled through overtime, additional shifts, temporary staff, improved productivity, rescheduling, queues/waiting lists, price changes, outsourcing or investment in new capacity. Short-term flexibility is faster; permanent expansion can reduce long-run unit cost but is risky if demand falls.

fragments.label: Capacity shortages
fragments.text: Use forecasts and contribution from lost orders to value the shortage.

fragments.label: Capacity shortages
fragments.text: Price increases may ration demand and raise contribution, but can damage market share and relationships.

fragments.label: Capacity shortages
fragments.text: New capacity needs finance, employees, permissions and lead time.
Why outsource

fragments.label: Why outsource
fragments.text: Outsourcing may give rapid flexible capacity, specialist expertise, lower cost and access to technology while management focuses on core activities. It converts some fixed cost into variable contractual cost and can avoid risky investment for temporary demand.

fragments.label: Why outsource
fragments.text: Examples include overflow production, delivery, payroll, IT support, call centres and specialist design.

fragments.label: Why outsource
fragments.text: The decision should compare total cost, including contracting, monitoring, transport, coordination and failure—not wage rates alone.
Outsourcing risks and control

fragments.label: Outsourcing risks and control
fragments.text: The business loses some direct control over quality, delivery, data and employment practices. Dependence on a supplier can create disruption or bargaining risk; hidden knowledge may leak; customers may dislike remote service; internal employees may lose jobs or morale.

fragments.label: Outsourcing risks and control
fragments.text: Set service-level measures, quality standards, data/security requirements, escalation processes and exit provisions.

fragments.label: Outsourcing risks and control
fragments.text: Retain strategic knowledge and alternative supply where failure would threaten the whole business.

fragments.label: Outsourcing risks and control
fragments.text: A cheap supplier is not low cost if defects, delays and reputational harm are substantial.
Make-or-buy judgement

fragments.label: Make-or-buy judgement
fragments.text: Keep an activity inside when it is a core source of differentiation, contains sensitive knowledge, needs close coordination or suppliers are unreliable. Outsource when specialist scale/skill, flexible volume and lower total cost outweigh control and dependence risks.

fragments.label: Make-or-buy judgement
fragments.text: Assess the time horizon: outsourcing may bridge a peak while investment may suit permanent growth.

fragments.label: Make-or-buy judgement
fragments.text: Consider stakeholder impact, reversibility, contract enforcement, supplier financial health and fit with brand promises.
How is capacity utilisation calculated?

fragments.label: How is capacity utilisation calculated?
fragments.text: Actual output divided by maximum possible output, multiplied by 100.
Why can full capacity raise unit cost rather than lower it?

fragments.label: Why can full capacity raise unit cost rather than lower it?
fragments.text: Overtime, congestion, errors, breakdowns and missed maintenance may outweigh fixed-cost spreading.
What is excess capacity?

fragments.label: What is excess capacity?
fragments.text: Actual output below what existing resources are capable of producing.
Name two flexible responses to a temporary capacity shortage.

fragments.label: Name two flexible responses to a temporary capacity shortage.
fragments.text: Examples include overtime, extra shifts, temporary staff, outsourcing, rescheduling or a waiting list.
Why might outsourcing convert fixed cost to variable cost?

fragments.label: Why might outsourcing convert fixed cost to variable cost?
fragments.text: The business pays the supplier for work used rather than owning and staffing permanent capacity.
When should an activity usually stay in-house?

fragments.label: When should an activity usually stay in-house?
fragments.text: When it is core to differentiation, sensitive, tightly integrated or too risky to depend on an external supplier.

Finance is needed before trading begins, during daily operations and when the business changes or grows. The central exam distinction is between profit and cash: a profitable business can still become illiquid if the timing of receipts and payments is poorly managed.

fragments.label: Finance
fragments.text: Funds required to start, operate, invest in and grow a business.

fragments.label: Start-up capital
fragments.text: Finance required before and during launch to acquire initial assets and fund operations until receipts are sufficient.

fragments.label: Working capital
fragments.text: Finance available for day-to-day operations; in accounting terms, current assets minus current liabilities.

fragments.label: Capital expenditure
fragments.text: Spending on non-current assets expected to benefit the business for more than one year.

fragments.label: Revenue expenditure
fragments.text: Spending on day-to-day expenses and items consumed within normal operations.

fragments.label: Liquidity
fragments.text: The ability to meet short-term debts and payments when they fall due.

fragments.label: Illiquidity
fragments.text: Insufficient available cash or near-cash resources to meet immediate obligations.

fragments.label: Liquidation
fragments.text: The legal process of closing a business and selling its assets to pay creditors.

fragments.label: Profit
fragments.text: The surplus of total revenue over total cost during a period.

fragments.label: Cash flow
fragments.text: Cash received and paid by a business over a period.
Why new businesses need finance

fragments.label: Why new businesses need finance
fragments.text: Before receiving reliable sales cash, a start-up may need premises deposits, equipment, technology, licences, research, initial inventory, recruitment, training, launch promotion and professional fees. It also needs a working-capital buffer for wages, rent, utilities and suppliers during low early sales or customer credit periods.

fragments.label: Why new businesses need finance
fragments.text: Underestimating start-up cost can force emergency borrowing on poor terms.

fragments.label: Why new businesses need finance
fragments.text: Timing matters: equipment may be a one-off capital need while several months of wages are recurring revenue expenditure.

fragments.label: Why new businesses need finance
fragments.text: Contingency finance recognises that forecasts are uncertain, but unused borrowing can still cost interest or fees.
Why established businesses need finance

fragments.label: Why established businesses need finance
fragments.text: Existing firms need finance to replace assets, expand capacity, enter markets, develop products, acquire another business, fund seasonal inventory, survive a temporary cash shortage or restructure. The purpose determines suitable duration and risk.

fragments.label: Why established businesses need finance
fragments.text: Match long-lived assets with long-term finance so repayment is spread across the benefit period.

fragments.label: Why established businesses need finance
fragments.text: Use short-term finance for temporary working-capital timing gaps, not permanent losses.

fragments.label: Why established businesses need finance
fragments.text: Growth often increases finance needs before generating cash: more inventory, employees and credit sales must be funded.
Start-up and working capital

fragments.label: Start-up and working capital
fragments.text: Start-up capital includes the initial non-current assets and cash needed to reach normal trading. Working capital cycles through cash, inventory, sales and customer receipts while short-term payments to suppliers and employees fall due. Too little working capital interrupts operations; too much may indicate idle cash, slow inventory or weak credit control.

fragments.label: Start-up and working capital
fragments.text: Inventory is a current asset but may be slow to sell or lose value.

fragments.label: Start-up and working capital
fragments.text: Trade receivables are recorded assets but do not pay bills until customers pay.

fragments.label: Start-up and working capital
fragments.text: Trade credit from suppliers delays cash outflow but creates a current liability.
Capital and revenue expenditure

fragments.label: Capital and revenue expenditure
fragments.text: Capital expenditure buys or improves long-term productive assets such as premises, machinery, vehicles or major systems. Revenue expenditure keeps the business operating, including wages, rent, utilities, routine repairs, materials and promotion. The same category is not determined only by price: purpose and duration of benefit matter.

fragments.label: Capital and revenue expenditure
fragments.text: A new delivery vehicle is capital expenditure; its fuel and routine servicing are revenue expenditure.

fragments.label: Capital and revenue expenditure
fragments.text: Capital decisions often require larger, longer-term finance and appraisal; revenue needs recur and are managed through working capital.
Cash and profit are different

fragments.label: Cash and profit are different
fragments.text: Credit sales increase revenue and may increase profit before cash arrives. Buying an asset creates a cash outflow but is not normally treated as a full immediate operating cost in profit. Borrowing creates a cash inflow but is not sales revenue; repaying loan principal is a cash outflow but not a cost of earning current sales. Owner drawings/dividends also use cash.

fragments.label: Cash and profit are different
fragments.text: A profitable fast-growing firm can fail if customers pay slowly while suppliers and employees require earlier payment.

fragments.label: Cash and profit are different
fragments.text: A loss-making firm may temporarily show positive cash flow after a loan or asset sale, but the underlying model remains weak.

fragments.label: Cash and profit are different
fragments.text: Always identify whether the item changes cash, profit, both or neither in the period.
Liquidity and business survival

fragments.label: Liquidity and business survival
fragments.text: Liquidity is about timing and access, not only total asset value. A firm unable to pay a supplier, employee, tax authority or lender may lose essential inputs, face legal action or be forced into liquidation even if its property and equipment exceed its debts.

fragments.label: Liquidity and business survival
fragments.text: Forecast cash by period and identify the size and duration of the maximum shortage.

fragments.label: Liquidity and business survival
fragments.text: Improve credit control and inventory conversion before relying only on new debt.

fragments.label: Liquidity and business survival
fragments.text: Maintain stakeholder trust: early negotiation is usually better than breaking payment promises.
Estimating the finance requirement

fragments.label: Estimating the finance requirement
fragments.text: Calculate what will be paid, when it will be paid, when customer cash is expected and what contingency is needed. Separate fixed-asset cost from working capital and distinguish a one-off shortage from a recurring operating deficit.

fragments.label: Estimating the finance requirement
fragments.text: Purpose: asset, start-up, seasonal inventory, temporary gap or loss recovery.

fragments.label: Estimating the finance requirement
fragments.text: Amount: include installation, training, tax, initial losses and contingency, not purchase price alone.

fragments.label: Estimating the finance requirement
fragments.text: Duration: match the finance term to the period of benefit and cash generation.

fragments.label: Estimating the finance requirement
fragments.text: Risk: test lower sales, later receipts and higher costs before deciding the safe commitment.
How is working capital calculated?

fragments.label: How is working capital calculated?
fragments.text: Current assets minus current liabilities.
Why can credit sales create profit before cash?

fragments.label: Why can credit sales create profit before cash?
fragments.text: Revenue is recognised when the sale occurs, while customer payment may arrive later.
Give one capital and one revenue expenditure example for a vehicle.

fragments.label: Give one capital and one revenue expenditure example for a vehicle.
fragments.text: Buying the vehicle is capital expenditure; fuel or routine servicing is revenue expenditure.
Why is inventory not equivalent to cash?

fragments.label: Why is inventory not equivalent to cash?
fragments.text: It must first be sold and collected, may take time and may not realise its recorded value.
Can a loan improve cash without improving profit?

fragments.label: Can a loan improve cash without improving profit?
fragments.text: Yes. It is a financing inflow, not revenue earned from trading.
What three dimensions should define a finance need?

fragments.label: What three dimensions should define a finance need?
fragments.text: Purpose, amount and duration, with risk/timing also tested.

No source of finance is universally best. A recommendation must match the purpose, amount and time period, then weigh cost, repayment, cash-flow risk, security, ownership and availability for the specific legal form and business.

fragments.label: Internal finance
fragments.text: Funds generated from within the business or its owners rather than an outside provider.

fragments.label: External finance
fragments.text: Funds provided by an outside individual or organisation.

fragments.label: Retained profit
fragments.text: Profit kept in the business after tax and owner distributions for reinvestment.

fragments.label: Equity finance
fragments.text: Permanent capital raised in exchange for ownership shares.

fragments.label: Debt finance
fragments.text: Borrowed finance that normally requires interest and repayment.

fragments.label: Overdraft
fragments.text: Permission to withdraw more from a bank account than its balance, up to an agreed limit.

fragments.label: Trade credit
fragments.text: A supplier's agreement allowing the buyer to pay after delivery.

fragments.label: Debt factoring
fragments.text: Selling trade receivables to a specialist for immediate cash at a discount, often with collection services.

fragments.label: Leasing
fragments.text: Paying to use an asset owned by another organisation for an agreed period.

fragments.label: Hire purchase
fragments.text: Obtaining an asset through a deposit and instalments, with ownership usually passing after the final payment.

fragments.label: Venture capital
fragments.text: Equity investment and often expertise supplied to a high-risk business with strong growth potential.

fragments.label: Crowdfunding
fragments.text: Raising relatively small amounts from many people through a platform, using donation, reward, lending or equity models.

fragments.label: Microfinance
fragments.text: Small-scale financial services for entrepreneurs who lack access to conventional banking.

fragments.label: Collateral
fragments.text: An asset pledged to a lender that may be claimed if the borrower fails to repay.
Internal sources

fragments.label: Internal sources
fragments.text: Retained profit has no mandatory interest or repayment and preserves control, but is unavailable to start-ups, may be insufficient and has the opportunity cost of lower owner distributions or reserves. Selling unused assets releases tied-up capital and may reduce maintenance, but takes time and removes future capacity. Reducing inventory releases cash but can create stockouts. Owner funds are quick and signal commitment but increase personal exposure.

fragments.label: Internal sources
fragments.text: Internal does not mean costless: every use has an alternative and may reduce liquidity.

fragments.label: Internal sources
fragments.text: Sale and leaseback raises cash from an asset while retaining use, but creates recurring lease payments and gives up ownership.
Share and venture capital

fragments.label: Share and venture capital
fragments.text: A company can issue shares for permanent finance with no compulsory repayment, supporting risky long-term investment. Existing control and profit are diluted, investors expect dividends/capital growth and public issues involve disclosure and cost. Venture capital can add expertise, contacts and risk-bearing funds to a high-growth venture but demands significant ownership, influence and an eventual exit.

fragments.label: Share and venture capital
fragments.text: Only companies issue shares; a private company cannot offer shares to the general public.

fragments.label: Share and venture capital
fragments.text: A rights issue offers existing shareholders the opportunity to buy new shares, helping reduce unwanted control dilution.

fragments.label: Share and venture capital
fragments.text: Equity is useful where early cash flow cannot safely support fixed interest and repayment.
Loans, long-term debt and overdrafts

fragments.label: Loans, long-term debt and overdrafts
fragments.text: A term loan gives a known sum and repayment period and preserves ownership, but interest, repayment, covenants and collateral increase risk. Debentures or long-term loan securities can raise large, long-duration finance for companies. An overdraft is flexible for fluctuating short-term needs because interest is charged on the amount used, but rates may vary and the facility can be reduced or recalled.

fragments.label: Loans, long-term debt and overdrafts
fragments.text: Debt is more dangerous where existing borrowing is high or cash flow is volatile because interest must be paid even without profit.

fragments.label: Loans, long-term debt and overdrafts
fragments.text: A fixed long-term asset should not normally depend on an overdraft that can be withdrawn at short notice.
Trade credit and debt factoring

fragments.label: Trade credit and debt factoring
fragments.text: Trade credit delays supplier payment, matching cash outflow more closely to sale receipts. It may be easy and interest-free within terms, but late payment loses discounts, damages trust and can stop supply. Factoring converts receivables to immediate cash and may outsource collection, but the business receives less than face value and customer relationships may be affected.

fragments.label: Trade credit and debt factoring
fragments.text: Both sources address working-capital timing rather than creating profitable demand.

fragments.label: Trade credit and debt factoring
fragments.text: Good credit control may be cheaper than permanent use of factoring.
Asset finance: leasing and hire purchase

fragments.label: Asset finance: leasing and hire purchase
fragments.text: Leasing avoids a large purchase outflow, may include maintenance and eases upgrades, but the user may pay more over time and does not own the asset. Hire purchase spreads payments and normally ends in ownership, but requires a deposit and interest and the asset may be repossessed after missed instalments.

fragments.label: Asset finance: leasing and hire purchase
fragments.text: Lease technology prone to obsolescence or needed for a limited period.

fragments.label: Asset finance: leasing and hire purchase
fragments.text: Buy/hire-purchase an asset with long useful life and high utilisation when ownership benefits outweigh financing cost.
Grants, crowdfunding and microfinance

fragments.label: Grants, crowdfunding and microfinance
fragments.text: Grants/subsidies need no repayment but are limited, competitive and conditional. Crowdfunding can test demand and build publicity, but platform fees, public disclosure, campaign work and failure risk remain; the legal obligation depends on donation, reward, debt or equity form. Microfinance provides small loans and services where conventional collateral is unavailable, but amounts are limited and rates/repayment still matter.

fragments.label: Grants, crowdfunding and microfinance
fragments.text: Do not call every crowdfunding contribution a donation.

fragments.label: Grants, crowdfunding and microfinance
fragments.text: Conditions must fit the business: a location grant is poor finance if moving harms customers or supply.
Matching duration and purpose

fragments.label: Matching duration and purpose
fragments.text: Short-term finance—overdraft, trade credit and factoring—suits temporary working-capital gaps. Medium-term loans, hire purchase or leasing may suit vehicles and equipment. Long-term loans, shares, retained profit, debentures or venture capital suit expansion and long-lived assets.

fragments.label: Matching duration and purpose
fragments.text: Maturity matching reduces refinancing risk and avoids paying long-term finance cost for a very short need.

fragments.label: Matching duration and purpose
fragments.text: A permanent trading loss should be corrected operationally rather than repeatedly covered by short-term borrowing.
Choosing and justifying a source

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: Use purpose, duration, amount, existing debt/gearing, cash-flow reliability, interest and fees, security, legal form, control, speed, flexibility and availability. Then compare the two strongest realistic options and give a conditional judgement.

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: A new sole trader cannot issue shares and may lack retained profit or collateral.

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: A profitable established company may fund moderate investment internally to preserve control.

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: A risky innovation with delayed cash generation may suit equity more than fixed loan repayments.

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: The cheapest quoted source may not be best after control, flexibility and failure risk.

fragments.label: Choosing and justifying a source
fragments.text: Need: $500,000 machine for eight years. Option A: long-term loan preserves ownership but creates fixed repayments. Option B: lease reduces initial cash and obsolescence risk but may cost more overall. Choose after applying cash reliability, technology life and control priorities.
What finance providers examine

fragments.label: What finance providers examine
fragments.text: Banks assess the amount and purpose, business plan, cash-flow forecast, past/forecast profit, existing borrowing, owner contribution, collateral, credit history and management experience. Equity investors examine market growth, competitive advantage, management team, scalability, forecasts, valuation, risks, governance and route to return.

fragments.label: What finance providers examine
fragments.text: Evidence reduces information risk but forecasts remain uncertain.

fragments.label: What finance providers examine
fragments.text: A strong application explains downside scenarios and how repayments or investor returns remain credible.
Why is retained profit not costless?

fragments.label: Why is retained profit not costless?
fragments.text: It has an opportunity cost and may reduce dividends, reserves or funds for another project.
What is the main difference between equity and debt?

fragments.label: What is the main difference between equity and debt?
fragments.text: Equity exchanges ownership for permanent capital; debt requires interest/repayment but normally preserves ownership.
When is an overdraft suitable?

fragments.label: When is an overdraft suitable?
fragments.text: For a short, fluctuating working-capital shortage with a credible near-term inflow.
How does factoring improve cash flow?

fragments.label: How does factoring improve cash flow?
fragments.text: It converts receivables into immediate cash at a discount and may transfer collection work.
How does hire purchase differ from leasing?

fragments.label: How does hire purchase differ from leasing?
fragments.text: Hire purchase normally ends in ownership after instalments; leasing pays for use while another party owns the asset.
What evidence does a lender prioritise?

fragments.label: What evidence does a lender prioritise?
fragments.text: Repayment cash flow, purpose, forecasts, existing debt, owner commitment, collateral, credit history and management ability.
Name five finance-choice factors.

fragments.label: Name five finance-choice factors.
fragments.text: Purpose, duration, amount, cost, cash risk, control, security, legal form and availability are valid factors.

Cash-flow forecasts organise expected cash receipts and payments by time period so managers can predict shortages and act early. Marks come from correct calculations plus interpretation: identify when, why and by how much cash is short, then judge a realistic response.

fragments.label: Cash inflow
fragments.text: Cash received by the business during a period.

fragments.label: Cash outflow
fragments.text: Cash paid by the business during a period.

fragments.label: Net cash flow
fragments.text: Total cash inflows minus total cash outflows for a period.

fragments.label: Opening cash balance
fragments.text: Cash available at the start of a period, equal to the previous period's closing balance.

fragments.label: Closing cash balance
fragments.text: Opening balance plus net cash flow at the end of a period.

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast
fragments.text: An estimate of future cash inflows, outflows and balances arranged by period.

fragments.label: Trade receivable
fragments.text: A customer that owes the business money after buying on credit, or the amount owed.

fragments.label: Trade payable
fragments.text: A supplier that the business owes after buying on credit, or the amount owed.

fragments.label: Bad debt
fragments.text: A receivable unlikely to be collected.

fragments.label: Overtrading
fragments.text: Expanding sales and operations faster than available working capital can support.
Cash-flow forecast structure

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast structure
fragments.text: List cash inflows, total them, list cash outflows and total them. Net cash flow is total inflows minus total outflows. Add net cash flow to opening balance to obtain closing balance. The closing balance automatically becomes the next period's opening balance.

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast structure
fragments.text: A negative net cash flow does not always create a negative closing balance if enough cash was available at the start.

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast structure
fragments.text: A positive net flow can still leave a negative closing balance after a severe earlier shortage.

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast structure
fragments.text: Use brackets or a minus sign consistently and carry balances forward exactly.

fragments.label: Cash-flow forecast structure
fragments.text: Opening balance $4,000; inflows $18,500; outflows $23,000. Net cash flow = −$4,500. Closing balance = $4,000 − $4,500 = −$500, so at least $500 plus a safety buffer is needed before period end.
Typical inflows and outflows

fragments.label: Typical inflows and outflows
fragments.text: Inflows include cash sales, receipts from credit customers, owner capital, loans, share issues, grants and asset sales. Outflows include cash purchases, supplier payments, wages, rent, utilities, promotion, tax, asset purchases, interest, loan repayment and owner withdrawals/dividends.

fragments.label: Typical inflows and outflows
fragments.text: Classify by when cash moves, not when the sale or cost is recorded for profit.

fragments.label: Typical inflows and outflows
fragments.text: A loan is a cash inflow but not trading revenue; an asset purchase is a cash outflow but not normally a full immediate operating cost.
Uses of cash-flow forecasts

fragments.label: Uses of cash-flow forecasts
fragments.text: Start-ups estimate finance needed and timing; managers plan payments, negotiate overdrafts, schedule investment and test decisions; banks judge borrowing size, duration and repayment; managers identify excess cash for debt repayment or investment.

fragments.label: Uses of cash-flow forecasts
fragments.text: Scenario analysis can test lower sales, late customer payment, higher material cost or delayed launch.

fragments.label: Uses of cash-flow forecasts
fragments.text: Forecasting early gives more and cheaper response options than waiting until a payment is missed.

fragments.label: Uses of cash-flow forecasts
fragments.text: Compare actual with forecast regularly to improve assumptions and control.
Limitations of forecasts

fragments.label: Limitations of forecasts
fragments.text: Forecasts rely on sales, payment timing and cost assumptions. New firms lack history, external shocks occur and managers may be over-optimistic to obtain finance. A monthly total can hide a shortage in the middle of the month.

fragments.label: Limitations of forecasts
fragments.text: Use conservative scenarios, sensitivity tests and frequent updates.

fragments.label: Limitations of forecasts
fragments.text: A forecast is a decision tool, not cash itself and not proof of future solvency.

fragments.label: Limitations of forecasts
fragments.text: Quality depends on accurate records and coordination between marketing, operations and finance.
Causes of cash-flow problems

fragments.label: Causes of cash-flow problems
fragments.text: Low or seasonal sales, low contribution, excessive spending, poor records, late-paying customers, bad debts, high inventory, rapid growth, large asset purchases, loan repayments and unexpected shocks can all cause shortages. Diagnose timing versus structural profitability.

fragments.label: Causes of cash-flow problems
fragments.text: A timing gap may be solved with short-term finance.

fragments.label: Causes of cash-flow problems
fragments.text: A recurring deficit from low margins needs price, cost, product or capacity change; more borrowing only postpones it.

fragments.label: Causes of cash-flow problems
fragments.text: Overtrading is common when apparently successful credit sales consume inventory and labour cash before collection.
Increasing or accelerating inflows

fragments.label: Increasing or accelerating inflows
fragments.text: Strengthen credit checks, set shorter terms, invoice promptly, chase overdue accounts, offer an economically justified early-payment discount, require deposits, increase cash sales, factor debts, sell unused assets or seek suitable finance.

fragments.label: Increasing or accelerating inflows
fragments.text: Tighter credit may lose customers to rivals.

fragments.label: Increasing or accelerating inflows
fragments.text: Factoring and discounts sacrifice part of revenue for faster, more certain cash.

fragments.label: Increasing or accelerating inflows
fragments.text: An asset sale improves cash once but may reduce future capacity or create lease cost.
Reducing or delaying outflows

fragments.label: Reducing or delaying outflows
fragments.text: Negotiate longer supplier terms, delay non-essential capital spending, lease rather than buy, reduce inventory, schedule orders, cut waste or overhead, and agree loan timing. Protect activities essential to quality and future revenue.

fragments.label: Reducing or delaying outflows
fragments.text: Breaking supplier terms may remove discounts, damage trust or stop deliveries.

fragments.label: Reducing or delaying outflows
fragments.text: Cheaper materials may create defects and customer loss.

fragments.label: Reducing or delaying outflows
fragments.text: Delaying a productive asset may preserve cash but prolong high operating cost.
Choosing a cash-flow response

fragments.label: Choosing a cash-flow response
fragments.text: Quantify the maximum deficit, start date and duration. Choose a source large enough and available in time, then compare its cost and side effects. Combine immediate relief with a correction to the underlying cause.

fragments.label: Choosing a cash-flow response
fragments.text: Temporary seasonal deficit: overdraft plus tighter collection may fit.

fragments.label: Choosing a cash-flow response
fragments.text: Rapid growth: longer-term working-capital finance and revised credit/inventory systems may be needed.

fragments.label: Choosing a cash-flow response
fragments.text: Persistent loss: revise price, volume, product and cost; do not rely only on finance.
How is net cash flow calculated?

fragments.label: How is net cash flow calculated?
fragments.text: Total cash inflows minus total cash outflows for the period.
How is closing balance calculated?

fragments.label: How is closing balance calculated?
fragments.text: Opening balance plus net cash flow.
Can net cash flow be negative while closing balance stays positive?

fragments.label: Can net cash flow be negative while closing balance stays positive?
fragments.text: Yes, if the opening cash balance is larger than the period's net outflow.
Why is a credit sale not an immediate cash inflow?

fragments.label: Why is a credit sale not an immediate cash inflow?
fragments.text: The customer pays later even though revenue may be recorded when the sale occurs.
What is overtrading?

fragments.label: What is overtrading?
fragments.text: Growth in sales and operations that outpaces the working capital available to fund it.
What is the danger of delaying suppliers?

fragments.label: What is the danger of delaying suppliers?
fragments.text: Lost discounts, damaged trust, tighter future credit or interrupted supply.
Why does a forecast need regular revision?

fragments.label: Why does a forecast need regular revision?
fragments.text: Actual demand, timing and costs differ from assumptions, and new information improves the next decision.

Cost information supports pricing, output and investment decisions. AS questions commonly require accurate contribution, break-even and margin-of-safety calculations followed by interpretation of what changes the risk and whether the simplifying assumptions are realistic.

fragments.label: Fixed cost
fragments.text: A cost that does not change with output in the short run, including when output is zero.

fragments.label: Variable cost
fragments.text: A cost that changes directly with the level of output or sales.

fragments.label: Total cost
fragments.text: Total fixed cost plus total variable cost.

fragments.label: Average cost
fragments.text: Total cost per unit of output.

fragments.label: Direct cost
fragments.text: A cost that can be traced directly to a product, service, job or cost unit.

fragments.label: Indirect cost
fragments.text: A shared overhead that cannot be economically traced to one product or cost unit.

fragments.label: Contribution per unit
fragments.text: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; the amount each unit contributes to fixed cost and then profit.

fragments.label: Total contribution
fragments.text: Contribution per unit multiplied by units sold, or total revenue minus total variable cost.

fragments.label: Break-even output
fragments.text: The output at which total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero.

fragments.label: Margin of safety
fragments.text: Actual or forecast sales volume minus break-even output.

fragments.label: Semi-variable cost
fragments.text: A cost containing both a fixed element and a variable element.
Classifying costs

fragments.label: Classifying costs
fragments.text: Fixed cost is unchanged across a relevant short-run output range, such as rent or salaried management. Variable cost rises with output, such as direct material or piece-rate labour. Direct/indirect is a different classification based on traceability, so a cost can be fixed and direct or variable and indirect depending on context.

fragments.label: Classifying costs
fragments.text: Some costs are stepped or semi-variable: an extra supervisor or machine may be needed after a capacity threshold.

fragments.label: Classifying costs
fragments.text: Classify using the case and time period rather than memorising one label for every wage or utility cost.

fragments.label: Classifying costs
fragments.text: Accurate classification matters because contribution and break-even use variable cost, not all cost per unit.
Using total, average and marginal information

fragments.label: Using total, average and marginal information
fragments.text: Total cost supports profit and cash planning; average cost informs long-run pricing and efficiency comparison; marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. Decisions may fail if managers use historic averages for a short-run order whose relevant extra cost is different.

fragments.label: Using total, average and marginal information
fragments.text: Price normally needs to cover total cost in the long run.

fragments.label: Using total, average and marginal information
fragments.text: A special order above variable cost can add contribution when spare capacity exists, but it may affect regular customers or trigger extra fixed cost.

fragments.label: Using total, average and marginal information
fragments.text: Cost data should be current, relevant and interpreted with qualitative evidence.
Contribution

fragments.label: Contribution
fragments.text: Each unit's contribution first covers fixed cost. Once total contribution equals fixed cost, the business breaks even; further contribution becomes profit. A product with positive contribution can support the business even if allocated average cost appears high.

fragments.label: Contribution
fragments.text: Contribution is not profit until fixed cost has been covered.

fragments.label: Contribution
fragments.text: Higher price or lower variable cost increases contribution, reducing break-even output if fixed cost is unchanged.

fragments.label: Contribution
fragments.text: Capacity, demand and competitor response determine whether the planned number of units can actually be sold.

fragments.label: Contribution
fragments.text: Price $30; variable cost $18; fixed cost $24,000; sales 2,500 units. Contribution per unit = $12. Total contribution = $30,000. Profit = $30,000 − $24,000 = $6,000.
Break-even calculations

fragments.label: Break-even calculations
fragments.text: Break-even output divides fixed cost by contribution per unit. Margin of safety shows how far expected/actual sales can fall before loss begins. A higher margin usually means lower operating risk, but it says nothing by itself about cash timing, quality or future demand.

fragments.label: Break-even calculations
fragments.text: Round break-even output up to the next whole unit when a fraction is produced.

fragments.label: Break-even calculations
fragments.text: State units, not dollars, unless the question requests break-even revenue.

fragments.label: Break-even calculations
fragments.text: Profit at a chosen output can be calculated as total contribution minus fixed cost.

fragments.label: Break-even calculations
fragments.text: Fixed cost $45,000; price $25; variable cost $10. Contribution = $15. Break-even = 45,000 ÷ 15 = 3,000 units. At sales of 4,200, margin of safety = 1,200 units.
Constructing and reading a break-even chart

fragments.label: Constructing and reading a break-even chart
fragments.text: Put output on the horizontal axis and cost/revenue on the vertical. Fixed cost is horizontal within the range. Total cost starts at fixed cost and rises by variable cost per unit. Total revenue starts at zero and rises by selling price. The intersection is break-even; loss lies where total cost exceeds revenue and profit where revenue exceeds cost.

fragments.label: Constructing and reading a break-even chart
fragments.text: The vertical gap between total revenue and total cost at an output is profit or loss.

fragments.label: Constructing and reading a break-even chart
fragments.text: Margin of safety is the horizontal gap between actual/forecast output and break-even output.

fragments.label: Constructing and reading a break-even chart
fragments.text: Label axes, lines, break-even and the relevant output clearly.
How changes move break-even

fragments.label: How changes move break-even
fragments.text: Higher fixed cost raises the total-cost intercept and break-even output. Higher variable cost steepens total cost, reduces contribution and raises break-even. Higher price steepens revenue, increases contribution and lowers break-even—if sales volume does not fall. A lower price has the reverse arithmetic effect but may increase demand.

fragments.label: How changes move break-even
fragments.text: Mechanisation often raises fixed cost while lowering variable cost: it may raise break-even but improve profit at high output.

fragments.label: How changes move break-even
fragments.text: Use revised calculations for a 'what if' decision and then discuss whether the assumed sales are realistic.
Uses of cost and break-even data

fragments.label: Uses of cost and break-even data
fragments.text: Managers can set target sales, compare locations or production methods, assess a price/cost change, judge a new product and present evidence to lenders. The model makes relationships visible and supports sensitivity analysis.

fragments.label: Uses of cost and break-even data
fragments.text: It helps answer 'what must be sold?', not 'what will be sold?'.

fragments.label: Uses of cost and break-even data
fragments.text: Combine with market research, capacity, cash-flow, quality and stakeholder evidence.
Limitations of break-even analysis

fragments.label: Limitations of break-even analysis
fragments.text: The model usually assumes constant price and variable cost, fixed cost unchanged within the range, all output sold, one product or constant sales mix, and accurate linear estimates. In reality discounts, overtime, stock, capacity steps and uncertainty change the lines.

fragments.label: Limitations of break-even analysis
fragments.text: Multi-product businesses require an assumed sales mix; if that mix changes, the calculated break-even changes.

fragments.label: Limitations of break-even analysis
fragments.text: Inflation and external shocks can make the data quickly outdated.

fragments.label: Limitations of break-even analysis
fragments.text: The simplicity is valuable for comparison, but should not be mistaken for a forecast of actual demand.
How is contribution per unit calculated?

fragments.label: How is contribution per unit calculated?
fragments.text: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit.
What happens to contribution before break-even?

fragments.label: What happens to contribution before break-even?
fragments.text: It accumulates to cover fixed cost.
How is break-even output calculated?

fragments.label: How is break-even output calculated?
fragments.text: Fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.
How is margin of safety calculated?

fragments.label: How is margin of safety calculated?
fragments.text: Actual or forecast output minus break-even output.
Where does total cost start on a break-even chart?

fragments.label: Where does total cost start on a break-even chart?
fragments.text: At the fixed-cost value on the vertical axis when output is zero.
Why might a price rise lower calculated break-even but reduce actual profit?

fragments.label: Why might a price rise lower calculated break-even but reduce actual profit?
fragments.text: The higher price raises contribution, but demand may fall enough to reduce total contribution.
Name two major break-even assumptions.

fragments.label: Name two major break-even assumptions.
fragments.text: Examples: constant price/variable cost, fixed cost unchanged, all output sold, constant sales mix and linear relationships.

A budget is an agreed target for future revenue, cost, cash or activity. Budgeting supports planning and control only when assumptions are realistic, managers understand responsibility and variances are investigated rather than mechanically rewarded or punished.

fragments.label: Budget
fragments.text: A quantified plan or target for a future period that managers aim to achieve.

fragments.label: Forecast
fragments.text: An estimate of what is likely to happen based on assumptions and evidence.

fragments.label: Budget holder
fragments.text: The manager responsible for agreeing, controlling and explaining performance against a budget.

fragments.label: Variance
fragments.text: The difference between an actual result and its budgeted result.

fragments.label: Favourable variance
fragments.text: A difference that, considered alone, tends to improve profit compared with budget.

fragments.label: Adverse variance
fragments.text: A difference that, considered alone, tends to reduce profit compared with budget.

fragments.label: Incremental budgeting
fragments.text: Setting a new budget by adjusting the previous period's figure.

fragments.label: Zero-based budgeting
fragments.text: Starting each budget from zero and requiring activities and spending to be justified.

fragments.label: Flexible budget
fragments.text: A budget adjusted to the actual or revised level of activity so performance can be compared fairly.
Why businesses use budgets

fragments.label: Why businesses use budgets
fragments.text: Budgets convert objectives into resource limits and performance targets. They support planning, coordination, allocation, communication, motivation and control. Comparing actuals with budget highlights where investigation and corrective action may be needed.

fragments.label: Why businesses use budgets
fragments.text: A sales budget influences production, staffing, purchasing and cash budgets, so assumptions must be coordinated.

fragments.label: Why businesses use budgets
fragments.text: A budget does not itself reduce cost; managers must act on the information.

fragments.label: Why businesses use budgets
fragments.text: Participation can improve information and acceptance, but negotiation may create budget slack.
Budget versus forecast

fragments.label: Budget versus forecast
fragments.text: A forecast states the latest expected outcome; a budget states an approved plan or target. If demand is now expected to fall, the forecast may change even while the original budget remains the benchmark. Confusing them removes the ability to compare what was planned with what is now expected and what actually occurred.

fragments.label: Budget versus forecast
fragments.text: Forecasts should be updated as evidence changes.

fragments.label: Budget versus forecast
fragments.text: Budgets can also be revised when assumptions fundamentally change, but managers should record why.
Types of functional budget

fragments.label: Types of functional budget
fragments.text: A revenue/sales budget sets expected quantity, price and revenue. Production/purchasing budgets plan output and inputs. Cost budgets set permitted spending; a profit budget combines revenue and cost; a cash budget schedules receipts, payments and balances. A master budget coordinates the overall plan.

fragments.label: Types of functional budget
fragments.text: An apparently favourable cost budget can be misleading if output was below plan.

fragments.label: Types of functional budget
fragments.text: Cash and profit budgets differ because credit timing, loans and asset purchases affect cash differently.

fragments.label: Types of functional budget
fragments.text: Every budget needs assumptions, a period, responsible holder and measurable lines.
Incremental budgeting

fragments.label: Incremental budgeting
fragments.text: Incremental budgeting takes last period's figure and adjusts for inflation, growth or known change. It is quick, stable and easy for recurring activities, but carries forward inefficiency, encourages spending to protect next year's allocation and may not reflect new priorities.

fragments.label: Incremental budgeting
fragments.text: Best where operations are stable and prior figures were efficient.

fragments.label: Incremental budgeting
fragments.text: Challenge large inherited items and assumptions rather than applying one percentage mechanically.
Zero-based and flexible budgeting

fragments.label: Zero-based and flexible budgeting
fragments.text: Zero-based budgeting asks managers to justify activities and spending from zero, which can redirect resources and expose waste but demands time and judgement and may undervalue long-term support functions. Flexible budgeting recalculates allowed variable cost/revenue for actual activity, making performance comparison fairer, but requires reliable cost behaviour data.

fragments.label: Zero-based and flexible budgeting
fragments.text: A flexible budget is not permission to ignore all overspending; it separates volume effects from efficiency or price effects.

fragments.label: Zero-based and flexible budgeting
fragments.text: Zero-based review may be applied periodically to selected discretionary areas rather than every line every year.
Calculating and classifying variances

fragments.label: Calculating and classifying variances
