fragments.text: Variance is actual minus budget in numerical size, then classified by its effect on profit. Actual revenue above budget is normally favourable; below is adverse. Actual cost below budget is normally favourable; above is adverse. State both amount and F/A label.

fragments.label: Calculating and classifying variances
fragments.text: Revenue budget $120,000 and actual $132,000 gives a $12,000 favourable revenue variance.

fragments.label: Calculating and classifying variances
fragments.text: Material-cost budget $50,000 and actual $56,500 gives a $6,500 adverse cost variance.

fragments.label: Calculating and classifying variances
fragments.text: A favourable label is not automatically good overall: lower material cost may result from lower output or poorer quality.
Investigating variances

fragments.label: Investigating variances
fragments.text: Revenue variance may arise from price, volume, product mix, promotion, competition or economic change. Cost variance may arise from input price, usage/waste, output, productivity, quality, supplier terms or inflation. Controllability and interdependence matter before judging a manager.

fragments.label: Investigating variances
fragments.text: Investigate material, recurring and controllable differences first.

fragments.label: Investigating variances
fragments.text: A sales promotion may create favourable revenue but adverse promotion and distribution costs.

fragments.label: Investigating variances
fragments.text: Use non-financial evidence such as defects, delivery and satisfaction to interpret the number.
Behavioural benefits and problems

fragments.label: Behavioural benefits and problems
fragments.text: Agreed challenging targets can focus effort and provide achievement feedback. Imposed or unrealistic budgets can demotivate, encourage short-term cuts, data manipulation, departmental conflict and spending of unused allowances. Managers may build slack by understating revenue or overstating cost.

fragments.label: Behavioural benefits and problems
fragments.text: Combine participation with evidence, review and strategic priorities.

fragments.label: Behavioural benefits and problems
fragments.text: Avoid rewarding one budget line when actions damage another department or long-term objective.

fragments.label: Behavioural benefits and problems
fragments.text: Treat significant adverse variances as questions to diagnose, not automatic proof of poor management.
Limitations and effective use

fragments.label: Limitations and effective use
fragments.text: Budgets can become outdated as demand, price, supply or technology changes. Preparation and monitoring cost time; qualitative factors are omitted; short-term financial targets can discourage training, maintenance and innovation. Effective systems update forecasts, use flexible comparison, coordinate departments and link financial with non-financial measures.

fragments.label: Limitations and effective use
fragments.text: The value of tighter control depends on uncertainty: a start-up may need frequent revisions, while a stable process can use firmer standards.

fragments.label: Limitations and effective use
fragments.text: Review the action taken after variance investigation, not only whether the original number was met.
What is the difference between a budget and forecast?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a budget and forecast?
fragments.text: A budget is an approved plan/target; a forecast is the latest estimate of what is likely to happen.
When is a revenue variance favourable?

fragments.label: When is a revenue variance favourable?
fragments.text: When actual revenue exceeds budget, considered alone.
When is a cost variance favourable?

fragments.label: When is a cost variance favourable?
fragments.text: When actual cost is below budget for a comparable level of activity, considered alone.
Why can incremental budgeting preserve inefficiency?

fragments.label: Why can incremental budgeting preserve inefficiency?
fragments.text: It starts from prior spending, so unnecessary activities can be carried forward.
What does zero-based budgeting require?

fragments.label: What does zero-based budgeting require?
fragments.text: Activities and spending must be justified from a zero starting point.
Why use a flexible budget?

fragments.label: Why use a flexible budget?
fragments.text: To adjust the budget to actual activity and separate volume differences from efficiency or price performance.
What is budget slack?

fragments.label: What is budget slack?
fragments.text: Deliberately making a target easier, such as understating expected revenue or overstating expected cost.

External influences are forces outside the business that change demand, costs, risk and strategic choices. The current A2 syllabus is broader than a simple PEST checklist: it includes political/legal changes, macroeconomic policy, demographic and social change, technology, competitors/suppliers, international trade and MNCs, plus environmental audits and sustainability.

fragments.label: Privatisation
fragments.text: Transfer of a business/activity from public/state ownership to private ownership.

fragments.label: Nationalisation
fragments.text: Transfer of privately owned business/activity into state ownership/control.

fragments.label: Fiscal policy
fragments.text: Government decisions on taxation and public spending.

fragments.label: Monetary policy
fragments.text: Policy influencing interest rates, credit conditions and/or money supply.

fragments.label: Supply-side policy
fragments.text: Measures intended to improve productive capacity and efficiency.

fragments.label: CSR
fragments.text: A business approach that considers social, ethical and environmental responsibilities as well as financial outcomes.

fragments.label: Environmental audit
fragments.text: A systematic review of a business's environmental impacts and performance.
Political and legal influences

fragments.label: Political and legal influences
fragments.text: Employment law, competition law, consumer protection, health/safety, marketing restrictions and ownership policy can change business costs and freedom of action. Regulation may raise compliance cost yet also build trust or prevent unfair competition. Political stability can influence investment risk.
Economic influences

fragments.label: Economic influences
fragments.text: Economic growth can increase demand but may create inflation/capacity pressure. Inflation raises costs and affects real incomes. Higher interest rates increase borrowing cost and can reduce consumption/investment. Tax/spending, supply-side and exchange-rate policies affect firms differently depending on debt, imports, exports and customer income sensitivity.
Social, demographic and CSR influences

fragments.label: Social, demographic and CSR influences
fragments.text: Age structure, migration, education, family patterns and lifestyle changes alter workforce supply and customer demand. CSR can strengthen reputation, recruitment and stakeholder trust, but may raise short-term costs. Pressure groups can influence reputation and policy even without legal authority.
Technology, competitors and suppliers

fragments.label: Technology, competitors and suppliers
fragments.text: Automation, AI and digital systems can improve productivity, information and customer reach but require investment, skills and cybersecurity. Competitor actions influence price, innovation and promotion; supplier bargaining power, quality, reliability and lead time affect cost and continuity.
International influences and MNCs

fragments.label: International influences and MNCs
fragments.text: Trade agreements can lower barriers and open markets; protectionism can protect domestic firms but raise import costs. Exchange rates affect export competitiveness and imported inputs. MNCs may bring jobs, investment and technology but can also pressure local firms/resources and repatriate profits.
Environmental and sustainability pressures

fragments.label: Environmental and sustainability pressures
fragments.text: Climate change, resource scarcity, pollution controls and stakeholder expectations influence product, process and location decisions. Environmental audits identify impacts and targets. Sustainable investment may cost more initially but reduce waste/energy cost and improve long-run legitimacy.
monetary=interest/credit
fiscal=tax/spending
supply-side=capacity/productivity
social/demographic=demand+labour
international=trade/exchange/MNC
sustainability=long-run resource/stakeholder impact

Business strategy is the long-term direction used to achieve corporate objectives. High-level answers must move through strategic analysis, strategic choice and implementation. The syllabus includes blue ocean strategy, scenario planning, SWOT, PEST, Porter, core competence, Ansoff, force-field analysis, decision trees, corporate planning/culture, transformational leadership, strategic change, contingency planning and crisis management.

fragments.label: Strategy
fragments.text: A long-term direction/plan for achieving major business objectives.

fragments.label: Core competence
fragments.text: A distinctive capability that creates customer value and is difficult for competitors to imitate.

fragments.label: Blue ocean strategy
fragments.text: Creating uncontested market space/value rather than competing head-on in an existing market.

fragments.label: Scenario planning
fragments.text: Preparing responses to several plausible future conditions instead of relying on one forecast.

fragments.label: Contingency plan
fragments.text: A prepared response for a foreseeable disruptive event.

fragments.label: Force-field analysis
fragments.text: A framework identifying forces driving change and forces restraining it.
Strategic management process

fragments.label: Strategic management process
fragments.text: Analysis asks where the business is now; choice compares possible strategic routes; implementation allocates people, finance, operations and controls to deliver the chosen strategy. An analytically attractive strategy can still fail if resources, culture or stakeholder support are weak.
SWOT and PEST

fragments.label: SWOT and PEST
fragments.text: SWOT separates internal strengths/weaknesses from external opportunities/threats. PEST scans broad external forces. Their value comes from connecting factors—for example using a strength to exploit an opportunity—not merely listing them.
Porter's five forces and core competence

fragments.label: Porter's five forces and core competence
fragments.text: Five forces assess rivalry, threat of entrants/substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Strong forces tend to reduce industry attractiveness. Core competence focuses internally on hard-to-copy capabilities that create customer value, so the two frameworks answer different strategic questions.
Ansoff matrix

fragments.label: Ansoff matrix
fragments.text: Market penetration uses existing products/existing markets; market development existing products/new markets; product development new products/existing markets; diversification new products/new markets. Risk usually rises as the firm moves further from its existing knowledge, but actual risk depends on capability and evidence.
Decision trees and force fields

fragments.label: Decision trees and force fields
fragments.text: Decision trees combine probabilities and financial outcomes to calculate expected values. Force-field analysis identifies drivers and restraints around change. Both structure judgement but rely on estimates and do not capture every qualitative factor.

fragments.label: Decision trees and force fields
fragments.text: Expected value of an outcome = probability x payoff; add weighted outcomes for each option.
Blue ocean and scenario planning

fragments.label: Blue ocean and scenario planning
fragments.text: Blue ocean seeks new value/market space that makes direct competition less relevant, but demand is uncertain. Scenario planning builds flexible responses to alternative futures and is valuable under uncertainty, though it is time-consuming and cannot predict every event.
Implementation and change

fragments.label: Implementation and change
fragments.text: Corporate culture may support or resist strategy. Transformational leadership can create vision and commitment. Implementation requires communication, resources, milestones and control. Contingency/crisis planning reduces reaction time when disruptions occur but plans must be updated/tested.
strategy=analysis->choice->implementation
Porter=industry pressure
core competence=internal distinctive capability
Ansoff=product x market
force field=drivers/restraints
strategy must be implementable

Organisational structure determines reporting relationships, authority, communication and decision speed. You must compare functional, hierarchical/flat/narrow and matrix structures, understand grouping by product/function/geography, and analyse delegation, accountability, span of control, centralisation/decentralisation and line/staff relationships.

fragments.label: Span of control
fragments.text: The number of subordinates directly managed by one manager.

fragments.label: Chain of command
fragments.text: The route through which authority/instructions pass through an organisation.

fragments.label: Delegation
fragments.text: Passing authority for a task/decision to a subordinate while ultimate accountability remains with the manager.

fragments.label: Accountability
fragments.text: Being answerable for results/decisions.

fragments.label: Centralisation
fragments.text: Decision authority concentrated at senior/head-office level.

fragments.label: Decentralisation
fragments.text: Decision authority distributed to lower levels, divisions or locations.

fragments.label: Delayering
fragments.text: Removing one or more management levels from the hierarchy.
Tall/narrow and flat structures

fragments.label: Tall/narrow and flat structures
fragments.text: Tall structures have more levels and often narrower spans: close supervision and clear promotion routes but slower communication and higher management cost. Flat structures reduce layers and often widen spans: faster communication and more delegation but heavier manager workloads.
Functional structure

fragments.label: Functional structure
fragments.text: Groups specialists such as marketing, finance and operations. It supports expertise and economies of specialisation but can create silos and slow cross-functional coordination.
Matrix structure

fragments.label: Matrix structure
fragments.text: Employees report across two dimensions such as function and project/product. It improves cross-functional collaboration and resource sharing, but dual authority can create conflict and unclear priorities.
Delegation and accountability

fragments.label: Delegation and accountability
fragments.text: Delegation develops employees and frees managers for higher-level work. It succeeds when objectives, authority, resources and competence are clear. The manager can delegate authority but normally remains ultimately accountable for outcomes.
Centralisation versus decentralisation

fragments.label: Centralisation versus decentralisation
fragments.text: Centralisation supports consistency, strategic control and standardisation. Decentralisation can improve local responsiveness, motivation and decision speed. The right balance depends on size, risk, staff skill, geographic spread and need for common standards.
Line and staff relationships

fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: Line managers have direct authority for core operational results; staff specialists advise/support with expertise. Conflict can occur if line managers see advice as interference or staff specialists lack operational context.
span=direct reports
chain=authority route
delegation=authority passed
centralise=control/consistency
decentralise=local speed
matrix=dual relationships

Communication is effective only when the intended meaning is understood and produces the required response. You need to select among spoken, written, electronic and visual methods, identify barriers, explain how communication affects efficiency and recommend improvements.

fragments.label: Communication
fragments.text: Transfer of information and meaning from sender to receiver.

fragments.label: Feedback
fragments.text: A response indicating whether the message was received/understood.

fragments.label: Communication barrier
fragments.text: A factor that delays, distorts or prevents understanding of a message.

fragments.label: Formal communication
fragments.text: Communication through recognised official channels.

fragments.label: Informal communication
fragments.text: Unofficial communication outside formal organisational channels.
Spoken communication

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Fast, rich and allows immediate questions/feedback. It is useful for sensitive or complex discussion but may leave no permanent record and can be impractical for a large dispersed audience.
Written communication

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: Provides a permanent record and allows precise/detail-heavy messages. It can be slower to create/read and lacks immediate feedback unless another channel is used.
Electronic and visual communication

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: Email, messaging, intranets and collaboration systems provide speed/scale but can create overload, distraction and security issues. Visual charts/diagrams can make patterns clearer but may oversimplify detail.
Barriers

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Jargon, language/cultural differences, status, too many hierarchy levels, noise, overload, poor technology, wrong channel and lack of feedback can distort meaning. The exam expects the consequence: errors, delay, conflict, weak decisions or lower productivity.
Improving communication

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: Choose the channel according to urgency, complexity, confidentiality, audience size and need for a record; simplify language; encourage feedback; train staff; improve systems; shorten unnecessary chains; and clarify responsibility for messages.
Communication and efficiency

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Good communication reduces duplicated work, errors and coordination delay and helps staff understand objectives/change. However, too many meetings/messages can waste time, so 'more communication' is not always better.
spoken=rich/fast
written=record/detail
electronic=speed/scale
visual=pattern clarity
feedback checks understanding

Leadership is influencing and guiding people toward objectives. The current syllabus focuses on leadership roles/qualities, trait, behavioural, contingency, power-and-influence and transformational theories, plus Goleman's emotional-intelligence competencies. Evaluation should always depend on situation rather than assuming one universal best style.

fragments.label: Leadership
fragments.text: Influencing and guiding people towards organisational objectives.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: An approach focusing on personal characteristics associated with effective leaders.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: The idea that effective leadership depends on the situation.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Leadership that creates a compelling vision and motivates significant organisational change.

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Ability to understand/manage one's own emotions and recognise/respond effectively to others' emotions.
Leadership roles and qualities

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: Directors shape strategic direction/governance; managers translate plans into coordinated action; supervisors lead frontline work; worker representatives communicate employee interests. Important qualities include communication, judgement, integrity, adaptability and ability to motivate—but importance varies by context.
Trait theory

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: Looks for personal characteristics linked with leadership. It can help selection/development but risks assuming qualities alone determine success and may underplay context and learned behaviour.
Behavioural approaches

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Focus on what leaders actually do, such as task-focused versus people-focused behaviour. Behaviour can be developed and adapted, but the same behaviour may not work with every workforce/task.
Contingency theory

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: No single leadership approach is always best. Urgency, employee competence, task structure, risk, culture and degree of change influence what works. A crisis may require faster central direction; expert creative teams may perform better with autonomy.
Power and influence

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Leaders influence through formal position, expertise, control of rewards/resources, relationships and credibility. Coercive power may gain short-term compliance but damage trust/commitment.
Transformational leadership

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Creates vision, challenges old assumptions and inspires followers to support major change. It can increase commitment during transformation but fails if the vision is unrealistic or implementation/resources are weak.
Goleman's emotional intelligence

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Self-awareness means understanding one's emotions/impact; self-management means regulating reactions; social awareness means recognising others' needs/perspectives; social skills cover communication, relationship-building, conflict management and influence.
trait=characteristics
behavioural=what leader does
contingency=depends on situation
transformational=vision/change
EI=self+social awareness/management

HRM strategy connects workforce decisions to long-term performance. You must compare hard and soft HRM, evaluate flexible contracts, diagnose and improve employee performance, understand Management by Objectives (MBO), and analyse how IT/AI changes HRM.

fragments.label: Hard HRM
fragments.text: An approach treating labour mainly as a resource/cost to be planned and controlled to meet business needs.

fragments.label: Soft HRM
fragments.text: An approach treating employees as assets whose commitment, development and participation create performance.

fragments.label: MBO
fragments.text: Management by Objectives: managers and employees agree measurable objectives, monitor progress and review results.

fragments.label: Flexible working
fragments.text: Employment arrangements allowing labour time/location/contract to adapt to employee or business needs.
Hard versus soft HRM

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: Hard HRM emphasises workforce numbers, productivity and cost; soft HRM emphasises motivation, development, trust and involvement. Real firms may combine both. Suitable balance depends on skill scarcity, service quality, cost pressure and culture.
Flexible contracts and working

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Temporary, zero-hours, part-time, full-time, annualised hours, flexitime, home working, shifts, job sharing, compressed hours and gig work allow labour to match demand or widen recruitment. Risks include insecurity, coordination difficulty, legal/reputation issues and weaker loyalty/training continuity.
Measuring poor performance

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: Indicators include productivity, absence, labour turnover, error/defect rates, complaints and missed targets. Causes may be skill gaps, poor equipment, unclear goals, workload, weak motivation, leadership or reward systems. Diagnose the cause before choosing a solution.
Improving performance

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Training, coaching, better job design, participation, clearer targets, technology, reward changes, wellbeing support or better recruitment may help. Evaluate cost, implementation time and whether the problem is individual or systemic.
Management by Objectives

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: Managers and employees agree objectives aligned with higher business goals, measures/timescales, then review progress. Benefits: clarity, participation, alignment and performance evidence. Risks: target gaming, narrow focus, measurement difficulty and time spent negotiating/reviewing.
IT and AI in HRM

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: Systems automate applicant screening, scheduling, payroll, training and performance analytics. Benefits include speed/consistency; risks include algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, inaccurate data and loss of human judgement/trust.
hard=labour resource/cost
soft=people/assets
flexibility matches labour to need
MBO=agreed objectives
AI HRM=efficiency + bias/privacy risk

Marketing analysis converts market information into decisions. The A2 syllabus focuses on price, income and promotional elasticity; product development and R&D; and sales forecasting using four-period centred moving averages plus qualitative forecasting.

fragments.label: PED
fragments.text: Price elasticity of demand: responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.

fragments.label: YED
fragments.text: Income elasticity of demand: responsiveness of demand to a change in consumer income.

fragments.label: Promotional elasticity
fragments.text: Responsiveness of demand/sales to a change in promotional spending/activity.

fragments.label: Sales forecast
fragments.text: An estimate of future sales over a stated period.

fragments.label: R&D
fragments.text: Research and development activity aimed at creating/improving products, processes or knowledge.
Price elasticity of demand

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. Demand is elastic when absolute PED >1 and inelastic when absolute PED <1. It helps pricing/revenue decisions but estimates depend on time period, competitors and other conditions.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: PED = %ΔQd / %ΔP
Income and promotional elasticity

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: YED helps predict how demand changes with income: positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods. Promotional elasticity estimates how sales respond to promotional changes and can guide budgets, but past responsiveness may not persist.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text:
YED = %Δdemand / %Δincome
Promotional elasticity = %Δdemand / %Δpromotion spending
Product development and R&D

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: Ideas can come from customers, employees, competitors, suppliers, research and new technology. Development commonly includes idea generation/screening, concept/design, prototype/testing and launch. R&D can create differentiation and future revenue but is expensive, uncertain and potentially imitable.
Why forecast sales

fragments.label: Why forecast sales
fragments.text: Forecasts influence staffing, capacity, purchasing, inventory, cash-flow and finance. Underforecasting can cause lost sales/capacity problems; overforecasting can create excess inventory/cost.
Four-period centred moving averages

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: First calculate averages for successive four-period blocks. Because four is an even number, each average falls between actual time periods; centre it by averaging adjacent four-period moving averages. This produces a trend value aligned with an actual period.
Qualitative forecasting

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Uses expert judgement, sales-force/customer insight, Delphi-style opinion or market knowledge when reliable historical data are limited or conditions are changing. It captures factors a time series may miss but is subjective.
PED=price responsiveness
YED=income responsiveness
promotion elasticity=response to promo
4-period MA needs centring
forecast drives capacity/finance/inventory

Marketing strategy coordinates objectives, research, resources and the marketing mix into a coherent plan. You must understand marketing plans, make consistent strategic choices, analyse IT/AI, and evaluate international market selection, entry methods and standardisation versus local adaptation.

fragments.label: Marketing plan
fragments.text: A documented set of marketing objectives, research, budgets/resources, actions and controls.

fragments.label: Positioning
fragments.text: The intended perception of a product/brand relative to alternatives in the target customer's mind.

fragments.label: Market entry strategy
fragments.text: Method used to enter a foreign market, e.g. exporting, licensing/franchising, joint venture or direct investment.

fragments.label: Pan-global strategy
fragments.text: A largely standardised marketing approach across countries.

fragments.label: Local adaptation
fragments.text: Changing the offer/marketing mix for local culture, law or market conditions.
Marketing planning

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: A plan converts objectives into target markets, budgets, responsibilities, mix decisions and controls. It improves coordination and measurement but can become rigid or outdated if assumptions/data change quickly.
Coordinated strategy

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: Segmentation, targeting and positioning should guide product, price, promotion and distribution. The mix must be internally consistent and feasible within finance/operations resources. A premium position combined with constant deep discounting can damage coherence.
IT and AI

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Digital platforms support CRM, recommendations, automated advertising, personalisation, dynamic analysis and experimentation. Benefits include targeting and measurable data; risks include privacy, algorithmic bias, inaccurate data, cybersecurity and platform dependence.
Selecting international markets

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Assess size/growth, income, culture, competition, regulation, political/economic risk, distribution, exchange rates and strategic fit. A large market is not automatically attractive if entry barriers/adaptation costs are high.
Entry modes

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: Exporting requires lower commitment/control; licensing/franchising can expand quickly but sacrifices control/know-how; joint ventures provide local knowledge while sharing control/profit; wholly owned investment gives high control but requires high capital and risk exposure.
Standardisation versus adaptation

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Pan-global standardisation can reduce design/promotion cost and create consistent brand identity. Local adaptation improves cultural/legal relevance but raises complexity/cost. The best balance depends on similarity of customer needs and regulation.
plan=objectives+research+resources+mix+control
strategy must be coordinated
entry mode trades control vs capital/risk
global standardise vs local adapt
AI=data efficiency + privacy/bias risk

Location and scale shape cost, responsiveness, risk and long-run competitiveness. You must analyse local/national/international location decisions, offshoring and reshoring, globalisation, and internal/external economies and diseconomies of scale.

fragments.label: Offshoring
fragments.text: Moving business activities or production to another country.

fragments.label: Reshoring
fragments.text: Returning previously offshored activity to the home country.

fragments.label: Economies of scale
fragments.text: Reductions in average/unit cost as scale increases.

fragments.label: Diseconomies of scale
fragments.text: Increases in average/unit cost caused by excessive size/complexity.

fragments.label: External economies
fragments.text: Cost advantages gained because the industry/region grows, not because one firm alone becomes larger.
Location factors

fragments.label: Location factors
fragments.text: Important factors include labour skill/cost, land/rent, suppliers, transport, infrastructure, energy, customers, government incentives/tax, law/political stability and sustainability. Weighting depends on the business model—a data centre, luxury retailer and heavy manufacturer should not prioritise the same factors.
Offshoring

fragments.label: Offshoring
fragments.text: Can lower labour/input cost, access specialist suppliers and place production nearer growing markets. Risks include longer supply chains, quality/control problems, exchange/political risk, cultural/communication issues and reputational concerns.
Reshoring

fragments.label: Reshoring
fragments.text: May improve responsiveness, quality control, supply-chain resilience and home-market reputation. It can also increase direct labour/property cost. Automation can make reshoring more viable by reducing labour-cost differences.
Globalisation and location

fragments.label: Globalisation and location
fragments.text: Trade liberalisation, digital coordination and global logistics allow firms to split design, production and service across countries. This increases choice but also creates dependence on international networks exposed to tariffs, pandemics, geopolitical tension and currency movement.
Internal economies of scale

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale
fragments.text: Purchasing (bulk discounts), technical (specialised machinery), managerial (specialist managers), financial (access/cost of finance), marketing (spread fixed promotion cost) and risk-bearing/diversification can reduce unit cost as the firm grows.
External economies and diseconomies

fragments.label: External economies and diseconomies
fragments.text: Industry clusters can provide specialist labour, suppliers, infrastructure and knowledge. But very large businesses may suffer communication, coordination, motivation and bureaucracy problems, causing unit costs to rise. Growth is beneficial only while economies outweigh diseconomies.
offshore=move abroad
reshore=bring back
internal economies=firm growth
external economies=cluster/industry
diseconomies=complexity raises unit cost

Quality management aims to deliver outputs fit for purpose and consistent with customer expectations. You must distinguish quality control, quality assurance and Total Quality Management and explain how benchmarking can identify performance gaps and support improvement.

fragments.label: Quality control
fragments.text: Inspection/testing of output to identify defects, often after or at stages of production.

fragments.label: Quality assurance
fragments.text: Systems and procedures designed to prevent defects by building quality into processes.

fragments.label: TQM
fragments.text: A whole-organisation culture of continuous quality improvement where everyone is responsible for quality.

fragments.label: Benchmarking
fragments.text: Comparing performance/processes with a strong external or internal reference to identify improvement gaps.

fragments.label: Continuous improvement
fragments.text: Ongoing repeated efforts to improve process, quality, cost or customer value.
Why quality matters

fragments.label: Why quality matters
fragments.text: Consistent quality can reduce returns/rework, strengthen reputation, support repeat purchase and premium positioning, and reduce waste. But 'maximum specification' is not always optimal if customers will not pay for it; quality is about meeting target expectations reliably.
Quality control

fragments.label: Quality control
fragments.text: Inspection detects defects before they reach customers and provides measurable standards. It can be expensive and often finds errors after resources have already been wasted; responsibility may become concentrated in inspectors rather than the workforce.
Quality assurance

fragments.label: Quality assurance
fragments.text: Standards, procedures, training and process checks aim to prevent errors at source. It can improve consistency and reduce rework but requires design, documentation, staff commitment and supplier consistency.
Total Quality Management

fragments.label: Total Quality Management
fragments.text: TQM makes quality everyone's responsibility and emphasises customer focus, prevention and continuous improvement. Potential gains include lower defect cost and stronger culture; barriers include training/time cost, employee resistance and difficulty maintaining commitment.
Benchmarking process

fragments.label: Benchmarking process
fragments.text: Identify what to improve, select a comparator/best practice, measure gaps, understand the reasons, adapt practices, implement and review. It can provide external targets but data may be unavailable and blindly copying another firm can fail because objectives/resources differ.
Quality and finance/strategy

fragments.label: Quality and finance/strategy
fragments.text: Quality investment can raise short-run costs but reduce warranty, scrap and complaint costs and improve demand/reputation. The judgement depends on defect cost, customer expectations, competitive position and required investment.
QC detects
QA prevents
TQM=everyone+continuous improvement
benchmark=compare->gap->adapt
quality must fit customer expectations

Operations strategy turns resources and processes into long-term capability. The current syllabus includes resource constraints, flexibility, process innovation, IT/AI, ERP, lean production and Critical Path Analysis (CPA). This topic is highly integrative because operations choices depend on HR, marketing and finance.

fragments.label: ERP
fragments.text: Enterprise Resource Planning: an integrated information system linking major business functions through shared data.

fragments.label: Lean production
fragments.text: An approach that seeks customer value using less waste, delay, inventory and non-value activity.

fragments.label: Kaizen
fragments.text: Continuous incremental improvement involving employees.

fragments.label: JIT
fragments.text: Just-in-time: materials/components arrive close to when needed, minimising inventory.

fragments.label: Critical path
fragments.text: The sequence of zero-total-float activities determining minimum project duration.

fragments.label: Total float
fragments.text: How long an activity can be delayed without delaying overall project completion.

fragments.label: Free float
fragments.text: How long an activity can be delayed without delaying the earliest start of a following activity.
Resource constraints and flexibility

fragments.label: Resource constraints and flexibility
fragments.text: Operations decisions depend on available finance, skilled labour and expected demand. Flexibility may mean changing volume, delivery time or specification quickly. It can improve customer response but may require spare capacity, multi-skilled employees, adaptable equipment or responsive suppliers—all with costs.
IT, AI and process innovation

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Automation, sensors, predictive maintenance, scheduling systems and AI can improve speed, consistency and information. Risks include capital cost, cybersecurity, skill shortages, inaccurate models and reduced flexibility if technology is too specialised.
ERP

fragments.label: ERP
fragments.text: ERP links purchasing, inventory, sales, finance, HR and production to shared real-time data. It can reduce duplicated entry and improve planning/coordination. Implementation can be expensive and disruptive; poor data, weak training or badly redesigned processes can cause failure.
Lean production tools

fragments.label: Lean production tools
fragments.text: Kaizen = continuous small improvements; quality circles = employee groups solving process/quality issues; simultaneous engineering = functions/stages work in parallel; cell production = teams handle a family of products; JIT reduces inventory; waste management removes non-value activity.
Lean trade-offs

fragments.label: Lean trade-offs
fragments.text: Low inventory cuts holding cost and exposes problems but increases dependence on reliable suppliers/transport. Employee involvement can improve ideas/motivation but change may create resistance. Lean should reduce waste, not blindly remove every buffer needed for resilience.
Critical Path Analysis

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis
fragments.text: Create the network, calculate earliest/latest times, identify activities with zero total float and find minimum duration. Float helps managers allocate resources and focus monitoring on activities where delay threatens completion.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis
fragments.text:
Total float = latest finish - earliest start - duration
Free float = earliest start of next activity - earliest start of current activity - duration
CPA evaluation

fragments.label: CPA evaluation
fragments.text: Benefits: shows dependencies, critical tasks, minimum duration and scheduling flexibility. Limitations: activity times are estimates; resource constraints are not automatically solved; complex projects change and require updates; unexpected events can create a new critical path.
flexibility=volume/time/spec
ERP=integrated shared data
lean=remove waste
JIT=low inventory+supplier risk
critical path=zero total float
CPA=dependencies+time

Financial statements communicate performance over a period and financial position at a date. At A2 you must interpret the statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position, understand relationships between them, and know inventory valuation using net realisable value and straight-line depreciation.

fragments.label: Gross profit
fragments.text: Revenue minus cost of sales.

fragments.label: Profit from operations
fragments.text: Gross profit minus operating expenses.

fragments.label: Net current assets
fragments.text: Current assets minus current liabilities.

fragments.label: Net realisable value
fragments.text: Expected selling value of inventory less the costs necessary to complete/sell it.

fragments.label: Depreciation
fragments.text: Allocation of a non-current asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

fragments.label: Retained earnings
fragments.text: Profits retained in the business rather than distributed to owners.
Statement of profit or loss

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss
fragments.text: Shows performance over a period. Typical flow: revenue -> cost of sales -> gross profit -> operating expenses -> profit from operations -> finance/tax/other items -> profit for the year. Trace a change through every affected subtotal rather than discussing one line only.
Statement of financial position

fragments.label: Statement of financial position
fragments.text: A snapshot at a specific date showing non-current assets, current assets, current liabilities, net current assets, non-current liabilities and equity/reserves. It indicates resources controlled and financing obligations.
How the statements connect

fragments.label: How the statements connect
fragments.text: Retained profit can increase equity/reserves. Depreciation reduces profit and reduces the carrying value of non-current assets. Inventory valuation affects both current assets and cost of sales/profit. The statements therefore must be analysed together.
Inventory valuation and NRV

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and NRV
fragments.text: Inventory may become damaged, obsolete or fall in selling price. Reporting it above what can be recovered overstates assets and potentially profit. NRV reflects expected recoverable amount after costs needed to complete/sell.
Straight-line depreciation

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: The same depreciation expense is charged each year across useful life. It reduces reported profit and the carrying amount of the asset but is not itself a current-year cash payment.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life
Using statements strategically

fragments.label: Using statements strategically
fragments.text: Statements provide evidence of profitability, liquidity, asset use and financing but are mainly historical. Managers/investors should combine them with ratios, cash-flow forecasts and non-financial information.
gross profit=revenue-cost of sales
operating profit=gross profit-operating expenses
SFP=snapshot
NRV=recoverable inventory value
straight-line=equal annual charge

Ratio analysis converts financial-statement data into indicators of liquidity, profitability, efficiency, gearing and investor return. Calculation is only the first step: top answers compare, diagnose causes, explain consequences, propose actions and recognise limitations.

fragments.label: Liquidity
fragments.text: Ability to meet short-term obligations when they fall due.

fragments.label: Profitability
fragments.text: Ability to generate profit relative to revenue or capital employed.

fragments.label: Efficiency
fragments.text: How effectively working capital/assets are managed to support operations.

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Extent to which long-term capital relies on non-current debt.

fragments.label: ROCE
fragments.text: Operating profit generated as a percentage of capital employed.

fragments.label: P/E ratio
fragments.text: Market price per share relative to earnings per share, often reflecting market expectations.
Liquidity ratios

fragments.label: Liquidity ratios
fragments.text: Current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities. Acid test removes inventory because it may be less liquid. Very low ratios can signal payment risk; very high ratios may signal inefficient working capital. Industry context matters.

fragments.label: Liquidity ratios
fragments.text:
Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities
Acid test = (Current assets - Inventory) / Current liabilities
Profitability ratios

fragments.label: Profitability ratios
fragments.text: Gross margin reflects selling price and direct cost of sales; operating margin also reflects operating expenses. ROCE relates operating profit to long-term capital committed.

fragments.label: Profitability ratios
fragments.text:
Gross profit margin = Gross profit / Revenue x100
Operating profit margin = Profit from operations / Revenue x100
ROCE = Profit from operations / Capital employed x100
Efficiency ratios

fragments.label: Efficiency ratios
fragments.text: Inventory turnover indicates how often inventory is sold/used. Receivables days estimates collection speed from credit customers; payables days estimates payment time to suppliers. Faster is not automatically better if it causes stockouts, customer loss or supplier conflict.

fragments.label: Efficiency ratios
fragments.text:
Inventory turnover = Cost of sales / Average inventory
Receivables days = Trade receivables / Credit sales x365
Payables days = Trade payables / Credit purchases x365
Gearing

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Higher gearing means greater reliance on long-term debt and therefore more fixed interest/repayment risk. Debt can still improve owners' returns when operating returns exceed borrowing cost. Context includes cash-flow stability and interest rates.

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: Gearing (%) = Non-current liabilities / Capital employed x100
Investor ratios

fragments.label: Investor ratios
fragments.text: P/E indicates how highly the market values earnings; dividend yield compares cash dividend with market price; dividend cover indicates how many times profit covers the dividend and therefore how much safety/retention exists.

fragments.label: Investor ratios
fragments.text:
P/E = Market price per share / Earnings per share
Dividend yield = Dividend per share / Market price per share x100
Dividend cover = Profit for the year / Annual dividend
Interpreting and improving

fragments.label: Interpreting and improving
fragments.text: Use previous years, targets, competitors or industry averages. Then move from result -> possible cause -> consequence -> action. Improvements may have trade-offs: tighter receivables collection improves cash but may reduce customer attractiveness.
Limitations

fragments.label: Limitations
fragments.text: Ratios rely on historical accounts and accounting policies, can be distorted by one-off items/inflation/window dressing, omit many intangibles and can be misleading across different business models. They identify symptoms, not proven causes.
liquidity=short-term payment
margin=profit/revenue
ROCE=operating profit/capital
efficiency=inventory/receivable/payable
gearing=long-term debt exposure
ratios need benchmarks

Investment appraisal compares long-term projects using payback, Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) and Net Present Value (NPV). You must calculate each method, understand what it measures, compare its strengths/limitations and integrate qualitative strategic factors before recommending a project.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Time required for cumulative net cash inflows to recover the initial investment.

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: Average annual accounting profit as a percentage of average investment.

fragments.label: Discount factor
fragments.text: Factor converting a future cash flow into present value.

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: Total present value of future net cash flows minus the initial investment.

fragments.label: Time value of money
fragments.text: The principle that money available now is worth more than the same nominal amount received later.
Why appraise investments

fragments.label: Why appraise investments
fragments.text: Major capital projects tie up finance for years and involve uncertain future returns. Appraisal provides structured evidence on liquidity, return and value, helping compare alternatives and justify resource allocation.
Payback

fragments.label: Payback
fragments.text: Add net cash inflows until initial cost is recovered. Short payback is useful when liquidity/risk/technology change matter, but ignores cash flows after payback and usually ignores time value of money.

fragments.label: Payback
fragments.text: If £100k is invested and £80k has been recovered after year 2, with £40k in year 3, another £20k/£40k=0.5 year -> payback 2.5 years.
ARR

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: Uses average annual accounting profit and average investment, producing a familiar percentage. It considers profitability over the project life but uses accounting profit rather than cash and ignores timing of returns.

fragments.label: ARR
fragments.text: ARR = Average annual profit / Average investment x100
NPV

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: Discount each future net cash flow at the required rate and subtract the initial cost. Positive NPV means discounted inflows exceed the initial investment at that required return. Higher NPV generally adds more financial value, but forecasts and discount rate may be wrong.

fragments.label: NPV
fragments.text: NPV = sum of discounted net cash inflows - initial investment
Qualitative factors

fragments.label: Qualitative factors
fragments.text: Strategic fit, brand, employee impact, environmental effect, technological flexibility, legal constraints, risk and competitor reaction can outweigh a small numerical advantage. Quantitative appraisal supports judgement rather than replacing it.
Comparing methods

fragments.label: Comparing methods
fragments.text: Payback emphasises speed/liquidity, ARR accounting profitability and NPV timing/opportunity cost. Rankings can differ. Strong evaluation asks which criterion matters most for the business's objectives/risk and how reliable the forecasts are.
payback=recovery time
ARR=average profit/average investment
NPV=discounted flows-initial cost
NPV recognises time value
qualitative factors still matter

Finance and accounting strategy uses published financial information to support long-term decisions. You must assess performance over time/against competitors and analyse how debt/equity, dividend decisions, business growth and other strategies affect ratios. The key evaluation point is that accounts are useful evidence but not perfect objective truth.

fragments.label: Annual report
fragments.text: Financial statements plus narrative/governance/risk information reporting company performance and position.

fragments.label: Debt finance
fragments.text: Borrowed long-term finance with contractual interest/repayment.

fragments.label: Equity finance
fragments.text: Finance provided by owners/shareholders, affecting ownership and shareholder returns rather than creating contractual interest.

fragments.label: Dividend policy
fragments.text: The approach to distributing profit to shareholders versus retaining it for reinvestment.

fragments.label: Window dressing
fragments.text: Actions/accounting presentation intended to make reported position/performance look more favourable around reporting time.
Using accounts strategically

fragments.label: Using accounts strategically
fragments.text: Accounts reveal profitability, liquidity, efficiency, financing and resource position. Weak liquidity may constrain expansion; strong ROCE may support investment; falling margins may trigger cost/price/product changes. Financial evidence should be combined with market, HR and operations information.
Annual reports and stakeholders

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholders
fragments.text: Annual reports can contain statements, strategic commentary, risk, governance, sustainability and audit information. Investors, lenders, employees, suppliers and managers use different information. Narrative sections provide context but management may emphasise favourable aspects.
Debt versus equity

fragments.label: Debt versus equity
fragments.text: Debt avoids ownership dilution and can be cost-effective, but raises gearing and fixed interest/repayment risk. Equity can reduce debt pressure and strengthen finance capacity but dilutes control/earnings per share and may create dividend expectations. Choice depends on cash-flow stability, interest rates, investor appetite and desired control.
Dividend strategy

fragments.label: Dividend strategy
fragments.text: Higher dividends may attract income-seeking shareholders and signal confidence but reduce retained funds for investment/liquidity. Lower dividends support self-financed growth but may disappoint investors. Dividend decisions affect yield, cover and retained earnings.
Growth and ratio effects

fragments.label: Growth and ratio effects
fragments.text: Expansion can initially weaken liquidity or raise gearing because working capital/capital expenditure must be financed. Later economies/productivity/revenue may improve margins and ROCE. A short-term ratio decline after strategic investment is not automatically failure.
Limitations of published accounts

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts
fragments.text: Accounts are mostly historical, use estimates/accounting policies, can be affected by inflation, one-offs and window dressing, and omit many intangible strengths. Cross-company comparisons can be distorted by different business models/policies. Ratios diagnose symptoms but do not prove causes.
Integrated judgement

fragments.label: Integrated judgement
fragments.text: A finance strategy should support overall objectives. A business pursuing fast growth may accept temporarily higher gearing; a mature firm with stable cash might return more cash to shareholders. The recommendation must fit risk, cash generation and strategic opportunity.
accounts=evidence not strategy
debt=gearing+fixed interest
equity=dilution/no contractual interest
dividend=payout vs retained growth
growth may temporarily weaken ratios
ratios diagnose not prove
A focused revision guide to atomic structure.
Subatomic particles

fragments.label: Subatomic particles
fragments.text: Protons (+1), neutrons (0), electrons (−1, negligible mass). Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count.
Ionisation energy trends

fragments.label: Ionisation energy trends
fragments.text: Increases across a period (more protons, same shell); decreases down a group (extra shielding shells, greater distance).

Bond types

fragments.label: Bond types
fragments.text: Ionic — electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent — shared electron pair(s). Metallic — delocalised electrons attracted to a lattice of positive ions.
Intermolecular forces

fragments.label: Intermolecular forces
fragments.text: Weakest to strongest: van der Waals < permanent dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding (needs H bonded directly to N, O or F).

A focused revision guide to chemical energetics.
Enthalpy change ΔH

fragments.label: Enthalpy change ΔH
fragments.text: Exothermic releases energy (ΔH negative); endothermic absorbs energy (ΔH positive).
Hess's law

fragments.label: Hess's law
fragments.text: Enthalpy change is independent of route. Draw a cycle via a common intermediate and add/subtract arrows to find the unknown ΔH.
Bond energies

fragments.label: Bond energies
fragments.text: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
enthalpy changes

A focused revision guide to equilibria.
Dynamic equilibrium & Le Chatelier

fragments.label: Dynamic equilibrium & Le Chatelier
fragments.text: Forward/reverse rates become equal at equilibrium. A disturbance shifts equilibrium to partially oppose the change — more reactant → shifts to products; more pressure → shifts to fewer gas moles; more heat → shifts endothermic direction.
Kc

fragments.label: Kc
fragments.text: A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change its position or Kc.

fragments.label: Kc
fragments.text: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ

Reaction kinetics explains why some reactions happen faster than others, using collision theory as the underlying model. At AS level the focus is qualitative — explaining rate changes in terms of collision frequency and the proportion of particles with enough energy to react — while the quantitative treatment (rate equations, orders of reaction) comes in the A2 topic.

fragments.label: Activation energy (Ea)
fragments.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur.

fragments.label: Collision theory
fragments.text: The model stating that a reaction only occurs when particles collide with energy ≥ Ea and in the correct orientation.

fragments.label: Catalyst
fragments.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, without itself being used up.
Collision theory & activation energy

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Not every collision between particles leads to a reaction — only those with enough energy (≥ Ea) and the correct orientation actually react. This is why increasing the frequency or energy of collisions increases the rate.

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Weak collision (low energy) → particles bounce apart, no reaction

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Collision with E ≥ Ea and correct orientation → bonds break/form, reaction occurs
Factors affecting rate

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Concentration/pressure increase the number of particles per unit volume, so collisions happen more often. Surface area (for solids) exposes more particles to collide with. Temperature increases both the speed of particles and, more importantly, the proportion with energy ≥ Ea. A catalyst offers a lower-energy pathway, so a larger fraction of collisions now exceed the (lower) activation energy.

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Doubling the concentration of a reactant roughly doubles collision frequency (for a first-order reactant)

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: A platinum catalyst in the Contact process lowers Ea for SO₂ oxidation
The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: This is a graph of the number of particles (y-axis) against their kinetic energy (x-axis) at a given temperature — an asymmetric curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak, then tailing off. Raising the temperature shifts the peak right and flattens/broadens the curve, while the total area under the curve stays the same (same number of particles). Crucially, the area under the curve beyond Ea — the fraction of particles that can react — increases sharply even for a modest temperature rise.

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T1, only a small area of the curve lies beyond Ea

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T2 > T1, the curve flattens/shifts right, and a much larger area lies beyond Ea, even though Ea itself hasn't changed
Rate increases only if collisions occur more often AND/OR more collisions exceed Ea
Catalyst = lower Ea via alternative pathway, not used up
Temperature ↑ → M-B curve flattens/shifts right → more particles exceed Ea
