Use Born-Haber cycles and lattice energy, and consider entropy and Gibbs free energy to judge whether a reaction is feasible. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Lattice energy
fragments.text: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.

fragments.label: Atomisation enthalpy
fragments.text: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous atoms forms from the element in its standard state.

fragments.label: Electron affinity
fragments.text: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous atoms gains electrons to form gaseous anions.

fragments.label: Hydration enthalpy
fragments.text: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous ions becomes aqueous ions under standard conditions.

fragments.label: Entropy
fragments.text: A measure related to the dispersal of energy and the number of accessible arrangements.

fragments.label: Gibbs free-energy change
fragments.text: ΔG, the thermodynamic quantity used to judge feasibility at a stated temperature.
Born–Haber cycles

fragments.label: Born–Haber cycles
fragments.text: Build the ionic solid from elements through atomisation, ionisation, electron gain and lattice formation. Hess's law makes the signed sum equal to ΔHf°. If a second electron affinity or ionisation energy is needed, include it as a separate endothermic step.

fragments.label: Born–Haber cycles
fragments.text: Write a chemical equation beside every enthalpy term.

fragments.label: Born–Haber cycles
fragments.text: Use the syllabus convention: lattice formation is usually exothermic and negative.

fragments.label: Born–Haber cycles
fragments.text: Born–Haber balance: ΔHf°=sum of atomisation + ionisation + electron-affinity + lattice steps
Lattice and hydration trends

fragments.label: Lattice and hydration trends
fragments.text: Higher ionic charge and smaller ionic radius increase electrostatic attraction, making lattice energy and hydration enthalpy more negative. Comparing experimental and theoretical lattice energies can indicate extra covalent character caused by polarisation.

fragments.label: Lattice and hydration trends
fragments.text: Compare charge density, not only ionic size.

fragments.label: Lattice and hydration trends
fragments.text: A small highly charged cation strongly polarises a large anion.
Dissolving ionic solids

fragments.label: Dissolving ionic solids
fragments.text: An enthalpy-of-solution cycle combines lattice dissociation with hydration of each gaseous ion. ΔHsol° alone does not determine solubility because entropy also matters, but it explains the energetic balance.

fragments.label: Dissolving ionic solids
fragments.text: Reverse lattice formation when breaking the solid into gaseous ions.

fragments.label: Dissolving ionic solids
fragments.text: Include hydration once per mole of each ion in the formula.
Entropy and Gibbs energy

fragments.label: Entropy and Gibbs energy
fragments.text: Calculate ΔS°=ΣS°products−ΣS°reactants, convert J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when combining with ΔH, then use ΔG°=ΔH°−TΔS°. ΔG°<0 indicates thermodynamic feasibility under the stated conditions, not a fast rate.

fragments.label: Entropy and Gibbs energy
fragments.text: Temperature must be in kelvin.

fragments.label: Entropy and Gibbs energy
fragments.text: A positive ΔG° does not prove a reaction is impossible under all non-standard conditions.
What makes lattice energy more negative?

fragments.label: What makes lattice energy more negative?
fragments.text: Larger ionic charges and smaller ionic radii.
Why is the second electron affinity endothermic?

fragments.label: Why is the second electron affinity endothermic?
fragments.text: An electron is forced onto an already negative ion, so electrostatic repulsion must be overcome.
What does ΔG°<0 mean?

fragments.label: What does ΔG°<0 mean?
fragments.text: The process is thermodynamically feasible under the stated standard conditions; it says nothing about speed.
Which unit conversion is commonly missed in ΔG calculations?

fragments.label: Which unit conversion is commonly missed in ΔG calculations?
fragments.text: Convert ΔS from J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ if ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹.

Use standard electrode potentials to calculate cell potentials and predict whether a redox reaction is feasible. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Standard electrode potential
fragments.text: The emf of a half-cell relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions, written as a reduction.

fragments.label: Standard hydrogen electrode
fragments.text: The reference half-cell with E°=0.00 V.

fragments.label: Salt bridge
fragments.text: An ionic connection that completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality without bulk mixing.

fragments.label: Cell potential
fragments.text: The potential difference between two half-cells.

fragments.label: Faraday constant
fragments.text: The charge carried by 1 mol of electrons, approximately 9.65×10⁴ C mol⁻¹.

fragments.label: Electrolysis
fragments.text: Using electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox process.
Half-cells and standard conditions

fragments.label: Half-cells and standard conditions
fragments.text: Standard E° values refer to 298 K, solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³ and gases at 100 kPa, measured against the hydrogen electrode. Tables show reduction half-equations; a more positive E° means a greater tendency to be reduced.

fragments.label: Half-cells and standard conditions
fragments.text: An inert Pt electrode is needed when no conducting solid redox species is present.

fragments.label: Half-cells and standard conditions
fragments.text: Electrons travel through the wire; ions move through the salt bridge.

fragments.label: Half-cells and standard conditions
fragments.text: Cell potential: E°cell=E°cathode−E°anode
Cell notation and E°cell

fragments.label: Cell notation and E°cell
fragments.text: Write the oxidation half-cell on the left and reduction half-cell on the right, with phase boundaries | and a salt bridge ||. Calculate E°cell=E°right−E°left using reduction potentials. Balance electrons only for the overall equation; never multiply E° values by stoichiometric coefficients.

fragments.label: Cell notation and E°cell
fragments.text: The cathode is reduction and the anode is oxidation.

fragments.label: Cell notation and E°cell
fragments.text: Include states in half-equations.
Feasibility and limitations

fragments.label: Feasibility and limitations
fragments.text: A positive E°cell predicts a thermodynamically feasible forward reaction under standard conditions. Actual behaviour can differ because concentrations, gas pressures and temperature are non-standard, reactions are kinetically slow, or activation energy is high.

fragments.label: Feasibility and limitations
fragments.text: Choose the oxidising agent from the more positive reduction potential.

fragments.label: Feasibility and limitations
fragments.text: Do not use E° alone to predict rate.
Quantitative electrolysis

fragments.label: Quantitative electrolysis
fragments.text: Charge Q=It. Moles of electrons equal Q/F; use the balanced electrode half-equation to convert electron moles to product moles, then to mass or gas volume. Current in amperes is coulombs per second.

fragments.label: Quantitative electrolysis
fragments.text: Convert minutes to seconds.

fragments.label: Quantitative electrolysis
fragments.text: Use the electron coefficient from the half-equation, not the overall equation blindly.
Which half-cell is on the right in standard cell notation?

fragments.label: Which half-cell is on the right in standard cell notation?
fragments.text: The reduction half-cell (cathode).
Why are E° values not multiplied when a half-equation is scaled?

fragments.label: Why are E° values not multiplied when a half-equation is scaled?
fragments.text: Potential is an intensive quantity; scaling amount does not scale voltage.
What does positive E°cell predict?

fragments.label: What does positive E°cell predict?
fragments.text: Thermodynamic feasibility of the written cell reaction under standard conditions.
How are moles of electrons found from current and time?

fragments.label: How are moles of electrons found from current and time?
fragments.text: Calculate Q=It, then divide by F.

Work with Ka, Kw and pH for acids and bases, understand how buffers resist pH change, and use Ksp and partition coefficients. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Brønsted–Lowry acid
fragments.text: A proton donor.

fragments.label: Brønsted–Lowry base
fragments.text: A proton acceptor.

fragments.label: Ka
fragments.text: The acid-dissociation constant for HA⇌H⁺+A⁻.

fragments.label: Buffer solution
fragments.text: A solution that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.

fragments.label: Solubility product
fragments.text: Ksp, the equilibrium constant for dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid.

fragments.label: Partition coefficient
fragments.text: The equilibrium concentration ratio of a solute between two immiscible solvents at a fixed temperature.
Acid–base equilibria

fragments.label: Acid–base equilibria
fragments.text: For weak HA, Ka=[H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] and pKa=−log₁₀Ka. Set up an equilibrium table and use approximations only when justified. Kw=[H⁺][OH⁻]=1.00×10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K, so pH+pOH=14 at that temperature.

fragments.label: Acid–base equilibria
fragments.text: Strong describes extent of ionisation, not concentration.

fragments.label: Acid–base equilibria
fragments.text: Check any small-x approximation against the initial concentration.

fragments.label: Acid–base equilibria
fragments.text: pH: pH=−log₁₀[H⁺]
Buffers

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: An acidic buffer contains HA and A⁻. Added H⁺ is removed by A⁻; added OH⁻ is removed by HA. Use [H⁺]=Ka[HA]/[A⁻] or pH=pKa+log([A⁻]/[HA]), after accounting stoichiometrically for any added strong acid/base.

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: Use mole ratios when both components share the same final volume.

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: Buffer capacity is finite and greatest when both components are substantial.
Ksp and precipitation

fragments.label: Ksp and precipitation
fragments.text: Write the dissolution equation before the Ksp expression. For MX₂⇌M²⁺+2X⁻, Ksp=[M²⁺][X⁻]²; molar solubility s gives s(2s)². After mixing solutions, calculate diluted ion concentrations and compare ionic product Qsp with Ksp.

fragments.label: Ksp and precipitation
fragments.text: Qsp>Ksp predicts precipitation.

fragments.label: Ksp and precipitation
fragments.text: Stoichiometric coefficients become powers and concentration multipliers.
Partition and extraction

fragments.label: Partition and extraction
fragments.text: For solute X, Kpc=[X]organic/[X]aqueous using the stated order. Calculate amount remaining from equilibrium concentration ratios and phase volumes. Several small extractions remove more solute than one extraction with the same total solvent volume.

fragments.label: Partition and extraction
fragments.text: Use concentrations, not raw moles, in Kpc.

fragments.label: Partition and extraction
fragments.text: The solute must have the same molecular form in both solvents unless the question accounts for reaction.
How does an acidic buffer remove added H⁺?

fragments.label: How does an acidic buffer remove added H⁺?
fragments.text: Its conjugate base A⁻ reacts with H⁺ to form HA.
When does precipitation begin?

fragments.label: When does precipitation begin?
fragments.text: When the ionic product reaches Ksp; Qsp>Ksp favours solid formation.
Why are several extractions more effective?

fragments.label: Why are several extractions more effective?
fragments.text: Each fresh portion establishes a new partition equilibrium and removes a fraction of what remains.
What is the difference between strong and concentrated?

fragments.label: What is the difference between strong and concentrated?
fragments.text: Strong means nearly complete ionisation; concentrated means many moles per unit volume.

Determine rate equations and orders of reaction from experimental data, and link mechanisms and catalysis to kinetics in more depth. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Order of reaction
fragments.text: The exponent of a reactant concentration in an experimentally determined rate equation.

fragments.label: Rate constant
fragments.text: k, the proportionality constant in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.

fragments.label: Half-life
fragments.text: Time for a reactant concentration to fall to half its value.

fragments.label: Rate-determining step
fragments.text: The slow elementary step controlling the observed rate.

fragments.label: Activation energy
fragments.text: The minimum energy barrier along a reaction pathway.

fragments.label: Catalyst
fragments.text: A substance that increases rate by providing a lower-activation-energy route and is regenerated overall.
Rate equations from data

fragments.label: Rate equations from data
fragments.text: For rate=k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, compare experiments where one concentration changes and others stay constant. A doubled concentration causing unchanged, doubled or quadrupled rate indicates order 0, 1 or 2 respectively. Calculate k after finding all orders and derive its units from the overall order.

fragments.label: Rate equations from data
fragments.text: Order is experimental and need not match equation coefficients.

fragments.label: Rate equations from data
fragments.text: Use initial rates to avoid changing concentrations during the run.

fragments.label: Rate equations from data
fragments.text: Rate equation: rate=k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ
Concentration–time evidence

fragments.label: Concentration–time evidence
fragments.text: A zero-order graph [A] against t is linear; first-order gives constant half-life and ln[A] against t linear; second-order gives increasing half-life and 1/[A] against t linear. Gradient information can determine k where required.

fragments.label: Concentration–time evidence
fragments.text: Constant half-life is strong first-order evidence.

fragments.label: Concentration–time evidence
fragments.text: Initial tangent gradients give initial rates.
Mechanisms

fragments.label: Mechanisms
fragments.text: A proposed elementary mechanism must sum to the overall equation and reproduce the observed rate equation. Species in the slow step may determine rate; if an intermediate appears, use a preceding fast equilibrium or step relationship as directed to eliminate it.

fragments.label: Mechanisms
fragments.text: A catalyst may appear in the mechanism but cancels from the overall equation.

fragments.label: Mechanisms
fragments.text: Reject a mechanism that conflicts with experimental orders.
Temperature and catalysis

fragments.label: Temperature and catalysis
fragments.text: Arrhenius gives ln k=ln A−Ea/(RT), so a plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −Ea/R. A homogeneous catalyst shares a phase and may form intermediates; a heterogeneous catalyst adsorbs reactants, weakens bonds, allows reaction, then desorbs products.

fragments.label: Temperature and catalysis
fragments.text: Use kelvin and Ea in J mol⁻¹ with R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

fragments.label: Temperature and catalysis
fragments.text: Catalysts change rate, not ΔH or equilibrium position.
Does stoichiometry determine reaction order?

fragments.label: Does stoichiometry determine reaction order?
fragments.text: No; order is found experimentally unless an elementary step is explicitly considered.
What kinetic feature indicates first order?

fragments.label: What kinetic feature indicates first order?
fragments.text: A constant half-life as concentration decreases.
What must a valid mechanism reproduce?

fragments.label: What must a valid mechanism reproduce?
fragments.text: Both the overall equation and the experimental rate equation.
What does a catalyst change thermodynamically?

fragments.label: What does a catalyst change thermodynamically?
fragments.text: It changes neither ΔH nor equilibrium position; it lowers the activation barrier for both directions.

Extend Group 2 trends to explain thermal stability and solubility patterns in more quantitative detail. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Charge density
fragments.text: Charge per effective ionic volume; it falls down Group 2 as M²⁺ radius increases.

fragments.label: Thermal stability
fragments.text: Resistance of a compound to decomposition on heating.

fragments.label: Polarisation
fragments.text: Distortion of an anion's electron cloud by a cation.

fragments.label: Solubility
fragments.text: The maximum equilibrium amount dissolved in a specified solvent at a stated temperature.

fragments.label: Lattice enthalpy
fragments.text: The enthalpy change associated with forming an ionic lattice from gaseous ions.

fragments.label: Hydration enthalpy
fragments.text: The enthalpy change when gaseous ions become hydrated aqueous ions.
Ionic trends

fragments.label: Ionic trends
fragments.text: M²⁺ radius increases down the group while charge stays +2, so charge density and polarising power decrease. Lattice and hydration enthalpies become less negative in magnitude, but not always at the same rate.

fragments.label: Ionic trends
fragments.text: Explain trends through competing enthalpy changes, not a single memorised slogan.

fragments.label: Ionic trends
fragments.text: The anion is constant within a solubility series.

fragments.label: Ionic trends
fragments.text: Carbonate decomposition: MCO₃(s)→MO(s)+CO₂(g)
Hydroxide and sulfate solubility

fragments.label: Hydroxide and sulfate solubility
fragments.text: Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group because lattice enthalpy weakens faster than hydration enthalpy. Sulfates become less soluble because the hydration advantage falls more significantly relative to lattice change for the large sulfate ion.

fragments.label: Hydroxide and sulfate solubility
fragments.text: More soluble hydroxides give more alkaline saturated solutions.

fragments.label: Hydroxide and sulfate solubility
fragments.text: BaSO₄ is very insoluble and used as a sulfate test/contrast medium when appropriate.
Thermal stability

fragments.label: Thermal stability
fragments.text: Carbonates decompose to MO+CO₂; nitrates form MO+NO₂+O₂. Stability increases down the group because larger M²⁺ ions polarise the large anions less, so their internal covalent bonds are less weakened.

fragments.label: Thermal stability
fragments.text: Mg compounds decompose more readily than Ba compounds.

fragments.label: Thermal stability
fragments.text: Write balanced decomposition equations.
Applications and observations

fragments.label: Applications and observations
fragments.text: Use solubility rules to predict precipitates and observations. Magnesium hydroxide can neutralise acid; calcium compounds have agricultural/building uses; barium compounds require toxicity awareness, while insoluble BaSO₄ behaves differently from soluble Ba²⁺ salts.

fragments.label: Applications and observations
fragments.text: Link any use to a chemical property.

fragments.label: Applications and observations
fragments.text: Do not generalise toxicity without specifying the compound and solubility.
Why does thermal stability increase down Group 2?

fragments.label: Why does thermal stability increase down Group 2?
fragments.text: Larger M²⁺ ions have lower charge density and polarise carbonate/nitrate ions less.
What is the hydroxide solubility trend?

fragments.label: What is the hydroxide solubility trend?
fragments.text: It generally increases down Group 2.
What is the sulfate solubility trend?

fragments.label: What is the sulfate solubility trend?
fragments.text: It generally decreases down Group 2.
Why is 'lattice energy decreases' alone insufficient for solubility?

fragments.label: Why is 'lattice energy decreases' alone insufficient for solubility?
fragments.text: Dissolving balances lattice breaking against hydration, so both trends must be compared.

Understand transition metal complexes and ligands, the origin of colour, and their role as catalysts. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Transition element
fragments.text: A d-block element forming at least one stable ion with an incomplete d subshell.

fragments.label: Ligand
fragments.text: An ion or molecule donating a lone pair to a central metal ion.

fragments.label: Complex ion
fragments.text: A central metal ion bonded to surrounding ligands by coordinate bonds.

fragments.label: Coordination number
fragments.text: The number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion.

fragments.label: Ligand exchange
fragments.text: Replacement of one ligand in a complex by another.

fragments.label: Stability constant
fragments.text: An equilibrium constant for formation of a complex from a metal ion and ligands.

fragments.label: d-orbital splitting
fragments.text: Separation of d-orbital energy levels by the ligand environment.
Electronic structure and oxidation states

fragments.label: Electronic structure and oxidation states
fragments.text: Remove 4s electrons before 3d when forming first-row transition-metal ions. Variable oxidation states arise because 3d and 4s energies are similar. Use oxidation numbers, charge and ligand charges to identify the metal state.

fragments.label: Electronic structure and oxidation states
fragments.text: Zn is d-block but Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so it does not meet every characteristic transition definition.

fragments.label: Electronic structure and oxidation states
fragments.text: State electron configurations for the ion, not only the atom.

fragments.label: Electronic structure and oxidation states
fragments.text: Complex formation: Mⁿ⁺+xL⇌[MLₓ]ⁿ⁺
Complexes and ligand exchange

fragments.label: Complexes and ligand exchange
fragments.text: Common ligands include H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻ and bidentate ethanedioate/ethane-1,2-diamine. Coordination 6 is usually octahedral; coordination 4 may be tetrahedral or square planar. Ligand exchange changes colour, charge and sometimes geometry.

fragments.label: Complexes and ligand exchange
fragments.text: Count donor atoms, not ligand molecules, for coordination number.

fragments.label: Complexes and ligand exchange
fragments.text: Write balanced ionic equations for exchange.
Colour, redox and stability

fragments.label: Colour, redox and stability
fragments.text: Ligands split d orbitals; visible light promotes a d electron and the complementary colour is observed. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions usually lack d–d colour. Use E° values to judge redox direction. Large Kstab favours complex formation; chelating ligands often gain stability partly through entropy.

fragments.label: Colour, redox and stability
fragments.text: Colour depends on metal, oxidation state, ligand and geometry.

fragments.label: Colour, redox and stability
fragments.text: E° predicts feasibility, not reaction rate.
Catalysis

fragments.label: Catalysis
fragments.text: Homogeneous transition-metal catalysts use variable oxidation states and form intermediates, providing a lower-energy sequence. Heterogeneous metals provide adsorption sites; reactant bonds weaken, surface reaction occurs and products desorb, freeing sites.

fragments.label: Catalysis
fragments.text: A catalyst is regenerated by the end of the mechanism.

fragments.label: Catalysis
fragments.text: Explain poisoning as blocking active sites where relevant.
Which electrons are removed first from a first-row d-block atom?

fragments.label: Which electrons are removed first from a first-row d-block atom?
fragments.text: The 4s electrons are removed before 3d.
What does coordination number count?

fragments.label: What does coordination number count?
fragments.text: Coordinate bonds/donor atoms attached to the central ion.
Why are many transition-metal complexes coloured?

fragments.label: Why are many transition-metal complexes coloured?
fragments.text: Visible light is absorbed to promote electrons between ligand-split d levels.
Why can transition metals catalyse redox reactions?

fragments.label: Why can transition metals catalyse redox reactions?
fragments.text: They access multiple oxidation states and form intermediates, creating lower-energy pathways.

title: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry

fragments.text: Extend organic nomenclature to more complex molecules, understand aromatic (benzene) bonding, and optical isomerism. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Arene
fragments.text: An aromatic hydrocarbon containing a benzene ring.

fragments.label: Delocalisation
fragments.text: Electron density spread over several adjacent atoms rather than confined to one bond.

fragments.label: Chiral centre
fragments.text: Usually a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups.

fragments.label: Enantiomers
fragments.text: Non-superimposable mirror-image stereoisomers.

fragments.label: Optical activity
fragments.text: Rotation of plane-polarised light by a chiral sample.

fragments.label: Racemic mixture
fragments.text: An equal mixture of two enantiomers with no net optical rotation.
Naming complex molecules

fragments.label: Naming complex molecules
fragments.text: Choose the parent chain/ring containing the highest-priority functional group, number for the lowest relevant locants, and name substituents alphabetically. Recognise phenyl (C₆H₅–) as a substituent and distinguish benzyl/side-chain positions when structures are supplied.

fragments.label: Naming complex molecules
fragments.text: The suffix functional group controls the parent and numbering.

fragments.label: Naming complex molecules
fragments.text: Use commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and words.

fragments.label: Naming complex molecules
fragments.text: Benzene: C₆H₆: planar σ framework + six delocalised π electrons
Benzene structure

fragments.label: Benzene structure
fragments.text: Each carbon is trigonal planar and contributes one p orbital. Six π electrons are delocalised above and below the planar σ framework, making all C–C bonds equal and the ring more stable than a localised cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene model.

fragments.label: Benzene structure
fragments.text: Use a circle or equal bonds to represent delocalisation.

fragments.label: Benzene structure
fragments.text: Aromatic stability helps explain substitution rather than addition.
Chirality and enantiomers

fragments.label: Chirality and enantiomers
fragments.text: A carbon with four different substituents is chiral unless symmetry makes the whole molecule achiral. Draw mirror images with wedge/dash bonds and test superimposability. Enantiomers share most physical properties but rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions and may interact differently with chiral reagents.

fragments.label: Chirality and enantiomers
fragments.text: A carbon with two identical groups is not chiral.

fragments.label: Chirality and enantiomers
fragments.text: Do not confuse E/Z isomerism with optical isomerism.
Formation and mixtures

fragments.label: Formation and mixtures
fragments.text: Attack on a planar intermediate from either face can produce equal enantiomers and a racemic mixture. A single enantiomer may form when a chiral environment, catalyst or starting material differentiates the faces. Connect stereochemical reasoning to the mechanism supplied.

fragments.label: Formation and mixtures
fragments.text: A racemate contains molecules that are individually chiral.

fragments.label: Formation and mixtures
fragments.text: Zero net rotation results from cancellation, not absence of enantiomers.
What structural feature usually creates chirality?

fragments.label: What structural feature usually creates chirality?
fragments.text: A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups.
Why are benzene C–C bonds equal?

fragments.label: Why are benzene C–C bonds equal?
fragments.text: The six π electrons are delocalised around the ring.
Why is a racemic mixture optically inactive?

fragments.label: Why is a racemic mixture optically inactive?
fragments.text: Equal and opposite rotations from the two enantiomers cancel.
Are enantiomers structural isomers?

fragments.label: Are enantiomers structural isomers?
fragments.text: No; they have the same connectivity and are stereoisomers.

Understand the structure of benzene and its characteristic electrophilic substitution reactions. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Electrophile
fragments.text: An electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions.

fragments.label: Electrophilic substitution
fragments.text: A reaction replacing a ring hydrogen by an electrophile while restoring aromaticity.

fragments.label: Aromatic stabilisation
fragments.text: Extra stability from π-electron delocalisation around the ring.

fragments.label: Friedel–Crafts alkylation
fragments.text: Ring substitution introducing an alkyl group using a halogenoalkane and AlCl₃.

fragments.label: Friedel–Crafts acylation
fragments.text: Ring substitution introducing an acyl group using an acyl chloride and AlCl₃.

fragments.label: Directing group
fragments.text: A substituent influencing the positions favoured by further ring substitution.
Core arene reactions

fragments.label: Core arene reactions
fragments.text: Benzene reacts with Br₂/AlBr₃ or Cl₂/AlCl₃, concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ at about 25–60 °C, CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ with heat, or CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ with heat. Hydrogenation uses H₂ with Ni/Pt and heat. Learn product, reagent, catalyst and condition as one package.

fragments.label: Core arene reactions
fragments.text: Bromine water alone does not rapidly decolourise benzene.

fragments.label: Core arene reactions
fragments.text: Friedel–Crafts products retain the aromatic ring.

fragments.label: Core arene reactions
fragments.text: Nitrating electrophile: HNO₃+H₂SO₄→NO₂⁺+HSO₄⁻+H₂O
Electrophilic substitution mechanism

fragments.label: Electrophilic substitution mechanism
fragments.text: Generate the electrophile (for nitration, NO₂⁺). A curly arrow moves from the benzene π system to the electrophile, producing a positively charged intermediate; a base removes H⁺ and the C–H bond electrons restore delocalisation.

fragments.label: Electrophilic substitution mechanism
fragments.text: Curly arrows begin at an electron pair or bond.

fragments.label: Electrophilic substitution mechanism
fragments.text: Show the positive intermediate and restored ring.
Methylbenzene and side chains

fragments.label: Methylbenzene and side chains
fragments.text: Methylbenzene can undergo ring substitution more readily than benzene, side-chain radical halogenation under UV light, and complete side-chain oxidation with hot alkaline KMnO₄ followed by acid to benzoic acid, provided a benzylic hydrogen is present.

fragments.label: Methylbenzene and side chains
fragments.text: Conditions decide ring versus side-chain halogenation.

fragments.label: Methylbenzene and side chains
fragments.text: Oxidation shortens an oxidisable alkyl side chain to –COOH.
Directing effects

fragments.label: Directing effects
fragments.text: –NH₂, –OH and alkyl groups direct mainly to 2/4 positions; –NO₂, –COOH and –COR direct mainly to position 3. Use the substituent already on the ring to predict major isomers without claiming a single exclusive product.

fragments.label: Directing effects
fragments.text: Number positions relative to the existing substituent.

fragments.label: Directing effects
fragments.text: Directing effect and activation are related but not identical statements.
Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?

fragments.label: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
fragments.text: Substitution restores aromatic delocalisation; addition would permanently lose that stabilisation.
What is the electrophile in nitration?

fragments.label: What is the electrophile in nitration?
fragments.text: NO₂⁺, the nitronium ion.
How do –OH and –NO₂ direct further substitution?

fragments.label: How do –OH and –NO₂ direct further substitution?
fragments.text: –OH mainly directs 2/4; –NO₂ mainly directs 3.
What conditions favour side-chain chlorination of methylbenzene?

fragments.label: What conditions favour side-chain chlorination of methylbenzene?
fragments.text: Chlorine with UV light/free-radical conditions rather than AlCl₃ ring-substitution conditions.

Extend halogen compound chemistry to more complex mechanisms and reactivity patterns. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Halogenoarene
fragments.text: A compound with halogen directly bonded to an aromatic-ring carbon.

fragments.label: Halogenoalkane
fragments.text: A compound with halogen bonded to an sp³ carbon of an alkyl group.

fragments.label: Halogen carrier
fragments.text: A Lewis-acid catalyst such as AlCl₃ or AlBr₃ that helps generate an electrophile.

fragments.label: Partial double-bond character
fragments.text: Bond strengthening caused by overlap/delocalisation that makes a bond shorter and harder to break.

fragments.label: Nucleophile
fragments.text: An electron-pair donor.

fragments.label: Hydrolysis
fragments.text: Bond cleavage involving water or aqueous hydroxide.
Making halogenoarenes

fragments.label: Making halogenoarenes
fragments.text: React benzene or methylbenzene with Cl₂/AlCl₃ or Br₂/AlBr₃ to substitute a ring hydrogen. With methylbenzene, the alkyl group directs mainly to 2 and 4 positions. Write HCl or HBr as the other product.

fragments.label: Making halogenoarenes
fragments.text: The catalyst is a halogen carrier, not UV light.

fragments.label: Making halogenoarenes
fragments.text: State positional isomers where the directing effect matters.

fragments.label: Making halogenoarenes
fragments.text: Ring chlorination: C₆H₆+Cl₂ —AlCl₃→ C₆H₅Cl+HCl
Halogenoarene bonding

fragments.label: Halogenoarene bonding
fragments.text: In chlorobenzene, a chlorine lone pair overlaps with the ring π system, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character. The ring carbon is sp² and the bond is shorter/stronger than in chloroethane, so nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis is much harder.

fragments.label: Halogenoarene bonding
fragments.text: Do not explain the lower reactivity only by bond polarity.

fragments.label: Halogenoarene bonding
fragments.text: Delocalisation involves a chlorine lone pair and the aromatic system.
Ring versus side chain

fragments.label: Ring versus side chain
fragments.text: Cl₂/AlCl₃ gives ring substitution; Cl₂ under UV radical conditions attacks an alkyl side chain. The substrate and conditions must both be read before predicting the product.

fragments.label: Ring versus side chain
fragments.text: A halogen on the side-chain carbon is a halogenoalkane functional group.

fragments.label: Ring versus side chain
fragments.text: A halogen directly on the ring is a halogenoarene.
Comparative reaction reasoning

fragments.label: Comparative reaction reasoning
fragments.text: Halogenoalkanes can undergo nucleophilic substitution because their polar Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻ bond is accessible and breakable under suitable conditions. Halogenoarenes resist the same conditions because the aromatic carbon–halogen bond is strengthened and the planar electron-rich ring disfavors the usual pathway.

fragments.label: Comparative reaction reasoning
fragments.text: Compare bond strength, hybridisation/environment and mechanism.

fragments.label: Comparative reaction reasoning
fragments.text: Use named example pairs such as chloroethane/chlorobenzene.
Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloroethane to nucleophiles?

fragments.label: Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloroethane to nucleophiles?
fragments.text: Its C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character from delocalisation and is shorter/stronger on an sp² carbon.
What conditions chlorinate the aromatic ring?

fragments.label: What conditions chlorinate the aromatic ring?
fragments.text: Cl₂ with AlCl₃ as halogen carrier.
What conditions favour side-chain chlorination?

fragments.label: What conditions favour side-chain chlorination?
fragments.text: Cl₂ with UV light/free-radical conditions.
How is a halogenoarene identified?

fragments.label: How is a halogenoarene identified?
fragments.text: The halogen is directly bonded to an aromatic-ring carbon.

Understand the chemistry of phenol alongside alcohols, and further synthetic routes between them. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Phenol
fragments.text: A compound with –OH directly attached to an aromatic ring.

fragments.label: Phenoxide ion
fragments.text: C₆H₅O⁻, the conjugate base of phenol.

fragments.label: Acidity
fragments.text: Tendency to donate H⁺; stronger acids form more stable conjugate bases.

fragments.label: Diazonium salt
fragments.text: An aromatic compound containing the –N₂⁺ group, formed cold from a primary aromatic amine.

fragments.label: Azo compound
fragments.text: A coloured compound containing an –N=N– link between carbon groups.

fragments.label: Acylation
fragments.text: Introduction of an acyl group, often by reaction with an acyl chloride.
Alcohol acylation

fragments.label: Alcohol acylation
fragments.text: Alcohols react with acyl chlorides at room temperature to form esters and HCl. This is faster and more complete than acid-catalysed esterification. Name the ester by the alcohol-derived alkyl group followed by the acid-derived carboxylate.

fragments.label: Alcohol acylation
fragments.text: Acyl chlorides fume in moist air because hydrolysis releases HCl.

fragments.label: Alcohol acylation
fragments.text: Keep the carbonyl oxygen in the acyl fragment.

fragments.label: Alcohol acylation
fragments.text: Acylation: RCOCl+R′OH→RCOOR′+HCl
Making and reacting phenol

fragments.label: Making and reacting phenol
fragments.text: Phenylamine reacts with HNO₂ generated from NaNO₂/dilute acid below 10 °C to form a diazonium salt; warming with water gives phenol. Phenol reacts with Na or NaOH to form phenoxide, with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature to give 2-/4-nitrophenol, and with Br₂(aq) to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

fragments.label: Making and reacting phenol
fragments.text: Cold conditions stabilise the diazonium ion.

fragments.label: Making and reacting phenol
fragments.text: Bromination gives a white precipitate and decolourises bromine water.
Acidity

fragments.label: Acidity
fragments.text: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because negative charge in phenoxide is delocalised into the ring; ethoxide has no comparable stabilisation. Phenol is less acidic than carboxylic acids, whose carboxylate charge is delocalised equally over two electronegative oxygen atoms.

fragments.label: Acidity
fragments.text: Phenol reacts with NaOH but not normally Na₂CO₃.

fragments.label: Acidity
fragments.text: Use conjugate-base stability in explanations.
Activated ring and azo coupling

fragments.label: Activated ring and azo coupling
fragments.text: The –OH group donates electron density into the ring, activating it and directing substitution to 2,4,6 positions, so phenol nitrates/brominates under milder conditions than benzene. In alkaline solution, phenoxide couples with a diazonium ion to form an azo dye.

fragments.label: Activated ring and azo coupling
fragments.text: Compare conditions explicitly with benzene.

fragments.label: Activated ring and azo coupling
fragments.text: Show the –N=N– linkage in an azo product.
Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?

fragments.label: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
fragments.text: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation into the aromatic ring; ethoxide is not.
How is phenol made from phenylamine?

fragments.label: How is phenol made from phenylamine?
fragments.text: Diazotise below 10 °C with HNO₂, then warm the diazonium salt with water.
Why does phenol brominate without AlBr₃?

fragments.label: Why does phenol brominate without AlBr₃?
fragments.text: –OH donates electron density and activates the ring.
What links the rings in an azo dye?

fragments.label: What links the rings in an azo dye?
fragments.text: An –N=N– group.

Understand the reactions of acyl chlorides and acyl substitution reactions in more depth. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Acyl chloride
fragments.text: A reactive carboxylic-acid derivative with functional group –COCl.

fragments.label: Nucleophilic acyl substitution
fragments.text: Addition to a carbonyl followed by elimination of a leaving group.

fragments.label: Amide
fragments.text: A carboxylic-acid derivative containing –CONH₂, –CONHR or –CONR₂.

fragments.label: Electron-withdrawing group
fragments.text: A group that pulls electron density and can stabilise nearby negative charge.

fragments.label: Benzoic acid
fragments.text: C₆H₅COOH, an aromatic carboxylic acid.

fragments.label: Ester
fragments.text: A derivative containing –COOR.
Carboxylic acids

fragments.label: Carboxylic acids
fragments.text: Oxidise an alkylbenzene with a benzylic hydrogen using hot alkaline KMnO₄ then acidify to obtain benzoic acid. Convert RCOOH to RCOCl using PCl₅, PCl₃ with heat or SOCl₂. Methanoic and ethanedioic acids can be further oxidised under the syllabus reagents.

fragments.label: Carboxylic acids
fragments.text: Write observations/products for oxidising-agent tests where asked.

fragments.label: Carboxylic acids
fragments.text: SOCl₂ gives gaseous by-products that help drive formation.

fragments.label: Carboxylic acids
fragments.text: Acyl chloride hydrolysis: RCOCl+H₂O→RCOOH+HCl
Acidity trends

fragments.label: Acidity trends
fragments.text: Carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols and alcohols because carboxylate charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms. Electron-withdrawing chlorine substituents stabilise the carboxylate by an inductive effect; more/closer Cl atoms generally increase acidity.

fragments.label: Acidity trends
fragments.text: Compare conjugate bases, not the O–H bond alone.

fragments.label: Acidity trends
fragments.text: Inductive effect weakens with distance.
Acyl-chloride reactions

fragments.label: Acyl-chloride reactions
fragments.text: At room temperature RCOCl reacts with water→RCOOH, alcohol→ester, phenol→ester, NH₃→primary amide, and primary/secondary amines→substituted amides, releasing HCl. Extra ammonia/amine may neutralise HCl to an ammonium salt.

fragments.label: Acyl-chloride reactions
fragments.text: Identify the nucleophile and the group replacing Cl.

fragments.label: Acyl-chloride reactions
fragments.text: Phenol acylation does not require the same harsh conditions as direct carboxylic-acid esterification.
Addition–elimination mechanism

fragments.label: Addition–elimination mechanism
fragments.text: A nucleophile attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move to oxygen. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses, re-forming C=O and expelling Cl⁻; proton transfer yields the neutral product. Acyl chlorides hydrolyse far more readily than halogenoalkanes or halogenoarenes because the carbonyl activates the acyl carbon and Cl⁻ is a good leaving group.

fragments.label: Addition–elimination mechanism
fragments.text: Curly arrows must start at electron pairs/bonds.

fragments.label: Addition–elimination mechanism
fragments.text: Show intermediate charge and proton transfer clearly.
Why are carboxylic acids stronger than phenols?

fragments.label: Why are carboxylic acids stronger than phenols?
fragments.text: The carboxylate negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms and is more stabilised.
What are the two stages of acyl substitution?

fragments.label: What are the two stages of acyl substitution?
fragments.text: Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl, then elimination of Cl⁻ as C=O reforms.
What does an acyl chloride form with a primary amine?

fragments.label: What does an acyl chloride form with a primary amine?
fragments.text: An N-substituted amide, with HCl captured by excess amine where applicable.
Why are acyl chlorides highly reactive to water?

fragments.label: Why are acyl chlorides highly reactive to water?
fragments.text: The carbonyl carbon is strongly electrophilic and chloride is a good leaving group.

Understand phenylamine, azo dye formation, and the structure of amides and amino acids. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Amine
fragments.text: An ammonia derivative with one or more H atoms replaced by carbon groups.

fragments.label: Phenylamine
fragments.text: C₆H₅NH₂, a primary aromatic amine.

fragments.label: Diazotisation
fragments.text: Conversion of a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt using nitrous acid below 10 °C.

fragments.label: Zwitterion
fragments.text: A species carrying both positive and negative charges but no overall charge.

fragments.label: Peptide bond
fragments.text: The amide link –CONH– formed between amino acids.

fragments.label: Basicity
fragments.text: Tendency to accept a proton, governed by lone-pair availability.
Preparing amines

fragments.label: Preparing amines
fragments.text: Heat a halogenoalkane with excess ethanolic NH₃ under pressure for a primary amine; reaction with a primary amine can form a secondary amine. Reduce nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni, and reduce amides with LiAlH₄. Choose routes by the required carbon skeleton.

fragments.label: Preparing amines
fragments.text: Nitrile reduction adds/retains the nitrile carbon in the chain.

fragments.label: Preparing amines
fragments.text: Excess ammonia reduces further substitution.

fragments.label: Preparing amines
fragments.text: Primary amine salt: RNH₂+H⁺⇌RNH₃⁺
Basicity

fragments.label: Basicity
fragments.text: Amines accept H⁺ through the N lone pair. Alkyl groups donate electron density and usually make aliphatic amines stronger bases than NH₃. Phenylamine is weaker because its lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation.

fragments.label: Basicity
fragments.text: Compare lone-pair availability in the conjugate pair.

fragments.label: Basicity
fragments.text: Amides are much weaker bases because the N lone pair is delocalised into C=O.
Phenylamine and azo chemistry

fragments.label: Phenylamine and azo chemistry
fragments.text: Phenylamine reacts with bromine water to form 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine. With NaNO₂/dilute acid below 10 °C it forms a diazonium salt, which can warm with water to phenol or couple with activated rings such as phenol in alkaline conditions to form coloured azo compounds.

fragments.label: Phenylamine and azo chemistry
fragments.text: Temperature control prevents diazonium decomposition.

fragments.label: Phenylamine and azo chemistry
fragments.text: Show the azo –N=N– linkage between aromatic groups.
Amides and amino acids

fragments.label: Amides and amino acids
fragments.text: Acyl chlorides react with NH₃/amines to form amides. Amides hydrolyse under acidic or alkaline conditions to carboxylic-acid/carboxylate products and ammonium/amine products. Amino acids exist as zwitterions near neutral pH, form cations in acid and anions in alkali, and condense through –COOH and –NH₂ to form peptide links.

fragments.label: Amides and amino acids
fragments.text: Draw ionic forms with correct charges.

fragments.label: Amides and amino acids
fragments.text: Peptide hydrolysis restores amino-acid functional groups.
Why is phenylamine weaker than an alkylamine?

fragments.label: Why is phenylamine weaker than an alkylamine?
fragments.text: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring and is less available to accept H⁺.
Why is diazotisation kept below 10 °C?

fragments.label: Why is diazotisation kept below 10 °C?
fragments.text: Aromatic diazonium salts decompose more readily when warmed.
What forms when an amino acid is placed in acid?

fragments.label: What forms when an amino acid is placed in acid?
fragments.text: The amine is protonated, giving an overall cationic form.
What functional group is a peptide bond?

fragments.label: What functional group is a peptide bond?
fragments.text: An amide link, –CONH–.

Understand condensation polymers in depth, predict monomers from a repeat unit, and consider polymer degradability. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Addition polymerisation
fragments.text: Joining unsaturated monomers without eliminating a small molecule.

fragments.label: Condensation polymerisation
fragments.text: Joining bifunctional monomers while eliminating a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl.

fragments.label: Polyester
fragments.text: A condensation polymer containing –COO– links.

fragments.label: Polyamide
fragments.text: A condensation polymer containing –CONH– links.

fragments.label: Repeat unit
fragments.text: The smallest structural section that repeats along a polymer chain.

fragments.label: Biodegradable
fragments.text: Capable of breakdown by biological action under suitable conditions.
Addition versus condensation

fragments.label: Addition versus condensation
fragments.text: Addition polymers come from C=C monomers and their repeat units contain only atoms from the monomer. Condensation polymers need two functional groups per monomer; each link forms with loss of a small molecule. Name the link and show open bonds through repeat-unit brackets.

fragments.label: Addition versus condensation
fragments.text: The repeat unit must preserve chain connectivity.

fragments.label: Addition versus condensation
fragments.text: Do not include n copies of a small-molecule by-product inside the repeat unit.

fragments.label: Addition versus condensation
fragments.text: Polyester link: –O–C(=O)–
Polyesters

fragments.label: Polyesters
fragments.text: A diol plus a dicarboxylic acid forms –O–C(=O)– ester links with water loss; a diol plus a diacyl chloride can form the same links with HCl loss. Hydrolysis cleaves the ester link under acidic or alkaline conditions.

fragments.label: Polyesters
fragments.text: Cut the repeat unit through ester links to recover both bifunctional monomers.

fragments.label: Polyesters
fragments.text: Under alkaline hydrolysis, carboxylate salts form before acidification.
Polyamides and peptides

fragments.label: Polyamides and peptides
fragments.text: A diamine plus a dicarboxylic acid/diacyl chloride forms –NH–C(=O)– links. Amino acids can self-condense into polypeptides. Hydrolysis breaks amide links but generally needs stronger conditions than ester hydrolysis.

fragments.label: Polyamides and peptides
fragments.text: Restore –NH₂ and –COOH at the cut bonds when deducing monomers.

fragments.label: Polyamides and peptides
fragments.text: Account for protonation state under acidic/alkaline hydrolysis.
Properties and sustainability

fragments.label: Properties and sustainability
fragments.text: Condensation polymers containing hydrolysable links can be more degradable than C–C addition polymers, but real biodegradation depends on crystallinity, access, temperature and enzymes. Evaluate reuse, mechanical/chemical recycling, feedstock and energy use instead of assuming one disposal route is always best.

fragments.label: Properties and sustainability
fragments.text: Biodegradable does not mean instant breakdown everywhere.

fragments.label: Properties and sustainability
fragments.text: Link a property claim to a named structural feature.
What feature identifies a polyester?

fragments.label: What feature identifies a polyester?
fragments.text: Repeated ester links, –COO–, in the main chain.
How are monomers recovered from a polyamide repeat unit?

fragments.label: How are monomers recovered from a polyamide repeat unit?
fragments.text: Cut the C(=O)–N links and restore –COOH/acid-derivative and –NH₂ ends.
Why can condensation polymers be hydrolysed?

fragments.label: Why can condensation polymers be hydrolysed?
fragments.text: Their ester or amide links can react with water under suitable acid/base conditions.
Does biodegradable mean harmless or instantly decomposed?

fragments.label: Does biodegradable mean harmless or instantly decomposed?
fragments.text: No; breakdown depends on environment and products, so conditions and life-cycle effects matter.

Build a complete organic reaction map, plan multi-step synthetic routes, and deduce structures from given information. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Synthetic route
fragments.text: An ordered sequence converting a starting material into a target compound.

fragments.label: Functional-group interconversion
fragments.text: Changing one functional group into another while managing the carbon skeleton.

fragments.label: Selectivity
fragments.text: Preference for one reaction site or product over alternatives.

fragments.label: Protecting strategy
fragments.text: Temporarily masking a reactive group when necessary; only used when supported by the chemistry given.

fragments.label: Overall yield
fragments.text: The product of fractional yields for every step.

fragments.label: Retrosynthesis
fragments.text: Planning backwards from the target to plausible precursors.
Build a reaction map

fragments.label: Build a reaction map
fragments.text: Organise reactions by functional group: alkene, halogenoalkane, alcohol, carbonyl, nitrile, amine, carboxylic acid, acyl chloride, ester, amide and arene. For each arrow learn reagent, conditions, product and mechanism/observation where required.

fragments.label: Build a reaction map
fragments.text: Revise reversible arrows and oxidation stages explicitly.

fragments.label: Build a reaction map
fragments.text: Track carbon-count changes in nitrile and Friedel–Crafts steps.

fragments.label: Build a reaction map
fragments.text: Overall yield: overall %=100×(yield₁/100)(yield₂/100)⋯
Plan backwards

fragments.label: Plan backwards
fragments.text: Identify the target's key bond and functional group, then ask which immediate precursor produces it reliably. Continue backwards until reaching the given starting material, then check the route forward for compatible reagents and conditions.

fragments.label: Plan backwards
fragments.text: A route is invalid if an earlier reagent also destroys another required group.

fragments.label: Plan backwards
fragments.text: Prefer syllabus reactions with unambiguous products.
Deducing structures

fragments.label: Deducing structures
fragments.text: Combine molecular formula/unsaturation, chemical tests, oxidation/reduction products and spectroscopic evidence. Each observation constrains the structure: use all evidence and verify atom count, functional groups and possible isomers.

fragments.label: Deducing structures
fragments.text: A negative test is evidence too.

fragments.label: Deducing structures
fragments.text: State why each datum supports or excludes a feature.
Yield and practical choices

fragments.label: Yield and practical choices
fragments.text: Overall percentage yield equals the product of step yields as decimals×100. More steps usually lower overall yield and increase time/waste. Consider selectivity, hazardous reagents, separation of isomers, purification and whether a gaseous/by-product drives equilibrium.

fragments.label: Yield and practical choices
fragments.text: Do not add percentage yields.

fragments.label: Yield and practical choices
fragments.text: A shorter route is not automatically better if it lacks selectivity.
Mechanism-led predictions

fragments.label: Mechanism-led predictions
fragments.text: Use electrophile/nucleophile and bond polarity to predict unfamiliar reactions. Curly arrows show electron-pair movement, charges are conserved, and intermediates must connect reactant to product. Mechanistic consistency is a powerful structure check.

fragments.label: Mechanism-led predictions
fragments.text: Start arrows at electrons.

fragments.label: Mechanism-led predictions
fragments.text: Account for every atom and overall charge.
Why plan a synthesis backwards?

fragments.label: Why plan a synthesis backwards?
fragments.text: The target functional group suggests reliable immediate precursors, narrowing possible routes.
How are step yields combined?

fragments.label: How are step yields combined?
fragments.text: Multiply their decimal yields, then convert back to a percentage.
What must every curly arrow show?

fragments.label: What must every curly arrow show?
fragments.text: Movement of an electron pair from a bond/lone pair to its destination.
How should several analytical clues be used?

fragments.label: How should several analytical clues be used?
fragments.text: Intersect all constraints and then verify formula, functional groups and reactions against the proposed structure.

Interpret chromatography, ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra, combining evidence from several techniques to identify structures. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Chromatography
fragments.text: Separation by different affinities for stationary and mobile phases.

fragments.label: Rf value
fragments.text: Distance moved by a solute divided by distance moved by the solvent front.

fragments.label: Chemical shift
fragments.text: NMR signal position δ in ppm relative to a reference.

fragments.label: Integration
fragments.text: Relative area of a ¹H NMR signal, proportional to the number of equivalent protons.

fragments.label: Splitting
fragments.text: Signal multiplicity caused by coupling to neighbouring non-equivalent protons.

fragments.label: Chemical environment
fragments.text: The electronic surroundings that make nuclei equivalent or non-equivalent.

fragments.label: Molecular ion
fragments.text: The ion corresponding approximately to the intact molecule in a mass spectrum.
Chromatography

fragments.label: Chromatography
fragments.text: A component travels further when it has greater affinity for the mobile phase and weaker attraction to the stationary phase. In TLC/paper chromatography, Rf is dimensionless and only comparable under identical conditions. One spot can suggest purity but co-elution is possible.

fragments.label: Chromatography
fragments.text: Mark the solvent front immediately.

fragments.label: Chromatography
fragments.text: Measure from the baseline to the centre of each spot.

fragments.label: Chromatography
fragments.text: Rf: Rf=distance moved by solute/distance moved by solvent front
¹³C NMR

fragments.label: ¹³C NMR
fragments.text: The number of signals gives the number of distinct carbon environments, reduced by symmetry. Chemical-shift ranges indicate environments such as alkyl, C–O/C–X, C=C/aromatic and C=O. Routine proton-decoupled ¹³C spectra do not use peak integration to count carbons.

fragments.label: ¹³C NMR
fragments.text: Equivalent carbons produce one signal.

fragments.label: ¹³C NMR
fragments.text: Use the syllabus data table rather than memorised exact shifts.
¹H NMR

fragments.label: ¹H NMR
fragments.text: Count proton environments, use δ for functional surroundings, integration for relative proton numbers and the n+1 rule for n equivalent neighbouring protons on adjacent atoms. OH/NH signals may be broad/variable and disappear on D₂O exchange; they may not split predictably.

fragments.label: ¹H NMR
fragments.text: Simplify integration ratios to whole-number proton counts.

fragments.label: ¹H NMR
fragments.text: Apply splitting only between appropriate non-equivalent neighbouring protons.
Combining evidence

fragments.label: Combining evidence
fragments.text: Start with molecular formula or M⁺ and degree-of-unsaturation ideas, identify functional groups from IR/tests, then construct fragments from NMR integration/splitting and join them while matching every carbon/proton environment. Chromatography can distinguish mixture components and monitor purity.

fragments.label: Combining evidence
fragments.text: A final structure must explain every signal and observation.

fragments.label: Combining evidence
fragments.text: Predict the spectrum back from the proposed structure as a check.
Why can Rf values only be compared under the same conditions?

fragments.label: Why can Rf values only be compared under the same conditions?
fragments.text: Solvent, stationary phase and temperature affect the partitioning and travel distance.
What does the number of ¹³C signals show?

fragments.label: What does the number of ¹³C signals show?
fragments.text: The number of distinct carbon environments, accounting for symmetry.
What information does ¹H integration give?

fragments.label: What information does ¹H integration give?
fragments.text: The relative number of equivalent protons producing each signal.
What does a D₂O exchange peak reveal?

fragments.label: What does a D₂O exchange peak reveal?
fragments.text: An exchangeable O–H or N–H proton signal disappears.
How should a proposed structure be checked?

fragments.label: How should a proposed structure be checked?
fragments.text: Predict all expected NMR environments, integrations/splitting and ensure all other evidence is explained.
